articles.title: UK anti-migrant activist jailed for slashing Channel dinghy
articles.summary: Daniel Thomas, known as "Danny Tommo," slashed a dinghy with a knife while a French rescue worker was on board. The incident was livestreamed to a large social media audience amid growing tensions…

image.caption: Daniel Thomas, also known as "Danny Tommo," founded the anti-migrant group Patriot Platform [FILE: July 31, 2024]Image: Benjamin Cremel/AFP

blocks.text: A British anti-migrant activist has been sentenced to 15 months in prison for slashing a dinghy used by migrants crossing the English Channel while a French rescue worker was still on board.
Daniel Thomas, 37, also known as "Danny Tommo," pleaded guilty to criminal damage earlier this month. He was sentenced on Friday at Portsmouth Crown Court in southern England.

blocks.caption: British anti-migrant activist Danny Tommo was sentenced to 15 months in prison at Portsmouth Crown Court [FILE: September 29, 2026]Image: Justin Tallis/AFP

blocks.text: The activist, who founded the anti-immigration group Patriot Platform, livestreamed the September 22 incident on social media, where it was watched by a large audience.
What happened during the English Channel incident?
Thomas had followed an inflatable boat carrying dozens of migrants across the Channel on September 22.
After the migrants were transferred to another vessel and taken ashore, Thomas approached the empty dinghy, which a French rescue worker had boarded.
Video footage showed him repeatedly stabbing the boat with a knife. Judge James Newton-Price said he counted eight cuts.

blocks.caption: Migrants are rescued from the sea after a failed attempt to board a small boat to cross the English Channel to the UK near Dunkirk, northern France [FILE: July 30, 2026]Image: Gareth Fuller/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: During the livestream, Thomas could be heard saying "this is what needs to happen."
He also shouted "get off the boat, you've got time to get off the boat ... take them back, no more of these," according to prosecutor Joel Smith.
Newton-Price accepted that there was "no immediate danger" to the rescue worker. However, he said Thomas' aggressive behavior would have been highly alarming.
What did the judge say about Danny Tommo's actions?
Sentencing Thomas, Newton-Price said his actions amounted to "flagrant interference and a deliberate disruption" of the legitimate activities of British and French authorities in the Channel.
The judge highlighted the work of Britain's Border Force, Coastguard and volunteers from the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI).
"They do necessary, highly sensitive and difficult jobs, and which should not be disrupted by a publicity-seeker slashing with a knife a boat they were attempting to recover," he said.

blocks.caption: Migrants rescued at sea by the UK's Border Force disembark from a patrol vessel in Dover after attempting to cross the English Channel from France [FILE: May 21, 2025]Image: Ben Stansall/AFP

blocks.text: Thomas appeared by videolink from a prison in Winchester, southern England, where he has been held since late September after being denied bail.
He reportedly held his head in his hands when the sentence was announced.
Under current UK sentencing rules, Thomas may serve only a third of his 15-month sentence, including time already spent in custody.
The court also heard that he had five previous convictions, including one for kidnapping in 2016.
Who is Danny Tommo and what is Patriot Platform?
Thomas is a longtime ally of prominent far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon.
He has built a large online following and founded Patriot Platform, a group campaigning against migrants arriving in Britain in small boats.

blocks.caption: Far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, arrives at Southwark Crown Court in London facing charges of harassing two journalists [FILE: October 10, 2026]Image: Jordan Pettitt/Press Association/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Thomas gained prominence earlier this year by leading confrontational anti-migrant demonstrations in Portsmouth and the southeastern port of Dover.
Hundreds of protesters, many dressed in black and wearing face coverings, blocked roads and clashed with police.
The demonstrations have increasingly targeted police officers and rescue workers involved in responding to migrant boats arriving on British shores.
The UK government has condemned the protesters' "intimidating and thuggish behavior."
Thomas is also due to stand trial in London next June over several alleged offenses, including entering a restricted zone at a migrant processing center in Dover in March.
How many migrants cross the English Channel?
Successive British governments have struggled to stop migrants from making the dangerous journey across the English Channel, one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.
More than 41,000 people crossed the Channel in small boats last year.
Although the number of arrivals has since fallen, the crossings remain a major political issue in Britain.
Right-wing opposition parties and anti-immigration campaigners have continued to demand tougher measures to prevent migrants from reaching the country.

articles.title: Romualdez co-accused granted conditional immunity after surrender
articles.summary: The co-accused, president of a firm linked to Romualdez, was ordered to turn over the firm's records and remain in the country in exchange for his immunity.

blocks.text: November 21, 2026 | 10:16am
Former House speaker Martin Romualdez is shown under guard at the Quezon City Jail in this CCTV image released by the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology on Nov. 5, 2026.
BJMP CCTV via The STAR

MANILA, Philippines — Conditional immunity has been given to Felicito Guevarra, a co-accused of former House Speaker Martin Romualdez in a P7.44-billion plunder case, the Office of the Ombudsman said on Friday, November 20.
Following Guevarra’s surrender to the National Bureau of Investigation on Thursday, the Ombudsman said his immunity rests on his full and truthful testimony.
Guevarra was ordered to remain in the country and stay under the protection of the Department of Justice, as well as turn over all of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corp.’s records and devices.

"Mr. Guevarra personally handled Samchan’s operations. His testimony and records will help the prosecution trace the movement of funds alleged in the charge sheet. The charges against the other accused stand as filed,” the Ombudsman said.
Samchan is alleged to have aided and abetted Romualdez through money laundering.
The company has returned all earnings from questioned transactions to the Bureau of Treasury.

articles.title: Animator Clister Santos makes peace with his absent mother in 3D short
articles.summary: In ‘Sana’y Nandito Ka,’ Clister Santos turns his longing for his mother into an animated short film that confronts the unfinished business of their separate lives

blocks.text: When he was in senior high school, 25-year-old animator and filmmaker Clister Santos’ mother moved from Marikina to Bicol to live a life she had always wanted. Living with his grandmother since then has made him yearn for a maternal figure, affecting their relationship and making it more distant.

Now that he is producing films, Clister wrote, directed, and produced a 3D animated short film inspired by his relationship with his mother, told through the lens of a child acknowledging her decisions.

His 21-minute animated film Sana’y Nandito Ka follows 24-year-old Kyle as he reunites with his mother, Loren, after six years of separation, thanks to an election in their city. As they spend the day together, they confront the awkwardness, unspoken emotions, and lingering love. Their brief meeting makes Kyle recognize his feelings about his mother’s absence and feel a strange sense of familiarity as she leaves him again.

This material, however, was originally planned for production in 2024, as he first pitched it to the QCinema International Film Festival under the QCShorts production grant or short film category, hosted by Quezon City — a UNESCO Creative City of Film — but it was only shortlisted.
Fast forward to 2026: Clister got invited to present it again to the film festival for possible funding and selection.
“Tapos sabi ko, parang ayoko nang ituloy kasi parang ayoko na. Parang tapos na yung kuwento na ganyan-ganyan. Hindi ko na siya i-pursue,” Clister shared.
(I told myself I would discontinue it because I’m not interested anymore — the story has been written. I no longer want to pursue it.)

blocks.caption: BUS RIDE. A still from the film ‘Sana’y Nandito Ka.’ Photo courtesy of On’tus Films and Chanoma Studios

blocks.text: The same week of their pitching, his mother invited him to Bicol for Holy Week. There, he visited their town for the first time in six years, which led him to realize the film should approach a mother’s story with empathy rather than anger.
“Pagka-uwi, sabi ko, sige, i-rewrite ko yung buong screenplay. Tapos nag-iba na yung angulo ko sa kuwento,” Clister said.
(When I got home, I told myself I would rewrite the screenplay, then I changed the angle of my story.)
Lo and behold, he was selected as one of five finalists out of 395 submissions from Filipino filmmakers globally in the same category at the film festival, receiving a P700,000 production grant.

Currently working at an advertising agency, Clister is no stranger to animation, having earned a multimedia arts degree with a concentration in animation at CIIT College of Arts and Technology in 2024.

His thesis film Ili-Ili (Little One) even won first place in the animation category of the CCP Gawad Alternatibo and was selected as a finalist at the BFI Flare: London LGBTQIA+ Film Festival in the year of his graduation.
He has also been one of the animators on full-length animated films in the country, such as Avid Liongoren’s Zsazsa Zaturnnah vs. the Amazonistas of Planet X and Carl Papa’s 58th and Patay Gutom.
His decision to pursue an animation program wasn’t easy, though, as he originally planned to study architecture or civil engineering, his parents’ preferred paths.
Thankfully, he competed in the 2018 National Digital Arts Awards (NDAA) in the animation contest under the student category, getting the second-place award in high school.
Little did he know, first-place winners were given scholarships to pursue a college degree program of their choice.

“Since yung nanalo ng first place nung batch namin, college na sila, sa akin nila binigay yung scholarship kasi magte-take pa lang ako ng college. Tapos, in a way, na-take ko pa rin yung animation,” Clister narrated.
(Since the first-place winners in our batch were already college students, they gave me the scholarship because I was about to enter college. In a way, I was able to take animation.)

blocks.caption: WINNER. Clister (middle) receives the Special Prize award of NDAA 2018, receiving a full scholarship at CIIT College of Arts and Technology in 2019. Photo courtesy of CIIT College of Arts and Technology

blocks.text: When he finished his degree two years ago, his mother couldn’t attend his graduation. Clister understood his mother’s absence. For him, it wasn’t because she didn’t care, but because she was already living out her dream of a happy life.
“After years of watching her unhappy, I couldn’t be angry about that. I still can’t,” his director’s statement reads.
The young animator-filmmaker told Rappler that working on the film made him understand his mother’s decisions — why she left him and why she did it — six years ago.
His personal narrative pushed him to tell a familiar story through an animated short film, as it is what he knows best as a storyteller.
Clister shared that he pursued this treatment because most animated films in the country are only for children or fantastical, featuring characters with powers, monsters, or aliens.
His treatment of the story was even questioned by some jurors because they thought the script was intended for live action.
“Ito yung gusto kong i-try ma-push, kahit papaano, na ma-introduce sa Philippines na puwede pala yung mga ganitong kuwento sa animation,” he told Rappler.
(I want to introduce that these kinds of stories can also be told in animated films in the Philippines.)

“It’s just na hindi lang dapat nalilimitahan yung puwedeng ikuwento sa animation. Kasi parang never pa ako nakakita ng 3D animation na parang slice of life lang, parang makikita [mo lang siya] sa live action,” he added.
(We must not limit the stories told in animation. I think I haven’t seen a 3D animation that features a slice of life; it is only done in live action.)

blocks.caption: BEHIND THE SCENE. Zaijian Jaranilla and Meryll Soriano perform in front of two cameras as the production team captures a scene for ‘Sana’y Nandito Ka.’ Photo by Roaze Alcaide

blocks.text: His approach to animation follows, however, the practices of other animation productions in the country: performance-first. This style requires actors to act first in front of a camera, which serves as a reference for the animation.
The young filmmaker chose 3D animation deliberately because it is rare in independent filmmaking in the Philippines, with most pursuing 2D.

The first 3D animated entry in the QCShorts stars Zaijian Jaranilla — who last starred in the 3D animated film RPG Metanoia almost 16 years ago — as the son, and Meryll Soriano as the mother. The cast also includes Harvey Bautista and Jeula Agbayani.

Clister worked on the animation alone in his previous films. For Sana’y Nandito Ka, however, he teamed up with over 20 animators — mostly students — and together they completed every shot of the film in three months.
When asked why he changed his approach this time, he said it was for convenience because film and voice actors usually record voices for animated films.

“Tapos, i-acting namin yun, ibi-video namin yung sarili namin, parang dina-dub namin yung [boses] nila. Tapos ang nangyayari, inconsistent siya sa emosyon ng iba’t ibang shots. So hindi siya nagtutugma every time,” Clister said.

(We will take a video of ourselves acting it, dubbing their voices, which serves as a reference for our animation. And then what happens is, it’s inconsistent with the emotions of the different shots. So it doesn’t match up every time.)

Through this treatment, the young animator expressed surprise at observing specific performance choices by the actors on set. He analyzed their acting intent, examining subtle details such as eye blinks and gaze directions.

blocks.caption: TEAM WORK. Young Filipino animators collaboratively animate their scenes for the film. Photo by Roaze Alcaide

blocks.text: “TV actors, film actors, alam nila yung camera, ganyan. May mga intention sila sa pag-act nila. Dinala ko sa animation na mas guide siya sa mga animators,” Clister added.
(They are television and film actors, so they know how to act in front of the camera. They have their own intentions when they act. I brought it into animation so animators had a guide.)
As the short film runs at QCinema until November 22 across select Quezon City cinemas, Clister hopes audiences will appreciate the true intention of the story.
“Sana mayroon ding part na makita nila sa sarili nila kay Kyle or even kay Loren, yung mama sa [kuwento], yung nais [na iparating ng] film,” Clister noted.
(I hope they also see a part of themselves in Kyle or even in Loren, the mother in the film, which we wanted to convey in the film.)

blocks.caption: CAST. Animator Clister Santos (center) poses with actors (from left) Zaijian Jaranilla, Jeula Agbayani, Harvey Bautista, and Meryll Soriano after wrapping up their shoot in August 2026. Photo by Roaze Alcaide

blocks.text: Clister shares that part of being an adult is to sometimes seek a parental figure. “[But] just have to live [a] life na di sana tayo nababurden lagi na na-held back tayo ng mga what-ifs natin sa buhay,” he added.
(But you just have to live a life where we do not feel burdened or held back by our what-ifs.)
With the short film’s title translated as “I Wish You Were Here” in English, Clister wants to highlight a story of two people trying to be seen and taking a leap of faith to start over.

“I’m not making this film to resolve anything,” Clister writes in his director’s statement. “I’m making this because I think there are lots of us who want to hug our mothers back a little too late.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: DOTr eyes barrier-less tollways pilot testing before end of 2026
articles.summary: The Department of Transportation is eyeing to implement a barrier-less tollways system across all toll roads before the end of the year.

blocks.text: Published November 21, 2026 9:33am
The Department of Transportation (DOTr) is eyeing to implement a barrier-less tollways system across all toll roads before the end of the year.

In an order, Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon said the plan is “in line with our shared commitment to modernizing our road networks, eliminating bottlenecks at toll plazas, and delivering a seamless, world-class travel experience for the motoring public.”
With this, Dizon said that the full implementation of a “Barrier-less/Multi-Lane Free Flow (MFF) Program” across all expressways has become an “urgent national priority.”
“To achieve these benefits, we are targeting the pilot test/proof of concept of the MLFF Program across all expressways before the end of this year,” the Transportation chief said.
Dizon further said that the success of a barrier-less system relies heavily on “near-universal” adoption of cashless payments and “robust backend infrastructure.”
Thus, the DOTr ordered toll roads operators to submit a comprehensive “Action Plan and Readiness Assessment” for the expressways under their jurisdiction.
The following key components should be included in the submission:

• Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Penetration Strategies: Concrete, time-bound initiatives to aggressively increase RFID/ETC adoption among motorists (e.g., expanded installation sites, digital onboarding, promotional incentives, and public information campaigns)

• Infrastructure and Technology Readiness: Current status and deployment timelines for gantries, Automatic Number/License Plate Recognition (ALPR/ANPR) cameras, high-speed RFID readers, and system integration
• Operational and Enforcement Protocols: Proposed mechanisms for handling non-registered vehicles, insufficient balances, and interoperability across different expressway operators
• Implementation Timeline and Milestones: A month-by-month roadmap detailing testing phases, dry ruins, and target dates for full live operation.

“Given the tight timeline and the immediate need to alleviate traffic congestion for our commuters, kindly submit your comprehensive report to this office on or before 21 December 2026 through the Toll Regulatory Board,” Dizon said.
The Transportation chief said that transitioning to a barrier-less system is “no longer merely an operational upgrade; it is an economic necessity.”

“By removing physical toll barriers, we can significantly reduce travel time, lower fuel consumption and carbon emissions caused by idling vehicles, and maximize the overall throughput and efficiency of our expressway infrastructure,” he said. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Can you afford to study in Europe? A Filipino’s guide to scholarships, costs
articles.summary: From Erasmus+ scholarships and tuition grants to choosing budget-friendly university cities and navigating healthcare, here is what Filipino students need to know about studying in Europe

items: The European Higher Education Fair (EHEF) Philippines 2026 provides an opportunity for students to explore academic programs, tuition, and scholarships from 51 European universities, with a focus on affordability and living costs in different cities.

Studying abroad offers benefits beyond academics, such as exposure to diverse cultures and perspectives, while the EU aims to strengthen partnerships with Philippine institutions through student exchanges and collaborative programs.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Eighty-five Filipino students have been accepted into the European Union’s (EU) Erasmus+ program in 2026, adding to the 364 Filipinos awarded Erasmus Mundus scholarships between 2021 and 2025, as interest in European higher education continues to grow.

The figures, shared by Agata Nowicka, deputy head of mission of the delegation of the European Union to the Philippines, point to expanding opportunities for Filipinos seeking to pursue higher education in Europe.
However, choosing where to study also means considering tuition, living costs, admission requirements, and healthcare arrangements.
For students considering the move, the choice of destination can make a significant difference to their budgets.

In Spain, for example, studying in smaller cities such as Granada and Santiago can be considerably cheaper than living in Madrid or Barcelona, according to Alberto Tello, education advisor at the Embassy of Spain in the Philippines.

For Filipinos weighing their options, the European Higher Education Fair (EHEF) Philippines 2026 can provide an opportunity to explore these choices and get information directly from universities. The fair, held until Saturday, November 21, at Robinsons Manila, allows prospective students to compare academic programs, ask about tuition and scholarships, and learn about admission requirements. Online sessions are scheduled for November 23-25.
The event brings together 51 European universities, 34 of which are participating onsite. They represent 13 EU member states and are joined by 23 Philippine partner institutions.
The cost of studying abroad depends not only on tuition fees but also on where students choose to live.

In Spain, major cities such as Madrid and Barcelona tend to have higher accommodation, transportation, and everyday expenses. Tello pointed to alternatives where students can find a wide range of academic programs at lower living costs.
“I can think about cities like in South Granada, in North Santiago, where you can study everything, and everything is probably way, way cheaper,” Tello told Rappler.
Spain has approximately 90 universities, offering courses across different fields, although the availability of programs and costs vary by institution.

Filipino students can also apply for government scholarships to attend public universities. According to Tello, these grants can cover tuition fees, while scholarships at private institutions may offer additional support, including accommodation, depending on the applicant’s financial circumstances.

Healthcare is another consideration when calculating the cost of living abroad. Tello said foreign residents in Spain, including eligible students holding valid residence permits, can access the country’s public healthcare system.
This can reduce the need for separate private health insurance, although students should check the specific healthcare and insurance requirements attached to their visa and residency arrangements.

Interest in European higher education has grown, with 364 Filipino students receiving Erasmus Mundus scholarships between 2021 and 2025, compared with 320 during the preceding six-year period from 2014 to 2020.
Another 85 Filipinos have been accepted into the Erasmus+ program in 2026, according to Nowicka. The figure remains subject to change as the year’s program activities continue.
Nowicka said the application process has not necessarily become more restrictive, but the program has become more professional as organizers improve their selection procedures and implementation.

Eligibility depends on the specific opportunity. Some programs are intended for graduates seeking master’s degrees, while others require applicants to be enrolled at universities that collaborate with European institutions.

The Erasmus Mundus program, in particular, supports students pursuing joint master’s degrees offered by European universities, giving participants the opportunity to study in different countries during their academic journey.

Spain, Poland, and Ireland are among the destinations attracting questions from Filipino students, Nowicka said. She cited the availability of English-language programs and historical connections between the Philippines and some European countries as possible factors influencing students’ choices.
Potential students attending EHEF 2026 can explore programs and scholarship opportunities from 13 EU member states:

items: Austria
Belgium

Ireland

blocks.text: The participating institutions will provide information on postgraduate programs, admission requirements, tuition fees, scholarships, research opportunities, and student life.

This year’s fair also introduces changes intended to make it easier for Filipino students and universities to establish connections. European universities participating in online seminars have been paired with Philippine institutions to encourage longer-term academic partnerships.
Universities are also being presented by country, allowing prospective students to compare the educational opportunities available in each destination.
For students who pursue international education, the benefits can extend beyond academic qualifications.
Nowicka said studying abroad exposes students to different cultures and perspectives, helping them develop confidence and experience that they can bring back to their communities.
The EU also hopes that stronger university partnerships will lead to more joint research projects, academic exchanges, and collaborative programs between European and Philippine institutions.
The EU’s cooperation with the Philippines includes commitments to student and staff exchanges under the Enhanced Partnership launched in July 2026.
For prospective applicants, the immediate challenge is identifying a program that matches their academic background, financial resources, and long-term goals.
Comparing destinations, understanding scholarship eligibility, and accounting for living expenses are important steps before committing to a university abroad. – Rappler.com

articles.title: DepEd distribution of MacBook units to run until March — Angara
articles.summary: The delivery of 231,725 new laptops to public school teachers, most of them Apple MacBooks, will run until March, with about a third expected to reach schools by the end of the year, Education…

blocks.text: November 21, 2026 | 9:20am

MANILA, Philippines — The delivery of 231,725 new laptops to public school teachers, most of them Apple MacBooks, will run until March, with about a third expected to reach schools by the end of the year, Education Secretary Sonny Angara said on Friday, November 20.
Angara also said the Department of Education (DepEd) would ask Congress for more funds in the 2027 budget to ensure all teachers would eventually have one device each.
The current rollout of new laptops covers fewer than three in 10 of the country's more than 840,000 public school teachers.
"Some of it will go into March because there are delivery schedules," Angara told reporters during a DepEd laptop distribution in Antipolo City, speaking in a mix of English and Filipino.

About 1,441 MacBook units were distributed to select teachers and staff of over 60 schools in the DepEd schools division office of Antipolo City on Friday, the latest batch of new laptops handed over to educators since DepEd first announced the procurement of thousands of new MacBook units.

DepEd began the distribution of new laptops on November 9 with a ceremonial distribution in Dagupan City, Pangasinan. The department has said deliveries would run from November to March across Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao.
Of the 231,725 laptops, 169,008 are MacBook Neo units and 62,717 are Windows-based machines. Another 3,646 MacBook Neo units are going to administrative staff.
DepEd said each MacBook unit cost P43,000 each with a five-year warranty.

Teachers who have never received a DepEd laptop are higher up on the priority list of those getting the new MacBook units. Next are teachers in schools that run education technology programs. After them come teachers who have had laptops before or whose units have broken down.

Asked how the new devices would be used in schools with poor internet access, Angara called these "little technical issues" that schools could pay for from their maintenance and operating budgets, which he said had been increased.
'One teacher, one laptop'
"Our plan is to ask Congress for funds so we are given the budget to reach our dream of one teacher, one laptop. That's the reality," Angara said.

He said the current batch was larger than what DepEd usually hands out. "These 231,000 [laptops] are no joke," he said. "I don't want to say once in a lifetime, but DepEd does not usually give out this many."
"We have to credit Congress for allowing that money, but once we're done crediting them, we will ask again, because that's what we need," he said. "It's a function of the budget."
Angara has said every teacher will have a computer before Marcos' term ends in 2028.

At a Senate finance committee hearing in October, DepEd asked for P147.93 billion on top of its proposed 2027 budget, including P13 billion for 267,155 more laptops for teachers and staff. The version of the budget approved by the House of Representatives gives DepEd and its attached agencies P969.79 billion.
The DepEd secretary said senators had already been furnished with the department's "wish list" and that he was hopeful as the Senate also raised the department's budget last year.
Angara previously served as Senate finance panel chairperson prior to being appointed as DepEd secretary mid-2024.

He said DepEd was also appealing to House members, since the budget would go back to them at the bicameral conference committee. "We know the process isn't over and there is still a lot to go through. There will be more debate," he said.

In lobbying for a higher budget, Angara cited the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) results, in which Filipino students posted the country's highest scores since it joined the test in 2018, though still below the OECD average. "We hope this continues and doesn't stall," he said.
The Senate is scheduled to begin plenary debates on the proposed 2027 national budget on Monday.

articles.title: Secret audio captures 'Crypto King' planning his own kidnapping, defence lawyer says
articles.summary: So-called "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski sounded "cool and collected" in a secret audio recording taken by his alleged kidnappers, according to one of their defence lawyers, who suggested the…

blocks.text: Toronto·New

So-called "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski sounded "cool and collected" in a secret audio recording taken by his alleged kidnappers, according to one of their defence lawyers, who suggested the recording was made as an "insurance policy" to show the kidnapping was a hoax.
Aiden Pleterski denies his kidnapping was a hoax on cross-examination at trial for alleged captors
Defence says secret audio captures 'Crypto King' planning his own kidnapping
In the recording — played for the jury on Friday — Pleterski discusses the value of luxury watches, gold bars and cars he says his former landlord, Sandeep Gupta, is hiding for him.
"This is the plan and a roadmap of how this kidnapping is going to play out," defence lawyer Leora Shemesh told Pleterski on cross-examination in Ontario Superior Court in Toronto.
"You are directing these men how you're going to do it and how you're going to sell it.”

Pleterski denied that. Instead, the 28-year-old testified that the recording was made after he was kidnapped and that he lied about Gupta hiding assets in order to sell the need for an in-person meeting with Gupta to his alleged kidnappers, where he hoped to escape.

items: 'Crypto King' faked kidnapping, created video for sympathy, defence says
Secretly recorded videos of 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski meeting alleged kidnapper played at trial

blocks.text: "I know it was taken before the confession video and it was taken after the initial beating," said Pleterski.
Shemesh is representing Alfredo Paladino who is on trial — along with Akil Heywood and Rakeem Henry — for allegedly kidnapping and extorting Pleterski in early December 2022.

From left, Alfredo Paladino, Akil Heywood and Rakeem Henry are accused of kidnapping and extorting the so-called 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski in December 2022. (Evan Mitsui/CBC, atlanticmastoronto/Instagram)
Pleterski previously testified that he was beaten, tortured and thought he was going to die during the three-day ordeal.

Shemesh previously called the kidnapping a "farce" Thursday, as she started her cross-examination, alleging Pleterski created a video pretending to be kidnapped in order to gain sympathy from his investors. He also denied both those assertions.

Pleterski was convicted of fraud last month in connection with more than $30 million he took from investors to trade on their behalf. Instead, he spent much of it on his lifestyle. He has yet to be sentenced.

items: 'Crypto King' or 'Lying King'? Aiden Pleterski says he was neither at alleged kidnappers' trial
'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski testifies about escape attempt during alleged kidnapping

blocks.text: The Crown is alleging Heywood lost a significant amount of money investing with Pleterski and was the "driving force" behind the kidnapping, while Paladino and Henry carried it out. Paladino and Henry are also charged with firearm and assault offences.
All three men have pleaded not guilty.
Beating or fighting?
On Friday, Shemesh also offered an alternative explanation for Pleterski's injuries.

She suggested they were the result of a fight he lost with "Slime," another alleged kidnapper — who is not part of this trial. The defence lawyer said "Slime" was upset because the plan to extract money from Gupta wasn't working and that police were involved.
"No one counted on Gupta calling 911, not even you," said Shemesh to Pleterski.
Again, Pleterski denied that and reiterated that he was kidnapped and beaten by his alleged captors.
Aiden Pleterski testified police took these photos of his injuries after his alleged kidnapping in early December 2022. (Ontario Superior Court)

Pleterski was previously shown photos of his injuries by the Crown and described how he received cuts, burns and bruises from multiple beatings, torture with cigarette burns and cuts with knives during his kidnapping.
However, when asked by Shemesh if he went to the hospital for treatment of these injuries, Pleterski confirmed that he did not.

items: 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski testifies he was beaten, tortured during alleged kidnapping
Crypto King's alleged kidnappers’ trial hears call Aiden Pleterski made to landlord asking for $3M

blocks.text: Shemesh completed her cross-examination on Friday.
Pleterski was testifying all week, and is expected to be back in the witness box on Monday morning for his third cross-examination, this time from Henry's lawyer.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nicole Brockbank is a reporter for CBC Toronto's Enterprise Unit. She digs up, researches and reports GTA-focused investigative and enterprise stories. nicole.brockbank@cbc.ca

articles.title: They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop
articles.summary: How convicted fraudsters made millions from detained immigrants, evaded efforts to shut down their bail business and left migrants behind bars.

blocks.text: Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.
But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.

Juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (£1,970) to a bond company, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS said it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.

What she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail company co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.
Their firm, Libre By Nexus, which was at one point the largest immigration bail company in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.

But public records and BBC interviews with clients and former employees reveal a tangle of interconnected operations continued - along with the flow of cash - while leaving immigrants stuck in detention centres.

Since President Donald Trump has returned to office after promising an immigration crackdown, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made over 1.2m arrests, and fast-tracked deportations. The administration has tried unsuccessfully to make it illegal to give migrants bail but the sharp increase in detentions has increased demand for bond companies to secure bail and their release.

Conditions in these centres can be poor. Held in custody, away from family, often scared to speak out, many have faced health problems and endured inadequate food or treatment, according to immigrant advocates and reports by the US government.

In the detention centre where Juarez was locked up, she and about 100 other detainees slept in bunks laid out in rows in a cacophonous room. The lights were left on all night and guards routinely woke everyone up for roll call. According to Castro and advocacy groups, detainees who caused trouble were put in "the hold" - solitary confinement.
The White House and officials from Homeland Security did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
For Juarez, the wait to be bailed out of detention seemed interminable.

In an email to the BBC, a spokesperson for LIS said Juarez "misunderstands" their services - that they are not bondsmen themselves, but they connect detained individuals to those who are licensed bondsmen. They said another company ultimately decided not to work with her.

An email sent by LIS, and reviewed by the BBC, said that the company had paid a cash bond to ICE on behalf of Juarez. The message was forwarded to Juarez as proof of payment a few days before her release.
But it was another bail agent, who was not affiliated with LIS, that got her out of detention - after her friends raised even more money to hire another company.
"I was losing it inside there," Juarez recalled, using an expletive.
"I lost everything. When I was released I had nightmares I was back inside."

Libre Immigration Services never paid back her deposit, despite sending messages promising a refund. A spokesperson told the BBC that they would refund Juarez's bail amount once her friend verified their details.
It is notoriously difficult for migrants like Juarez to make bail, which can be upwards of $7,000.

Once charged with illegal entry, a judge may grant bail, which allows the migrant to live freely while their case is heard, a process which can take years. Once a person's court case is completed, the bond amount is returned.

Bail agents, who are licensed to provide a down payment on bail and vouch that if the accused does not show up for court they will pay the rest, can help people get out of detention sooner. But many won't help migrants because they view them as too much of a flight risk. A 2024 government report found that a third of migrants not already in custody did not show up for court.
Libre by Nexus, also known as Nexus, was willing to take that risk.
Founded in 2013, its co-founders Michael Donovan and Richard Moore had served prison time in the 1990s and early 2000s for a string of fraud and forgery convictions.
Through his attorney, Donovan declined to comment. Moore did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
Although people with felony convictions are barred from holding a bond licence in many states, Nexus operated as a kind of middleman between immigrant clients and licensed bondsmen.

Holed up in detention in Louisiana after crossing the border, Rosa Murillo heard about Libre by Nexus from another inmate, and the 18-year-old Honduran's mother called them to arrange her $7,000 bail.
A Nexus employee picked her up and took her to a hotel room where she was told she would have to pay $420 a month and wear a GPS ankle monitor until her case was completed.
Federal regulators accused Nexus of implying, in their contracts, that the GPS bracelets were court-mandated, when they were actually the private company's requirement.
Murillo got a job as a waitress and tried to hide the ankle bracelet for fear that people might think she was a violent criminal.
Over the course of a decade, Libre by Nexus enabled more than 20,000 migrants like Murillo to be released on bail - and took in more than $230m in revenue, court documents show.
But the ankle bracelets were a constant source of annoyance for Nexus clients released from detention, according to two former employees who spoke to the BBC.
A former Nexus co-owner, Evan Ajin, told the BBC that the company stopped requiring released detainees to wear ankle bracelets in 2018.
But Mark Supetran, who was based in the Philippines and worked for the company for a few months in 2022, says the bracelets were still in use when he worked for the company.

Supetran said he would field 80 calls a day from people who were either going through the process themselves or were the loved one of someone who was. Telling them they would have to wear a tag on release was part of the conversation.
"Part of the script was to say something like: 'The client will be wearing an ankle monitor.' So that got me thinking, like, why?" he recalled. "It doesn't make sense, we're not the government."
Not getting refunds of bail deposits was another complaint. Another former employee told the BBC he was instructed to tell callers that they would get their money back once their case was completed.
"But that that was never the case," he told the BBC. "I mean, you had people calling me in almost every day like 'Hey, am I gonna get my money back? Am I gonna get my money back?'"
Ajin, the former Nexus co-owner, told the BBC that the contract clearly stated that monthly fees did not go towards their bond, but were programme fees, and so they could issue no refund.
The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), an agency created to stop predatory lending and other abusive financial practices, successfully sued Libre by Nexus and its parent company.

The lawsuit accused the firm of running a "predatory immigrant-services scam" that trapped victims into paying high, long-term fees. Nexus also misrepresented and concealed the terms, the lawsuit alleged, such as the non-refundable, monthly payments.
The judgment sided with the CFPB and a federal judge found the company liable for using predatory tactics against its clients in 2024, fining Nexus, its parent company, Ajin, Donovan and Moore $811m.
In addition to the hefty fine, the judge forbade the company from collecting on past debts.
Days after the 2024 order, Donovan sold a number of the company's assets, including customer lists and records - for $3.50.
As part of the agreement the buyer would also take on its debt.
Ajin says he ceased contact with everyone involved following the sale.

Moore is now in prison, after being convicted of filing fraudulent Nexus taxes. He and Donovan, who is also behind bars, are awaiting sentencing for insurance fraud and conspiracy. Donovan has also been charged with sexually abusing a boy under 12, but has not entered a plea in that case.

The purchaser of Nexus's assets was a Pennsylvania businessman named Vincent Smith, who had been sentenced to 10 months' probation in 2015 for conspiring with employees to write over $2m in fake bail bonds.
Smith called the new business Libre Immigration Services.
This March, the judge who issued the fine also ruled the sale of the company had violated her order by transferring the debts.

Judge Elizabeth Dillon voided the sale, but did not shut Libre Immigration Services down. She is due to review claims that LIS also violated the order by trying to build an app to collect debts from Nexus's old clients.
A former paralegal at Nexus, who went on to work for LIS, told the BBC about the app. She said after the sale, the lines between the two companies were blurred.
Another employee confirmed her account independently to the BBC, noting that the app was never finished because they could not obtain the client data.
A hearing date has not been set, and LIS has denied any wrongdoing, noting the company was never in possession of the client lists.
Libre Immigration Services continues to solicit immigrant clients and advertises its services online and on social media.
Its website features glossy photos of beaming families alongside the promise to "get your loved one released from a detention centre today!".

That wasn't Janie Aviles's experience. She had wired Libre Immigration Services $10,000 to help get her friend out of detention in Texas. But LIS did not pay his bail, Aviles said, until a month later, leaving him, like Juarez, in limbo.
When she called they offered various explanations and then stopped answering the telephone, she said.

Eventually she drove to the office listed on the website, which had shown a picture of LIS's logo hanging above the door. But on arrival, she found there was no storefront with the business's name and logo anywhere.
She said the company finally paid the bail a month after getting the funds, after she had reported them to the district attorney. No charges have been laid.
An LIS spokesperson said that "verification of significant information had to occur to prevent or minimise loss".
"The application was ultimately approved, and the cash bond was pledged to ICE. Presumably any delay related to the substantial bond amount and the heightened requirements of review."
They also said the office at that location was for business operations, and not client services, and that a sign had been ordered and would be installed, pending permits.
But the ordeal was enough to anger Aviles, who feared for her friend while he was stuck in detention. "I'm like 'This ain't right.'"

articles.title: [Vantage Point] The nickel wealth the Philippines gets to keep
articles.summary: Jobs and taxes must be measured across the entire lifespan of a mining project, with environmental cleanup fully funded before any profits leave our shores

blocks.text: Recent corporate write-downs and asset sales show that processing Philippine nickel carries steep hidden costs and financial risks. Before offering tax breaks or cheap electricity to attract refineries under the new ASEAN minerals agreement, Manila must ensure that investors carry the commercial risk and that genuine wealth—not just the environmental cleanup bill—stays in Filipino hands.
Just days before Southeast Asian leaders called on our region to earn more money from its valuable minerals, a major Japanese metals company showed us just how expensive and risky that goal can be.

Sumitomo Metal Mining reported an impairment charge of ¥42.55 billion (P17,025,663,405.00) on its Coral Bay Nickel processing plant in Palawan. Only two days later, the local mining giant Nickel Asia announced plans to sell its entire 10% share in a separate Philippine processing plant, Taganito HPAL, in Surigao del Norte.

(HPAL stands for high-pressure acid leaching. It uses sulfuric acid at high temperatures and pressure to extract nickel and cobalt from low-grade laterite ore. The resulting intermediate product requires further refining before it can be used in batteries. In this column, HPAL refers to the processing technology used at Taganito).
The regional leaders’ grand announcement arrived just as two experienced companies were marking down their Philippine nickel-processing investments.

The new minerals declaration, adopted by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) during the Manila Summit on November 15, lays out an ambitious plan. It asks member countries to work together across the entire supply chain—from digging up raw rocks and processing them into usable metals, to building finished goods like electric vehicle batteries, and eventually recycling them.

Joining this effort is completely optional, and the regional strategy still needs to be developed. On paper, the idea makes complete sense. Right now, countries such as the Philippines sell raw minerals to other countries and then buy back expensive finished electronics and cars.

Naturally, the region wants to keep more of that processing profit for itself. For the Philippines, however, the question is not whether the idea sounds good, but where the actual profit hides, who takes the financial risk to earn it, and how much of that money truly stays in our country. (READ: Riding the clean energy and AI wave: Marcos wants to go beyond ore exports)

When it comes to raw materials, the Philippines certainly has enough nickel to be taken seriously on the world stage. According to estimates from the United States Geological Survey, Philippine mine output contained 270,000 metric tons of nickel in 2025, which equals roughly 7% of the entire world’s nickel mine output.

By comparison, our neighbor Indonesia produced 2.6 million tons—nearly ten times our output. Meanwhile, United Nations trade records show that the Philippines earned about US$1.48 billion in 2025 just by shipping raw nickel ore and concentrates overseas. While one number measures the nickel contained in mine output and the other measures the value of ore exports, both figures tell a clear story. We have a very large and successful mining industry, yet we are competing right next door to an Indonesian giant whose massive size gives it an advantage that no diplomatic agreement can easily erase.

The troubles at the Coral Bay plant in Palawan offer a vital lesson about the hidden costs of running a factory. According to Sumitomo’s official briefing, the plant is expected to stop operating sometime between fiscal years 2028 and 2030.

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] The nickel wealth the Philippines gets to keep

blocks.text: When the company reviewed how much it would cost to safely dismantle the factory and restore the surrounding environment once it closes, those future cleanup costs pushed the plant’s accounting value higher than what the business could realistically earn back.

Low global prices for nickel and cobalt, rising factory expenses, and declining ore quality all hurt the plant’s outlook. While this ¥42.55 billion write-down is an accounting adjustment rather than a cash bill paid today, it serves as a critical reminder for government leaders. Policymakers must always include the end of a project’s life when calculating whether it is a good deal. A factory must earn enough money while it is open to pay for cleaning up the mess it leaves behind. (READ: Poor towns near nickel mines pay the price of energy transition – report)

The situation at the Taganito plant in Surigao del Norte sends a different kind of warning. Nickel Asia’s plan to sell its stake to Sumitomo is not a factory shutdown. It is simply one owner deciding to step away, and the deal still requires definitive agreements, regulatory compliance, and fulfillment of closing conditions.

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] The nickel wealth the Philippines gets to keep

blocks.text: Even so, Nickel Asia reported a P1.99 billion net accounting hit on the value of that factory investment. Yet in the first nine months of 2026, Nickel Asia’s revenue from simply digging up and selling raw nickel ore jumped by 39% to P29.12 billion.

In other words, the company generated sharply higher revenue selling raw rocks while simultaneously losing value on its factory shares. This does not mean mineral processing can never make money, but it shows that owning a profitable mine does not guarantee success when you try to build a factory farther down the supply chain.

Still, there is a strong argument for building processing plants here at home. Specialized factories using high-pressure acid leach technology can turn low-grade local ore into a semi-finished metal product that sells for much more than raw ore.

A healthy processing plant creates high-skilled jobs, brings business to local suppliers, generates tax money, and teaches Filipino workers advanced engineering skills. Working with neighboring ASEAN nations could also help these plants find steady buyers and secure loans.

However, a semi-finished metal is still several steps away from becoming a finished battery. Furthermore, a higher export price tag does not mean the Philippines actually gets rich if foreign machinery, imported chemicals, expensive electricity, and overseas bank loans absorb most of that money. We must judge every project by the wealth that remains in Filipino hands after all those bills are paid.

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] The nickel wealth the Philippines gets to keep

blocks.text: Before our government hands out tax breaks, discounted electricity, or public money to attract factory builders, officials must demand clear answers. Investors should prove their factory can survive even when global nickel prices drop to conservative, realistic levels.

The government needs to know what electricity rate and ore quality the plant requires just to break even, how much money will go directly to Filipino workers and local businesses, and how much tax the company will pay during and after its incentive period. Most importantly, officials must ask who will pay to maintain tailings facilities and restore the land if metal prices crash and the owners shut the doors early.

The public deserves to see these exact numbers so we can weigh the true benefits against the cost of taxpayer support. Jobs and taxes must be measured across the entire lifespan of the plant, with environmental cleanup fully funded before any profits leave our shores.

Manila should use the new ASEAN minerals declaration to negotiate smart deals that bring guaranteed buyers, new technology, and private funding—while ensuring that foreign investors, not Filipino taxpayers, carry the financial risk.

The Philippines can easily afford to say no to a metal refinery that only survives on cheap, taxpayer-funded electricity and overly optimistic price guesses. What we cannot afford is to celebrate higher export numbers as industrial progress, only to discover when the factory closes that the only thing our country kept was the cleanup bill. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 12 photographers with autism show Baguio how they see the world
articles.summary: At an exhibit beside a bonfire in Camp John Hay, Art Heals celebrates a dozen photographers whose work is opening conversations about creativity, livelihood, and independence

blocks.text: BAGUIO, Philippines – When I arrived at the Dap-ay of the John Hay Hotels, the fire was roaring, and so was the art.

Around the bonfire, black-and-white photographs stood on easels, illuminated against the evening darkness. There was a hallway filled with sunlight, a stack of firewood, a motorcycle, the rough bark of a tree, and familiar corners of Baguio that most of us probably pass without a second glance.
I moved from one photograph to another, admiring the angles, textures, and careful use of light. Some were beautifully simple. Others made me look twice.

blocks.caption: ART HEALS. An Art Heals sign welcomes guests to an outdoor photography exhibition at the Dap-ay of John Hay Hotels, where photographs by 12 artists with autism are displayed around a bonfire.

blocks.text: The photographs were the work of 12 people with autism, aged 16 to 33, participating in The Thinking Photographer, an exhibition organized by Art Heals as part of Project LENS, or Livelihood Empowerment through Nurturing Skills.

Their works were impressive enough to merit an exhibition on their own. But the organizers also wanted to turn artistic interests into practical skills and, eventually, opportunities to earn a living.
For families of children with autism, that possibility addresses a question that becomes more pressing with time. What opportunities will be available to their children when they become adults?
Photographer and designer Eros Goze mentored the participants in a workshop that grew from one session into two.
When I interviewed him beside the exhibition, he struggled to contain his emotions.

Goze admitted that he had initially been apprehensive about teaching photographers with autism. His previous workshops generally involved participants without autism, and he was uncertain how to adjust his approach.
“Challenge accepted,” he recalled telling himself.

blocks.caption: MENTOR. Photographer and mentor Eros Goze explains the composition techniques used by his students. From leading lines to texture and negative space, the photographs show how the participants interpreted his lessons in their own ways. Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

blocks.text: The participants already had some experience through Photography with a Difference, a program of the Autism Society Philippines (ASP) Baguio Chapter, which was supported by the Baguio Photographers Club under the leadership of the late Ompong Tan.

Goze built on that foundation, teaching composition techniques such as leading lines, contrast, texture, framing, negative space, and the rule of thirds. Instead of directing every shot, he gave the photographers assignments and allowed them to interpret the concepts independently.
The results surprised him.

As we walked around the exhibit, Goze enthusiastically pointed out how the participants had applied what they learned. One image explored the texture of tree bark. Another used the lines of a corridor to guide the viewer’s eye. Ordinary objects became studies in contrast and composition.
“Let the photos speak for themselves,” he said.
Some photographs had been taken using ordinary mobile phones. For Goze, understanding composition and developing an eye for an image mattered more than owning expensive equipment.
What pleased him most was that the participants could apply the lessons on their own. He gave them challenges, and they returned with their answers.
The experience even inspired him to consider another workshop, this time exploring photography with people who are blind. It remains an idea, but one he said he was willing to pursue.

Among the photographs, one immediately caught my attention. It showed a church steeple rising toward a sky filled with clouds and sunlight. I recognized it. It was the chapel at Brent International School, where I had worked for nine years.
Naturally, I wanted to meet the photographer.
His name was Manuel Martin Teodoro, a 22-year-old who goes by Sky. He enjoys nature photography and hopes to become a teacher for students with special needs.
When Goze asked him about his composition, Sky identified negative space, one of the techniques covered in the workshop.
I told Sky why I loved his photograph. That chapel had been part of my life for nearly a decade, and he had captured it in a way that made me appreciate it all over again.

Nearby, I met Carlo Bañez, 33, whose interest in photography goes back years. He enjoys photographing nature, people, and sporting activities, and hopes his images will encourage young people, particularly aspiring athletes.
When I asked what he liked about the workshop, he talked about taking pictures and going outdoors.
Then I asked how he felt seeing his work displayed.
“I feel proud of myself,” he answered.
And why shouldn’t he?
Carlo was among 12 photographers whose individual interests gave the exhibition its variety.

Nathan Carlos Clemente, 16, enjoys capturing people, emotions, and details others might overlook. Onel Osbert Gundran, 30, dreams of becoming an internationally recognized photographer, while John Ray Joaquin, 22, hopes to master the craft.
Lyera Joaquin, 29, wants to build a collection of beautiful images. Lynette Joaquin, 33, enjoys photography and paper crafts, while Andrei Nisperos, 21, is interested in both photography and drawing.

Emarnel Pasana, 26, loves documenting festivals and landscapes. Andres Joaquin Tano, 18, is drawn to nature photography, while Josef Noli Vizcocho, 33, enjoys close-up subjects, patterns, shadows, and symmetry.

Then there is Danielle Louise Marquez, 29, known online as Lori, a digital artist who enjoys finding stories in everyday surroundings. She describes herself as stubborn, creative, and observant, and wants to continue making art while developing greater independence.
She is also the daughter of Melan Ku Marquez, the woman behind Art Heals.

blocks.caption: Participants of The Thinking Photographer pose with their mentor, Eros Goze, during the Art Heals exhibition. The artists presented their black-and-white photographs after completing workshops on composition and visual storytelling. courtesy of Melan Ku Marquez

blocks.text: For Melan, Art Heals began with a personal belief in creativity.
“When I wrote my book as a legacy for my children, and we started Art Heals, we had one simple belief: that creativity has the power to heal, connect, and transform lives,” she said in her message.

Over the years, the organization explored artistic expression through workshops, exhibitions, and community collaborations. Eventually, Melan and her collaborators began thinking about what could come after those experiences.
“Art does not only heal. It can also empower,” she said.
That thinking led to Project LENS, which seeks to develop creative skills and eventually connect participants with livelihood opportunities.
For Melan, inclusion means more than accepting individuals as they are.
“It is giving them the opportunity to GROW and live meaningful lives,” she said.

The initiative addresses a concern shared by many families. Much of the attention surrounding autism focuses on childhood, particularly education, therapy, and early intervention. Yet the need for support does not disappear when a person turns 18.

Adults with autism may want to pursue careers, earn money, and make decisions about their own lives. Their opportunities depend partly on whether communities and employers recognize their abilities and accommodate their needs.
ASP Baguio chapter president Ma. Teresa Wanchakan addressed this concern during the fundraising dinner.

“These children grew up, supported, understood, and valued. They become adults. Young adults with autism who have beautiful talents, big dreams, and deep desire to be independent,” she told the gathering.
“The funds raised tonight will kickstart a vital livelihood project dedicated to adults with autism,” she added.
Wanchakan said the project aims to provide training and employment opportunities in creative fields.

The exhibition was therefore both a celebration of the photographers’ work and a fundraiser for an initiative whose success will depend on sustained training, partnerships, and actual livelihood opportunities.
John Hay Hotels general manager Roberto A. Garcia offered a distinctly Cordilleran perspective during his inspirational message.

“We call tonight Habi, the art of weaving. Watch any Cordillera weaver at her loom and you will notice that no two threads are the same. She never tries to make them identical. She knows the beauty of the cloth comes precisely from how different each thread is.”
Garcia had spent time studying the photographs and noticed how several photographers used windows, doorways, tunnels, and frames to compose their images.
“Our young photographers were not only showing us what they saw. They were showing us where they were standing when they saw it,” he said.
He connected that observation to his experience in hospitality, where making people feel welcome begins with recognizing the person in front of you.
But his most practical message concerned the future of Project LENS.

“Applause is wonderful, but it does not last. What lasts is a skill that has been cared for, and a livelihood that has been made possible. Those are the things that truly change a life, and a family.”
The photographs had drawn an appreciative audience. The challenge now was to create opportunities beyond the exhibition.
The evening brought together Art Heals, ASP Baguio, John Hay Hotels, Le Chef, and community supporters.
Chef Billy King and his team prepared dinner, while the Smooth Band and Cordillera Earth Beats provided music. The photographs were also offered at auction to raise funds for Project LENS.

Melan acknowledged the support of Garcia, chef Billy, Venus Tan of CBCC, the Youth Leadership Council of Baguio International School, and other partners. The Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry, represented by lawyer Rowena Tabanda, was also recognized for its involvement.

The support matters because meaningful opportunities for adults with autism cannot rest on families and advocacy organizations alone. Different individuals have different interests, abilities, and support needs, and no single livelihood program can serve everyone.
As I made another round of the exhibition, I found myself returning to the simplest photographs. Firewood. A corridor. A motorcycle. A familiar chapel.
The photographers had taken ordinary subjects and made deliberate decisions about light, perspective, and composition.
Their work deserved appreciation as photography, not merely because its creators were people with autism.
I remembered Carlo’s pride when he talked about his work and Sky explaining the technique behind his photograph of the Brent chapel.
As a journalist, I spend much of my time looking for stories. That evening, I met 12 people telling theirs through photographs.

I hope their work finds its way into homes, offices, galleries, and future exhibitions. Better yet, I hope some of them eventually get commissioned to photograph portraits, events, products, or whatever subjects interest them.
Their photographs deserve to be seen, and their skills deserve the chance to earn them a living.
The bonfire at the Dap-ay would eventually burn out.
I hope the opportunities being built around it won’t. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ANC fights to keep control of South Africa's key cities after election setback
articles.summary: The ANC appears reluctant to replicate its national power-sharing deal with the pro-business DA at the local level.

blocks.text: Image source, Gallo Images via Getty Images
The ANC got the most votes overall but lost control in more than half of the councils it won in 2021

The party that has dominated South Africa for more than 30 years is in a race against time to secure power-sharing deals in most of the country's cities after a massive drop in its support in this month's local elections.
The African National Congress (ANC) suffered its worst result since it came to power in 1994 when South Africa transitioned from the racist apartheid system to democracy.

It won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo, down from six in the last elections. It won the most votes in just two of the country's eight cities, compared with six in 2021.

At the national level, the ANC is sharing power with its long-time rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), but while there is still no official announcement, it appears that ANC party officials do not want to replicate this at the local level.
Parties have until 27 November to negotiate and form local governments.
What happened in the local election?
While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.

But in the country's economic powerhouse, Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and Pretoria, the picture is different. The pro-business DA got the most votes in both cities, as well as the province's other main region, Ekurhuleni.
Nationally, the party got 25% of the vote, up from 22% five years ago.
It also retained its majority in its power base of Cape Town, and got the most votes in Nelson Mandela Bay, where Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth) is located.

The left-leaning uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, came third, with 10% of the vote. This is a repeat of its performance in the 2024 national election, when it came in third and became the official opposition after the DA joined the coalition government.

It emerged as the biggest party in KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, securing 34% of the vote. However, this leaves it reliant on agreeing a coalition with other parties.
The only party to secure an overall majority in a city was the DA in Cape Town.
Why is the ANC apparently choosing smaller parties over the DA?
The DA and ANC have had an uneasy alliance since they entered a coalition, along with eight other political parties, in 2024.

The two, long-standing rivals due to their opposing policies, were forced into an agreement after the ANC lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since the end of apartheid. This became known as the Government of National Unity (GNU).
Despite this, the two parties have continued to disagree on key issues, and both sides have threatened to rip up their power-sharing deal.
Ahead of the local elections, analysts predicted that the two parties could team up at municipal level, mirroring the national arrangement.

blocks.caption: Image caption, ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba (left) and ANC chairperson Gwede Mantashe (right) look set to reach on agreement on co-governing some of South Africa's biggest cities

blocks.text: ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba (left) and ANC chairperson Gwede Mantashe (right) look set to reach on agreement on co-governing some of South Africa's biggest cities
The ANC seems to have rejected this, with state broadcaster SABC reporting that most of the party's top leaders see an agreement with the DA as a last resort.
Instead, the party has been courting smaller parties to try and form councils in South Africa's cities.

In Gauteng, numerous reports point to an arrangement between the party and the anti-immigrant ActionSA, which emerged as the third largest party in the province with 17%, leaving it as a potential kingmaker.
The DA has also been trying to reach arrangements with smaller parties, and the ANC, but looks set to assume the opposition benches at least in Gauteng.
ActionSA is unlikely to work with the DA as they cannot agree on the mayoral candidates in Johannesburg and Pretoria.
Does this signal a breakdown in the relationship between the ANC and DA nationally?

It's too early to tell. Neither the ANC nor DA have spoken publicly about the future of their arrangement on a national level amid the ongoing coalition talks but the ANC's reluctance to partner with the DA in key cities points to continued strain between the two.

While the GNU has remained intact since it was formed in 2024, there have been those in the ANC who have been angered by what they view as the DA's dual role as opposition and partner in the coalition government and have pushed for the arrangement to end.
A party insider told the Daily Maverick on Sunday that a nationwide agreement to work with the DA at municipal level "was overwhelmingly rejected" at a meeting held by ANC members.

While some experts predict that the DA may have to consider its position in the coalition government given the ANC's stance, political analyst Andre Duvenhage told the BBC there was a possibility that "a lot of asymmetrical coalitions" could emerge - parties working together in one area and being in opposition elsewhere.
Another political analyst, Sandile Swana, said that any party wanting to leave the GNU over the failure to secure deals locally would be "[shooting] yourself in the foot".
Would coalition governments improve services?
This is what voters want.

The decline in the ANC's support was seen as being mainly due to high levels of corruption and a loss of confidence in its ability to provide basic services, such as electricity, water and rubbish collection.
While some attribute the increase backing for the DA to its record of competent management in municipalities under its control, some have accused it of neglecting poorer areas and townships.
But the experience of coalition governments over the past 10 years does not inspire much confidence that things will improve.
Half of the country's cities have been governed through power-sharing agreements since 2016 and these types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic.
As agreements collapse and new ones are forged, the delivery of basic services has often been affected.
This has been particularly evident in Gauteng, where governance in all three cities has come under scrutiny in recent years partly because of unstable governments.

Experts agree that even after new arrangements take effect, it will take longer than a five-year term to resolve the issues facing many municipalities, particularly South Africa's biggest city Johannesburg.
"I think if we are really turning the ship around, we are talking about a 10-year period," Duvenhage said.
Swana echoed this, saying it would take a decade to "cleanse and purify" local councils and "reinstate them as "proper municipalities".
