articles.title: French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
articles.summary: The court has upheld the 2020 beating of the black music producer as an aggravated circumstance of racism.

blocks.text: Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.

Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.
Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.
Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.
All were told they could never serve in the police again.

The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.
Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.

This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.
Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.
The case was heard by a panel of five judges.
The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.
They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.

After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.
The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.
During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.
In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

articles.title: French police officers found guilty of racist assault on black music producer
articles.summary:
Beating of Michel Zecler in 2020 sparked outrage over police brutality after it was caught on security cameras

Three French police officers who beat a black music producer whom they said was…

blocks.text: Three French police officers who beat a black music producer whom they said was not wearing a face mask during the Covid pandemic have been found guilty of intentional, racist violence.

The brutal assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, was caught on security cameras in his building in 2020 and sparked outrage in France over police brutality. The trial this month was considered a turning point for the recognition of racist violence.
The officers were sentenced to between one and two years in prison, with additional years suspended. They were banned for life from serving in the police.

The officers had stopped Zecler outside his Paris music studio on 21 November 2020, accusing him of failing to wear a mandatory face mask. They pushed him into the entrance of his office and violently beat him in an assault recorded by his studio’s security cameras.

Zecler sustained about 30 punches and truncheon blows to the face and body over a five-minute period, according to the investigation. He was left with craniofacial trauma, a wound to the lip and scalp, and a complete rupture of his biceps tendon, leaving him unable to work for 45 days.

Zecler told the court the officers used a racist slur against him on several occasions during the beating. He said the attack had “completely devastated him” and had left a lasting physical and psychological impact.

The three officers, Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Pierre Plantier, 37, and Philippe Tondeux, 50, were found guilty of breaking into Zecler’s studio and committing intentional violence in a group. The judges decided racism was an aggravating factor in the attack.

The officers were also found guilty of forgery after they tried to cover up their actions by falsifying an official police report saying Zecler had been violent towards them. The police used that report to accuse Zecler of attacking them and trying to grab one of their weapons, but the video footage did not back up the claims, showing he was not violent.

The state prosecutor said that without the CCTV footage, the false police report on Zecler could have resulted in him being convicted of attacking a police officer in what would have been a serious miscarriage of justice.
The state prosecutor, who asked not to be named in the media, told the court the case had caused “immense harm to Michel Zecler but also to society as a whole”.
She said the officers had “betrayed” their uniform. She told the judges: “I ask you to believe Michel Zecler, to recognise him as a victim of these racist insults.”
The three police officers, who did not realise their attack was being recorded on security cameras, had apologised in court for beating Zecler, but denied racism.

Zecler’s lawyers and supporters said the trial had shone a spotlight on police violence in France, which victims and researchers say is systemic but authorities and law enforcement unions say is limited to isolated cases. Many members of the public who had come to support Zecler and watch the trial said it was a key moment in confronting institutionalised racism.

One of Zecler’s lawyers, Serge Money, said while summing up the case: “A verdict can force a society to really look at an injustice that up until now had been tolerated, minimised, and I dare to use the word: institutionalised.”
He said: “The Zecler trial is the trial of impunity, for all those who before him and after him will experience the same thing.”
Money told the court: “I want you to give voice to all those who didn’t have security cameras, and to all those who were not believed.”
Nine young performers who had been rehearsing in the basement at Zecler’s studio had been violently arrested when they came to assist Zecler.
Their lawyer, Seydi Ba, told the court that France needed to know how “police violence, lies and racism” would be considered by a court.

articles.title: B.C. restaurant group alleges $2.1M in missing staff tips, sues payment company executives
articles.summary: A B.C.-based restaurant group that operates Moxie's, Chop Steakhouse and Shark Club is suing six current and former executives and directors of a digital payment company over more than $2.1 million…

image.caption: A civil lawsuit from B.C.'s Northland Restaurant Group is targeting payment firm XTM’s former directors after millions in employee tip funds allegedly went missing across B.C. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: British Columbia

A B.C.-based restaurant group that operates Moxie's, Chop Steakhouse and Shark Club is suing six current and former executives and directors of a digital payment company over more than $2.1 million in funds allegedly owed to the group.
Northland Restaurant Group alleges money intended for employee tips was not properly safeguarded

A B.C.-based restaurant group that operates Moxie's, Chop Steakhouse and Shark Club is suing several former executives and directors of a digital payment company over more than $2.1 million in funds allegedly owed to the group.

Northland Restaurant Group and several affiliated companies filed a notice of civil claim in B.C. Supreme Court on Nov. 10, alleging that Ontario-based XTM Inc. failed to properly safeguard money entrusted to it for distribution to restaurant employees.
XTM went bankrupt and obtained creditor protection in February following a substantial shortfall in client funds, according to the court filing.
An Ontario court subsequently approved the sale of most of its business assets, including its digital payment platform, to a Calgary-based fintech company.

Northland is now seeking to recover losses from six people who served as XTM's directors or senior executives. They are Keith McKenzie, Randy Khalaf, Olga Balanovskaya, Michael Li, Jakob Ripshtein and Cary Strange.

items: More stories from Vancouver-South Coast

blocks.text: Northland alleges the defendants knew or should have known about the company's handling of client funds. It also alleges that they either assisted in breaches of trust or received money that should have been protected.
The allegations have not been proven in court.
The interior of a Shark Club Sports Bar and Grill in 2019. (Jackson Weaver/CBC)
How the payment system worked

According to the lawsuit, Northland entered into an agreement with XTM in August 2024 to use its digital payment platform — which at the time was known as AnyDay, now called GratiaPay — to distribute gratuities and petty cash reimbursements to employees working at restaurants.
Under the agreement described in the lawsuit, XTM was required to hold the deposited money separately from its own operating funds and use it only for payments to employees.
Any money that had not yet been transferred to employees' cards was supposed to remain Northland's property and be returned to the restaurant group upon request.
Missing tips leave some servers out of pocket
But Northland alleges XTM failed to follow those requirements.
The lawsuit says Northland learned on Jan. 30 that XTM had placed client money into a single pooled account rather than maintaining separate accounts as required.

items: Defendants accused of stealing money from Kamloops, B.C., Denny's deny wrongdoing

blocks.text: According to the lawsuit, the account contained approximately $12 million belonging to about 4,000 clients, with Northland and its affiliates among the largest.
Northland alleges roughly 75 per cent of that money, approximately $9 million, was no longer available.
More than $2.1M allegedly owed
According to the court filing, XTM signed an acknowledgement of debt on Feb. 2, confirming it owed Northland $2,161,647.07 as of Jan. 30.
The amount represented money Northland had deposited with XTM that had not yet been loaded onto employees' prepaid cards.
The lawsuit alleges XTM's CEO, Marilyn Schaffer, also promised to make a $50,000 repayment but Northland did not receive the money.
A tipping jar is seen at a coffee shop in Toronto. The lawsuit alleges that XTM owes Northland more than $2.1 million. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)
Northland says its lawyers formally demanded repayment on Feb. 7, but XTM did not respond.

Later that month, XTM obtained creditor protection and some of its assets, including the payment program, were acquired by Pateno Payments. According to the civil claim, Northland and other clients have been able to continue using that payment platform.
Northland is asking the court to order the return of any such funds and award damages, including punitive damages as well as legal costs.
Restaurants had to pay out of own pockets
Ian Tostenson, president and CEO of the B.C. Restaurant and Foodservices Association, estimates that about 3,000 businesses and nearly 15,000 employees were affected by XTM's financial troubles.
He said restaurant operators stepped in to cover the missing funds, paying employees out of their own pockets to ensure they received their tips.
“They recognized it's an important part of their compensation and so … was replaced by the businesses,” he said. “I have yet to meet an employer that did not pay the money back to their employees.”

items: Restaurants offered few answers as regulators scrutinize 3rd-party platform over missing tips

blocks.text: Tostenson said the case also highlights the need for restaurants to scrutinize third-party payment providers before trusting them with employee gratuities.
"In the case of XTM, we know these guys were around for quite a few years and so we didn't question their financial ability," he said.
"My advice to our industry is make sure you do a check out of any fintech company you want to do business with."

articles.title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
articles.summary: The Russian embassy in Denmark has denied the allegation, which has led to Russia's defence attaché being expelled.

blocks.text: Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.
Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.
Russia's Embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.

In a statement posted on social media, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".
Russian state media cites the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".
Danish media named the target of the assassination attempt as the rapper known as Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Vasiliev.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.
PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September.
Firearms and knives were found in the vehicle, PET said.
Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.

In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.

In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.
Russia's defence attaché must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said.

He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Denmark is already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians can still get a Schenegen visa in another country and travel to Denmark. Denmark wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.

articles.title: Bell says it's investigating cyberattack that led to potential theft of business customer data
articles.summary: Bell says it's investigating a cyber incident in which some enterprise client data may have been stolen. A spokesperson confirmed an "agentic" threat actor was able to access some of the company's…

image.caption: A Bell store in downtown Montreal pictured in May 2025. The company says it is investigating the theft of some business client data earlier this week. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Business

Bell says it's investigating a cyber incident in which some enterprise client data may have been stolen. A spokesperson confirmed an "agentic" threat actor was able to access some of the company's systems, including one used for ordering and supplying telecommunication networks.
Company says it was able to quickly contain 'agentic' attack on Tuesday
Bell says it's investigating a cyber incident in which some enterprise client data may have been stolen.
A Bell spokesperson confirmed with CBC News that an "agentic" threat actor was able to access some of the company's systems, including one used for ordering and supplying telecommunication networks.

Some client data, including business contact information like names, corporate email addresses, phone numbers, as well as IP addresses, were stolen in the attack, the company says. Its investigation has so far determined that things like files and PDFs, which would contain more sensitive information, were not affected.
Bell says it was quickly able to contain the threat in the attack, which took place on Tuesday.

"Upon learning of the breach, we immediately contained the incident and secured our systems. There has been no impact to customer services," public affairs manager Zoe Chapman said in an emailed statement. Bell said it is reaching out to affected customers directly.
The company says it's unclear at this point who the perpetrator is, as nobody has contacted the company claiming responsibility.

items: KPMG Canada client documents accessed in cybersecurity breach, accounting firm says

blocks.text: The telecom firm also says it has shared "indicators of compromise" — essentially, digital footprints that give evidence of an attack — with enterprise customers and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (CCCS). It's also reached out to the RCMP’s cybercrime unit and is pursuing its own investigation into the matter.

The incident comes after a string of cyberattacks targeting legal and financial firms in Canada through voice phishing ("vishing") scams, in which fraudulent phone numbers and voice-altering software can be used to contact potential victims by phone.
KPMG Canada confirmed earlier this week some of its clients' tax documents had been accessed in a breach, while four major law firms were targeted by a similar vishing incident in October.

articles.title: Calgary man who threatened to kill Prime Minister Mark Carney in TikTok, YouTube videos pleads guilty
articles.summary: A Calgary man who threatened to kill Prime Minister Mark Carney and one of his children in videos posted to social media pleaded guilty to a number of offences on Friday.

image.caption: Jamie Dacosta, left, pleaded guilty to threatening to kill Prime Minister Mark Carney. (YouTube, Jon Blacker/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
A Calgary man who threatened to kill Prime Minister Mark Carney and one of his children in videos posted to social media pleaded guilty to a number of offences on Friday.
Jamie Dacosta, 31, pleaded guilty to extortion, uttering threats, mischief over $5,000
WARNING: This story contains graphic details
“We’re going to slaughter Mark Carney,” said Jamie Dacosta in a YouTube video posted four days before the prime minister was set to visit Red Deer, Alta.
“We’re coming for you and your children.”
Jamie Dacosta, 31, pleaded guilty to extortion, uttering threats and mischief over $5,000.
Details of the crimes come from an agreed statement of facts (ASF) prepared by prosecutor William Tran and defence lawyer Adriano Iovinelli.

items: Calgary man accused of threatening to kill Prime Minister Mark Carney

blocks.text: According to the ASF, police first warned Dacosta in March after he posted a video to TikTok in which he threatened to slit the throat of one of Carney’s children and disfigure the prime minister.
'Slaughter Mark Carney'
Four months later, Dacosta posted another video, this one on his YouTube account, telling followers he was going to Ottawa.
“We are going to slaughter Mark Carney … hey man, I’ll break the rules for us,” he said in the video.
Two days later, on July 27, Dacosta threatened to hang the PM.

“Mark Carney, you know what we are going to do to you? We are going to put 6x6s on an upside-down cross, and we’re going to hang you upside down butt naked and we’re going to watch all the blood pour out of your skull,” Dacosta said.
Arrested day before Alberta visit

Carney was scheduled to visit Red Deer on July 29 for a housing announcement alongside Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Mayor Cindy Jefferies. That scheduling information was publicly available online, the ASF notes.
Calgary police and RCMP officers arrested Dacosta at his northeast home on July 28. During an interview with police after his arrest, Dacosta admitted to making the videos.
Friday’s plea also encompassed a six-month period of near-constant harassment Dacosta committed against employees of Tiremaxx, a local tire shop.

In October 2025, Dacosta bought a set of tires from the shop. After the tires were installed, he witnessed a routine test drive and became enraged, demanding $400 for what he believed to be damages caused during the drive.
6 months of harassment

When the company denied the damages and refused to pay, Dacosta spent the next six months threatening, extorting and posting racist comments to his YouTube channel against Tiremaxx owners and employees.
In July, Dacosta showed up at Tiremaxx with an axe and smashed its windows.
By then, he was demanding $10,000 from the company.
A pre-sentence report was ordered ahead of a sentencing hearing which will take place before Justice Clarissa Pearce next year.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Meghan Grant is a justice affairs reporter. She has been covering courts, crime and stories of police accountability in southern Alberta for more than 15 years. Send Meghan a story tip at meghan.grant@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous penalties’ on US tech firms that build datacenters abroad
articles.summary:
President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and says he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi

Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on…

blocks.text: Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.

In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.

Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.
At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.

“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.
He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.
“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.
“We want them to build it here.”

With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.

The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.

China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.

In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and said: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”
He added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”
Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.

“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president said. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran.

“I can’t speak to America,” he said, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.”
He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election.
“I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said.

Trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He said Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.”
And he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”

articles.title: What the new UK-EU deal could mean for future post-Brexit relations
articles.summary: The BBC's political and Europe editors analyse the new agreements between the UK and EU.

blocks.text: The United Kingdom and European Union agreed a deal on Friday covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, while European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.
The BBC's political editor Chris Mason and Europe editor Katya Adler analyse the new agreement and what it could mean for future relations between the UK and EU.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".

articles.title: Trump threatens 'tremendous tax' on U.S. tech companies that build AI data centres in other countries
articles.summary: U.S. tech companies that build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries will face "a tremendous tax," President Donald Trump said on Friday.

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump at a news conference in the White House on Friday. where he said American tech companies will face 'tremendous penalties' if they build AI data centres abroad. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
U.S. tech companies that build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries will face "a tremendous tax," President Donald Trump said on Friday.
U.S. president urged Americans to welcome data centre construction in their communities
U.S. tech companies that build artificial intelligence data centres in other countries will face "a tremendous tax," U.S. President Donald Trump said on Friday.

"We're not allowing data centres to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump said in a White House press briefing. "And we're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it."
Trump did not provide details on how he would enforce such a policy and said he hadn't yet told his own officials about his plan.
The president urged Americans to welcome data centre construction in their communities and extract concessions from the developers, repeating a point he made before the midterm elections.

items: U.S. further restricts China's access to AI chips in wake of Nvidia scandal
Trump says he's working on a 'fair' trade deal with Canada

blocks.text: "You ought to take advantage of the data centres," Trump said. "Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don't shut them off."
"We want them to build it here," he added.

With host communities across the U.S. turning against the gargantuan data centres, America's technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets or shower more money onto the communities willing to allow the server warehouses.

The U.S. Senate on Thursday approved bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation's energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.
The legislation's sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centres pay for the energy they use and upgrades to the larger transmission network.
Anger over data centres and rising electricity prices helped usher in a midterms wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.
Data centre backlash is a problem for Trump’s Republicans
Trump praised the Senate bill, which now goes to the House.
"It's going to cause tremendous amounts of new building," he said.

A tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data centre developers is expected to follow, even if Trump — a champion of the industry — stalls any federal crackdown. The data centres powering the AI boom have become politically toxic.

items: Data centres in the U.S. put out more carbon emissions in a year than Denmark, says Harvard study

blocks.text: The tech industry says it has gotten the message. Besides ramping up financial incentives, officials with Google and Meta said in interviews with The Associated Press they are trying to address mistrust by being more transparent with communities where they would like to build.

Companies are also making pledges to reduce their impact on the environment and offering assurances that data centres will boost local property values — all while maintaining AI is a positive force for the American economy.

The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China's abilities to use U.S. chips to train its best AI models.

articles.title: Former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia investigated by California state bar
articles.summary: California's state bar is investigating former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia after a complaint she represented herself as a lawyer without having ever passed the bar exam.

image.caption: Katie Zacharia arrives to hold her first and only press briefing as White House press secretary on Oct. 13. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
California's state bar is investigating former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia after a complaint she represented herself as a lawyer without having ever passed the bar exam.
Watchdog group filed complaint saying Zacharia misrepresented herself as a lawyer
The State Bar of California confirmed its investigation into Zacharia, who was removed from her role as press secretary after a rocky five days, in a letter to a watchdog group published Thursday.
In a statement on Thursday, the state bar declined to comment further but noted the existence of an investigation doesn't mean "a non-licensee" has practised law without authorization.
"Our investigations are confidential, so we cannot share anything more, regardless of whether or not a complainant has made their own disclosure," its email read.
New White House press secretary says she's a lawyer. Is she?
The watchdog group Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint last month, asking the state bar to investigate whether Zacharia broke the law by describing herself as a lawyer in interviews.
Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University's law school in California in 2011, but was never admitted to the bar.

"Zacharia may have thought she was just playing a lawyer on TV, but by repeatedly holding herself out as an attorney on news programs, she was pretending to have authority she lacks," Campaign for Accountability executive director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a statement.

items: Katie Zacharia fails to impress in brief debut as White House press secretary

blocks.text: The organization published a response from the state bar on Thursday. In that letter, the bar confirmed the complaint had been "forwarded for further investigation" and would be assigned to an investigator and legal adviser.

Under the state's business code, anyone "holding himself or herself out as practicing or entitled to practice law" without being an active licensee of the bar is guilty of a misdemeanor. The violation is punishable by up to a year in county jail, a fine of $1,000 or both."
Katie Zacharia listens to U.S. President Donald Trump outside the White House after her only briefing as press secretary last month. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)
U.S. President Donald Trump announced Zacharia's appointment as press secretary in October, following Karoline Leavitt's resignation from the role in August.
Zacharia held only one, shaky briefing before she was removed from her role, making her the shortest-serving White House press secretary in history.
She had also faced a flurry of headlines questioning whether she had misrepresented herself as a lawyer when she spoke as a commentator on television.
In an October interview, she said she was preparing to take the California bar exam at a time when she had just gotten married and was preparing to move to China to join her new husband.

Zacharia said it was appropriate to use the title when she was offering legal analysis and said she had worked as a lawyer in China. U.S. President Donald Trump had also described her as "an attorney."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Rhianna Schmunk is a senior writer covering domestic and international affairs at CBC News. Her work over the past decade has taken her across North America, from the Canadian Rockies to Washington, D.C. She routinely covers the Canadian courts, with a focus on precedent-setting civil cases. You can send story tips to rhianna.schmunk@cbc.ca.

articles.summary: The beloved hippo Fiona died Thursday at the Cincinnati Zoo after eating a knit hat that was accidentally tossed into her enclosure earlier this month. Here's a look back at the life of the famous…

image.caption: The beloved hippo Fiona, pictured in October 2017 with her mother at the Cincinnati Zoo, died Thursday after eating a knit hat that was accidentally tossed into her enclosure about 10 days earlier. (John Minchillo/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

The beloved hippo Fiona died Thursday at the Cincinnati Zoo after eating a knit hat that was accidentally tossed into her enclosure earlier this month. Here's a look back at the life of the famous hippo.
9-year-old's death Thursday sparks outpouring of grief at Cincinnati Zoo and beyond
Tributes are pouring in for Fiona, the beloved hippopotamus of the Cincinnati Zoo, who died Thursday after eating a knit hat that was accidentally tossed into her enclosure earlier this month.
Here's a look back at the life of the famous hippo, who became a social media darling after she survived a premature birth.
Against all odds
The zoo shared Fiona's miraculous survival story in videos and blog posts, capturing hearts around the world. Below, the baby hippo makes her media debut in the Hippo Cove at the zoo in May 2017.
(Liz Dufour/USA TODAY NETWORK/Imagn Images/Reuters)
Fiona weighed 13 kilograms when she was born six weeks prematurely in 2017. (Most hippos are born weighing between 23 and 50 kilograms.)
(John Minchillo/The Associated Press)
The hippo, pictured with mom, did more than help sell T-shirts, bobbleheads and ice cream at the zoo. She became a teaching tool in classrooms and libraries and the subject of a series of books.
Fiona on the day her book, Fiona the Hippo, launched on Aug. 7, 2018.
(Albert Cesare/ Enquirer/USA TODAY NETWORK/Imagn Images/Reuters)
Fiona sleeps in her enclosure beside a copy of Saving Fiona by the zoo's director Thane Maynard.
Visitors pose for photographs with a sleeping Fiona on June 26, 2018.
(John Minchillo/The Aasociated Press)
On her third birthday, Jan. 23, 2020, Fiona ate her specialty birthday cake. The zoo used that birthday as a way to raise money for Australian wildlife affected by recent bushfires.
Fiona enjoying the sunshine with Tucker in the Hippo Cove on April 18, 2025.
(Liz Dufour/USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images/Reuters)
A tragic end
On Thursday, Fiona died more than a week after she ate a visitor's hat that accidentally found its way into her enclosure, sparking an outpouring of grief in Cincinnati and beyond.
Here, a young man prepares to place a flower at a memorial for Fiona, as an adult stands nearby at the zoo on Friday.
(Obed Lamy/The Associated Press)
Flowers, handwritten notes, watermelons and other items are displayed at a memorial for Fiona.
