articles.title: Alto-backed study predicts major economic gains along proposed high-speed rail corridor
articles.summary: A new study commissioned by the group behind Eastern Canada's proposed high-speed rail line lays out the project's potential to benefit people's lives, their communities and the region's economy if…

image.caption: A high-speed train near Paris in 2022. France is among the countries considered by consultants studying the potential economic impact of Alto, Eastern Canada's proposed high-speed rail line. (Gonzalo Fuentes/Reuters)

blocks.text: Ottawa·New

A new study commissioned by the group behind Eastern Canada's proposed high-speed rail line lays out the project's potential to benefit people's lives, their communities and the region's economy if it's done right.
High-speed rail from Toronto to Quebec City will boost productivity, create jobs, consultant finds

A new study commissioned by the group behind Eastern Canada's proposed high-speed rail line lays out the project's potential to benefit people's lives, their communities and the country's economy if it's done right.
The report argues that Alto will be worth the massive investment because it will boost productivity by better connecting people living and working in the Toronto-Quebec City corridor.

The project was announced late last year with planned stops in Trois-Rivières, Laval, Montreal, Ottawa and Peterborough. Its CEO said this summer that it would likely add a stop in Kingston for some trains.

The government's latest cost estimate is $60 billion to $90 billion, and the federal budget watchdog said recently that could balloon by another $15 billion to $25 billion. Construction would start at the end of this decade or early next decade.

The study by Quebec consultants Aviseo said once fully up and running, Alto would generate about $24.5 billion worth of financial benefits annually by connecting Ontario and Quebec's major population centres.

Workers would have better access to jobs and employers would have a much wider talent pool to draw from if it took an hour or less to commute between Ottawa or Trois-Rivières and Montreal, or Peterborough and Toronto, it said.
Less travel time means more in-person learning, collaboration and networking, plus more leisure time for workers.
Aviseo's 2026 study compares driving times between major population centres along the proposed route, top, with the time it would take aboard an Alto train, bottom. (Aviseo)
That boost to productivity would draw investment and diminish the drag of an aging population on the economy.
"When workers and businesses produce more value per hour worked, wages can rise, prices can fall and governments can collect more revenue without raising tax rates," it said.
'Cost of doing nothing'

According to Aviseo, the growing communities along the proposed route will need to invest something like $50 billion in roads, airports and railways without Alto, and would still not benefit from faster travel between them.
"There's a cost of doing nothing," said Jean-Pierre Lessard, Aviseo's co-founder and partner.

items: Alto high-speed rail project could cost more than originally thought: budget watchdog
Montreal-Ottawa high-speed rail line could cross 1,700 properties, Alto predicts

blocks.text: The corridor between Toronto and Quebec City is home to 40 per cent of Canada's population and gross domestic product, but still lacks "a reliable, fast, frequent and affordable way to travel," according to the study.
The anticipated drop in private vehicle traffic that Alto would bring — about 6.8 million fewer trips by 2055, by Aviseo's estimate — would also reduce congestion and collisions.
Alto would also help boost tourism in communities within easy reach of its stations, according to the report.
Loud opposition
There has also been loud opposition to the project, with some warning of serious disruption and the spectre of private land expropriation, with little gain for some regions.
Quebec's premier and the federal Conservatives are against the project, while a source told CBC News in July that the Ontario government is also rethinking its support of Alto.

items: Could Quebec's new government derail plans for Alto's high-speed train project?
Quebec farmers challenge costs of Alto high-speed rail, propose new — slower — plan

blocks.text: Aviseo's study, which came the week after a farmer-backed study of a cheaper, slower train line, promises local benefits including a share of the estimated 5,000 jobs related to running and maintaining Alto.
That economic spillover could extend up to 110 kilometres from "station cities," according to the report.
Aviseo said its case studies of other rail projects suggest economic spillover can extend as far as 110 kilometres from a station. This study did not contemplate a stop in Kingston, Ont. (Aviseo)
An Alto spokesperson recently told CBC News that it plans to unveil a narrower proposed corridor between Ottawa and Montreal in the coming weeks.
The Crown corporation also intends to publish a business case early next year.
With files from Dan Taekema and Radio-Canada's Claudine Richard

articles.title: Dancing with the Stars Season 35 finale: What you can expect
articles.summary: The Dancing With The Stars Season 35 finale airs Tuesday, Nov. 24. Five stars remain: Olympic figure skater Amber Glenn, comedian and podcaster Connor Wood, Paralympic gold medallist Ezra Frech,…

image.caption: Five stars remain: Olympic figure skater Amber Glenn, comedian and podcaster Connor Wood, Paralympic gold medallist Ezra Frech, reality star Maura Higgins and actor Tatyana Ali. (Andrew Eccles/Disney)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

The Dancing With The Stars Season 35 finale airs Tuesday, Nov. 24. Five stars remain: Olympic figure skater Amber Glenn, comedian and podcaster Connor Wood, Paralympic gold medallist Ezra Frech, reality star Maura Higgins and actor Tatyana Ali.
5 finalists, 3 routines each and 1 mirrorball trophy up for grabs
Your last chance to hear "Thanks, Alfonso" is right around the corner. Well, until next season.

The Dancing With The Stars Season 35 finale airs Tuesday, Nov. 24. Five stars remain: Olympic figure Skater Amber Glenn, comedian and podcaster Connor Wood, Paralympic gold medallist Ezra Frech, reality star Maura Higgins and actor Tatyana Ali.
The three-hour finale will air live on Disney+ in Canada, with each couple performing three (yes, that's right, three) routines.

There's the judges' choice, where a judge assigns a specific dance style and song to each finalist. Then there's the instant dance, where couples find out what they're doing on the fly. And of course, there's the freestyle, where pretty much anything goes — it's a fan favourite for a reason.

items: How Dancing with the Stars became must-watch TV in the streaming era

blocks.text: Now, in typical reality television fashion, we're not nearing the end without a hint of internet drama.

Following a semifinal elimination that sent Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson home despite a streak of perfect scores, some viewers threatened boycotts, arguing the show has become a popularity contest since Connor Wood is at the bottom of the leaderboard.
Speaking to E! News, Shum said he thinks "social media is a little nuts" and that he hopes the show addresses it at some point.

"I think there's a good amount of bullying that doesn't feel really good, and I think the rest of the cast feels it," he said, sharing that he loved the experience and that every cast member "has been able to do something incredible in our own way."
Season 27 winner Bobby Bones defended Wood on TikTok, calling a "toxic" fraction of Dancing With the Stars fans "the biggest losers in the whole world" after seeing Shum speak out.
Whether you’re watching to see who wins or just here for the choreography, here’s what you can expect for the last night in the ballroom:
Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov
Judges' choice: Quickstep to Sing, Sing, Sing by Louis Prima.
Freestyle: Like a Prayer and Music by Madonna.
Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold
Judges' choice: Viennese Waltz to Willing and Able by Noah Kahan.
Freestyle: Singin' in the Rain by Gene Kelly and Umbrella by Rihanna.
Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach
Judges' choice: Salsa to Danza Kuduro by Don Omar feat. Lucenzo.
Freestyle: Numb by Linkin Park.
Maura Higgins and Mark Ballas
Judges' choice: Tango to Gallo Ciego by Orquesta Color Tango.
Freestyle: Diamonds Are a Girl's Best Friend by Marilyn Monroe and Irish folk songs The Parting Glass and Flowers of the Red Hill.
Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik
Judges' choice: Salsa to Jamaican (Bam Bam) by Hugel & Solto (FR).
Freestyle: Minnie the Moocher by Cab Calloway and Over the Rainbow by Judy Garland.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca

articles.title: GTA VI hauls in $3.79 billion US in massive 1st day of sales
articles.summary: Criminal duo Lucia and Jason's blitz through Vice City in Grand Theft Auto VI helped Take-Two Interactive, the publisher of the blockbuster game that is now a global cultural phenomenon, rake in…

blocks.text: Business·New

Criminal duo Lucia and Jason's blitz through Vice City in Grand Theft Auto VI helped Take-Two Interactive, the publisher of the blockbuster game that is now a global cultural phenomenon, rake in nearly $4 billion US in first-day sales.
Game said to have had production cost of $1 billion US or more
It’s been a long wait for GTA VI — but it's finally here

Take-Two Interactive, the ‌parent company of GTA developer Rockstar Games, is not a household name despite its portfolio of massive hits, including the Red Dead Redemption franchise and the NBA 2K basketball series.

GTA VI sold 32.5 million units in pre-release and garnered $3.79 US billion in day-one retail sales, Rockstar Games said ​on Friday. That is nearly five times the roughly $800 million ​— a figure unadjusted for inflation — that GTA V made on its first day in 2013.
Analytics firm Sensor Tower estimated ​the company sold 24.5 million copies of GTA VI and made $2.36 billion US in pre-order revenue.

items: Grand Theft Auto VI is a spectacular, cynical and sometimes shallow joyride through the American psyche

blocks.text: Take-Two ⁠had stayed tight-lipped about GTA ⁠VI demand since it opened for pre-orders in ‌June, limiting commentary to saying demand has been "unprecedented" or "far exceeding expectations."

"The title is so widely anticipated, consumers appear very, very excited, and all the press so far has been universally positive, but we still aren't ready to declare victory," CEO Strauss Zelnick said on Take-Two's earnings ⁠call earlier this month.
"We tend to avoid claiming success before it occurs," he said.
Massive hype
Take-Two has shelled out an estimated $1 billion US in production costs for GTA VI, making it one of the ‌most expensive entertainment projects.
A man is seen playing the newly released Grand Theft Auto VI video game at a launch event in London, England, on Thursday. (Kirsty Wigglesworth/The Associated Press)
Sensor Tower estimates that the game's promotional trailer, GTA VI "Extended Look," on Netflix in August helped drive a sixfold jump in pre-orders.
In Miami, which Vice City is based on, the city's NBA team celebrated the release on Wednesday with a Vice City-themed match.
Over the weekend, ​the company is hosting GTA VI: The Festival, with a star-studded lineup that includes Grammy-winning rapper Cardi B, hip-hop record ⁠producer Metro Boomin and rapper Travis Scott.
Anticipation for PC launch of game
Investors have been waiting to hear from Take-Two ⁠about its plans for a PC launch of GTA VI and an online version rollout.
The online, ⁠multiplayer ⁠component of a videogame is crucial ​in turning the title into a recurring revenue engine.
Some industry analysts are expecting the PC launch and online mode ​in 2027.
Brokerage TD Cowen named ⁠Take-Two one of its "Best Ideas" for 2027, with its analyst Doug Creutz upbeat about the company's financial prospects when the game releases online.

"The potential ceiling for GTA VI's long-term recurrent consumer spending performance is very high... 'when' and 'how big' the next GTA Online will be is the most important question for the stock, more so than GTA VI ⁠unit sales."

articles.title: Russian ornithologist jailed over small donations to Navalny's foundation
articles.summary: Sofia Rosenfeld has devoted her life to studying Arctic birds. A Russian court sentenced her to 3.5 years in a penal colony over donations to Navalny's foundation. Friends and family are fighting for…

image.caption: Renowned Russian ornithologist Sofia Rosenfeld on an expeditionImage: Privat

blocks.text: Boris Rosenfeld shows DW a photo of him with his daughter Sofia and can't hold back tears. "This was the last time we saw her. Then she left for Moscow, and this whole case began," he says.

Helives in Israel, while Sofia is in Russia. For more than a month now, she has been behind bars on charges of financing extremism. The case goes back to two donations totaling 2,000 rubles (about $30) to the late opposition politician Alexei Navalny'sAnti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), which the Russian authorities have since designated as extremist.
On October 7, a court in Moscow sentenced Rosenfeld to three and a half years in a penal colony.
A biologist who dedicated her life to Arctic birds

Rosenfeld is a prominent ornithologist who has devoted her life to studying and protecting Arcticbirds. "Sofia was an avid young naturalist from childhood. She loved birds, horses and dogs," her father said as he leafed through a photo album.
Sofia was a teenager when the family moved to Israel but she returned to Russia a few years later and now holds both Russian and Israeli citizenship.

She studied biology at Moscow State University and developed a significant scientific career in Russia. Her colleague, Alexandra Panyutina, who now also lives in Israel, explained that Rosenfeld was devoted to her work from an early age.
"Birds and the Arctic are the defining passions of her life," she said.

blocks.caption: Sofia and her father Boris Rosenfeld in Israel during her most recent visitImage: Privat

blocks.text: Rosenfeld was among the first Russian researchers to develop a systematic approach to monitoring migratory bird populations. To support her research, she even developed a special aircraft.

"They could fly at almost the same speed as the birds and observe them from a low altitude," says Dmitry (name changed), a colleague of Rosenfeld's. "It quickly became clear that this was a unique method."
Protecting birds in Russia and beyond

Rosenfeld is considered to be one of the leading figures in Russian ornithology. Her work has extended well beyond Russia and she has been deeply involved in international research projects. In the field of migratory bird conservation, cross-border cooperation is essential.
Helmut Kruckenberg, the head of the German Institute for Wetlands and Waterbird Research (IWWR), said Rosenfeld was highly respected within the international scientific community.
"She has done an enormous amount for nature conservation and for the protection of Siberian and Arctic species," he said. "What is happening to her is simply beyond comprehension for us."
More than 225 cases over donations to FBK across Russia

In the summer of 2021, when Russian authorities designated Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation, also known as FBK, as an extremist organization, Rosenfeld was on a remote Arctic expedition without a phone or access to the internet. Therefore, she did not cancel her regular donations to the FBK immediately, doing so only after her return to the Russian capital Moscow.

Her friend Olga (name changed) described Sofia as a person of absolute honesty. According to her, Rosenfeld's donations to Navalny's foundation reflected a genuine desire to fight corruption. Through her work in Russia's regions, she had seen plenty of it firsthand.
"She was never involved in political activism. Her donations were solely intended to support anti-corruption work," said her father Boris Rosenfeld. "It's unthinkable".

blocks.caption: Sofia Rosenfeld during an expedition Image: Privat

blocks.text: For him and others close to her, the sentence came as a shock. Although prosecutors had requested a five-year prison term, friends and colleagues expected that she would receive a fine at most.

There were reasons for that expectation. According to calculations by independent media outlet Mediazona, about 85% of convictions in the 225 cases involving donations to Navalny's foundation have so far resulted in non-custodial sentences. Yet Rosenfeld got three and a half years in a penal colony.
A year of court hearings and travel restrictions

Just a few months after Rosenfeld defended her doctoral dissertation in October 2025, her home was searched. She was also subject to travel restrictions. She continued to work but she had to cancel her annual summer expedition to the Arctic.

Even on the day of the sentencing, her conversations with her colleagues focused largely on science: "We discussed how the work could continue in Sofia's absence," Olga said. "But no one really believed she would end up in prison."
Leaving Russia was never an option
"The only thing we think about now is how to bring her here," Boris Rosenfeld says as he looks at the pictures from Sofia's last visit.

Friends and colleagues who spoke to DW say that his daughter never considered leaving Russia, even as the prospect of a prison sentence loomed. "Sofia would never have left. She simply can't imagine life without geese," says Dmitry.
Now, her family, friends and colleagues are campaigning to have her sentence overturned. More than 1,000 people have signed an appeal to Russia's Presidential Council for Human Rights.
Boris Rosenfeld is also hoping for support from Israel but so far Israeli consular officials have not been granted access to his daughter in detention.

The two continue to write to each other and he is trying to keep his spirits high: "She writes that she's trying to adjust to life in prison, and that it's hard," he says. "But she's a strong person."
This article was originally published in Russian.

articles.title: Repression against Iranian lawyers increases
articles.summary: At least 135 lawyers in Iran have been subjected to repressive measures over the past year. UN experts warn that this seriously jeopardizes the right of those accused to trial in a constitutional…

image.caption: The wall of Tehran's infamous Evin prison in March 2006Image: dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: UN human rights experts have called on the Iranian authorities to end the escalating persecution of independent lawyers. They warn that limiting access to legal representation increases the risk of arbitrary detention, coerced confessions and unfair trials.
"Independent lawyers are increasingly being prosecuted and intimidated for their professional work and for defending human rights," the experts said in a statement in mid-November.

They said that between September 2025 and September 2026, at least 135 lawyers were issued with a summons, arrested, detained, suspended, dismissed or banned from traveling. In January and February 2026, 23 lawyers, including five women, were reportedly arrested after nationwide protests.
Defending the politically persecuted is becoming dangerous

A current example is the case of Amirsalar Davoudi, a human rights lawyer who was arrested in October in the central Iranian city of Isfahan, where he was defending a client in the Revolutionary Court. According to Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), he was taken to hospital on November 9 after suffering a heart attack in custody.

blocks.caption: Nationwide anti-government protests in Iran in early 2026 were met with a violent crackdown, in which thousands diedImage: Sohrab/Middle East Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: "There is a long history to the persecution of and coercive measures taken against lawyers," Sina Yousefi, a 41-year-old lawyer and human rights activist, told DW.

In October 2022, Yousefi was arrested by security forces in Tabriz during the nationwide "Woman Life Freedom" protests. Later, he was sentenced to six months' imprisonment for "propaganda against the system." He has since left Iran, and now lives in the German capital Berlin.

"The pressure was already increasing on lawyers back then, because they were undertaking the defense of people who were arrested and publicly expressing their support for the demonstrators," said Yousefi. "The security services, judiciary, and criminal prosecution apparatus increasingly used targeted mechanisms to move against independent lawyers."

Even renowned and internationally known lawyers such as Nasrin Sotoudeh, who was co-awarded the Sakharov Prize in 2012, have been affected by this repression. In 2026, Sotoudeh was awarded the Vaclav Havel Human Rights Prizeafter being repeatedly arrested and imprisoned.

blocks.caption: The award-winning Iranian human rights lawyer Nasrin Sotoudeh has been arrested repeatedlyImage: Everett Collection/picture alliance

blocks.text: Yousefi said arrests and threats against lawyers working on political and human rights cases not only curtailed the rights of those accused to a defense, but also discouraged other lawyers from accepting such briefs. This, he added, compromised the fairness of trials.

Criminal proceedings have also been instigated, or other measures taken, against lawyers who undertook to represent demonstrators. Comments on social media about the violation of civil rights can also be cited as grounds for investigation and judicial proceedings.
Restrictions on the right to choose a lawyer

Yousefi also warned against tightening restrictions on a person's right to choose their own lawyer. According to the note to Article 48 of Iran's Code of Criminal Procedure, for people arrested on certain charges, access to lawyers of their own choosing is already restricted during the investigation phase. Defendants must resort to lawyers approved by the head of the judiciary. In some cases, even these lawyers are not granted access to all the files and evidence.

According to Yousefi, in many cases in which charges have been brought against demonstrators, lawyers have only been granted access to the files "when the preliminary investigations have been concluded and the evidence for the prosecution has been gathered — including confessions made during their imprisonment." Even then, he said, "their access to the records is limited and they have little time to prepare the defense."
Unbreakable: My fight for freedom in Iran
"In many cases," Yousefi added, "the judges ascribe greater importance to reports by security agents than to the defense. Verdicts are handed down predominantly on the basis of this."

Shabnam Moinipour, the program director at the Center for Supporters of Human Rights (CSHR) in the UK, sees the independence of the bar as a fundamental precondition for the effective defense of citizens. The organization monitors the situation of lawyers in Iran, documenting violations of their rights, and following up at an international level.

"A lawyer must be able to call into question the charges brought by the public prosecutor and the credibility of the security agencies' reports without fear of criminal prosecution," Moinipour told DW. "Because when a lawyer's freedom and professional activity are threatened, their client's right to defense is impaired."
Fear and self-censorship among lawyers

In Moinipour's view, when the decision as to which lawyers are approved is made by the most senior representative of the same court authority, it raises serious questions about the independence of the bar.

"This restriction has psychological as well as legal consequences," she stressed. "For the accused, it may reinforce a sense of being unprotected, as well as feelings of fear and mistrust. It can also prevent them from disclosing details of threats, torture, and illegal behavior."

Moinipour considers this practice incompatible with Iran's obligations as a member of the UN Human Rights Committee. International law stipulates that people must have immediate access to a lawyer of their own choosing, be able to communicate with them in confidence and be supplied with sufficient means to mount a defense.
All the Ayatollah's men — ensuring the regime's survival

Referring to a joint report by the Tehran-based Defenders of Human Rights Center and the International Bar Association's Human Rights Institute (IBAHRI), as well as the recent statement by UN human rights experts, Moinipour said: "Even without mass arrests, the actions taken against a limited number of lawyers can send a threatening message to others and restrict their professional activity. This phenomenon is described as a chilling or deterrent effect."

However, Moinipour stressed that, despite this pressure, "many lawyers in Iran continue to defend the rights of their clients and accept the risk of arrest, criminal prosecution, and professional restrictions. In doing so, they are prepared, if necessary, to pay a high price for this resistance."
This article was originally written in Persian.

articles.title: Baywatch's Erika Eleniak says OnlyFans has her 'calling the shots' after money woes
articles.summary: Original Baywatch star Erika Eleniak is opening up about work and money challenges — including nearly being evicted from her home — amid a recent career upswing since joining OnlyFans, the online…

image.caption: Erika Eleniak, seen at an event in Pasadena, Calif., in 2024, is seeing a career uptick since joining OnlyFans this summer, at a time she was nearly evicted from her home. (Willy Sanjuan/Invision/AP)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Original Baywatch star Erika Eleniak is opening up about work and money challenges — including nearly being evicted from her home — amid a recent career upswing since joining OnlyFans, the online subscriber platform known for its popularity with adult audiences.
Original Baywatch star faced eviction in 2026, but says she's since cleared the debt

Original Baywatch star Erika Eleniak is opening up about work and money challenges — including nearly being evicted from her home — amid a recent career uptick since joining OnlyFans, the spicy online subscriber platform.

Despite having "kept a toe in the door" of her film and TV career over the past two decades as well as teaching acting to others, Eleniak, a single mom, said her main focus has been to raise her daughter.
"I'm in this position where I'm not really acting anymore," Eleniak explained in an episode of the Miss Understood podcast released this week.
"You find yourself in that position where it's like, 'I need to make a certain amount of money in order to pay my overhead.' And so what do I do? Where am I going to make that kind of money?"
Actors Monte Markham, from left, Billy Warlock and Erika Eleniak appear in a scene from season one, episode seven of lifeguarding TV series Baywatch. (Baywatch/YouTube)

The 57-year-old started an OnlyFans account this past summer around the time she received an eviction notice for her condo, telling podcast host Rachel Uchitel she was able to settle her debts "after a couple of months."

An online platform where subscribers pay creators for custom photos and videos, OnlyFans is best known for its adult content and as a relatively safer space for sex workers to make a living, though it's also been singled out amid wider debates about combatting alleged sex trafficking and the reported exploitation of minors.

Only a fraction of top-tier OnlyFans creators — such as celebrities or those with pre-established social media followings — typically make it big, with a large majority of others believed to make up to $200 per month after the platform takes its commission.

Eleniak's among a growing wave of veteran actresses who have turned to the for-pay platform as a source of income, independence and to reconnect with fans. Others include 1980s-era soap divas Morgan Fairchild and Donna Mills, American Pie's Shannon Elizabeth and Battlestar Galactica's Tricia Helfer.

items: Morgan Fairchild, the icy diva you couldn't miss on 1980s TV, joins racy subscriber platform OnlyFans

blocks.text: Eleniak gained global fame fresh out of high school after landing the role of a rookie lifeguard on the Santa Monica-set Baywatch, which debuted in 1989 and also helped launch the career of Canada's Pamela Anderson.

Yet being on the show, coupled with her decision to pose in Playboy magazine, cast a shadow over her attempts to branch out with different types of roles, Eleniak said, noting later gigs where producers simply expected nudity from her.

Her credits span films like E.T., Under Siege and The Beverly Hillbillies to cameos on TV shows such as Full House, CSI: Miami and Desperate Housewives to reality competitions like Celebrity Fit Club, in which she participated just after childbirth and during her nearly decade-long stint living in Calgary.

items: Marmots on OnlyFans: Researchers turn to the internet for funding
How an Olympic medallist is using OnlyFans for additional income and independence

blocks.text: Now, with her daughter recently married, Eleniak is refocusing on acting and says she feels empowered making "fun and spicy everyday life" content on OnlyFans to interact with her loyal fanbase.
"I do my own content. I shoot my own stuff. I do my own everything," she said. "I feel like I'm the one that's calling the shots and it feels good to be the one in control."
Audiences will see Eleniak back on the beach again in the Baywatch reboot debuting in January, reprising her role as former-lifeguard-now-city-councilwoman Shauni McClain.

articles.title: Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment
articles.summary: The depiction of the birth of the goddess Athena above the Parthenon's entrance is considered a masterpiece of ancient art. Now, a German research team has pieced together all the surviving fragments.

image.caption: A digital reconstruction of the Parthenon's east pedimentImage: Vinzenz Brinkmann und Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann/Liebieghaus Skulpturensammlung

blocks.text: The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most important temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.
Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.

The Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.
'Very confident we've solved the mystery'

The east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.
For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.
But now there has been a breakthrough.

blocks.caption: The results of the research are on show at the Frankfurt exhibition 'Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle'Image: Norbert Miguletz/Liebieghaus Skulpturensammlung

blocks.text: After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.
Brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.
The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle."

Only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.
Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.

And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.
In 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.

Then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!"
Nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.
Brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go."

blocks.caption: The researchers are convinced that the Dioscuri — the sons of the king of the gods, Zeus — located in Rome’s Piazza del Quirinale are also copies of the group of figures from the eastern pedimentImage: Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: A handy tool: the iPhone

The researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.
Digitally fitting the fragments together led to another important discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.

The Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.

Using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most important fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.

Alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.
The dispute between Greece and Britain over the Parthenon sculptures
There is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.
Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.

blocks.caption: The landmark of Athens: the Acropolis with the ParthenonImage: Fokke Baarssen/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.

In the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.
Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.
Greece, however, considers them stolen.

For years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.
The exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
articles.summary: The US president provided little detail on the potential policy, saying others in his team were hearing about it for the first time.

blocks.text: Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.
"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.
Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.
Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.
"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.
"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."
But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.
"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.
Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.
Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.
As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.
"You ought to take advantage of the the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.
"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."
Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.
Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out.
In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.
Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.
Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".
Google has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Images of Canada's most wanted are AI-generated. How do we know they're accurate?
articles.summary: The new reveal of Canada's top 25 most wanted fugitives might look like something out of the Harry Potter movies. But while the moving images of the men and women used by the Bolo Program aren't…

image.caption: An image provided by the Bolo Program shows Canada top 25 most wanted fugitives, on Thursday. The images are all AI generated. (Bolo Program)

blocks.text: The lifelike images blink, turn their heads, cross their arms, squint and shrug.

To some, the new reveal of Canada's top 25 most wanted fugitives might be reminiscent of the Harry Potter posters warning that Sirius Black escaped from Azkaban. But while the moving images of the men and women used by the Bolo Program aren't magical, they also aren't real — they're AI.

"This year, with the help of AI, we bring our top 25 fugitives into this room, life-sized, moving as they might if you saw them on the street, at the supermarket, at [the] airport or anywhere else," Bolo Program executive director Max Langlois said in a Toronto news conference Thursday.
Behind him, AI-generated images of 25 people wanted for some of Canada's most serious crimes stood in sweatshirts and jeans, put their arms behind their backs, shuffled and sighed.
"If it feels uncomfortable, that's the point," Langlois added.

But some security and technology experts caution that the use of AI to present images of Canada's most wanted fugitives isn't without risks — such as the accuracy of the digital avatars, privacy concerns and whether there are enough safeguards around such third-party programs working with police.

The Bolo Program, which stands for "be on the lookout," has been partnering with police forces in some of Canada's biggest cities since 2018. The national initiative uses public awareness campaigns, new technologies and cash rewards to amplify police requests for the public's help in locating major crime suspects.

The program also uses gimmicks to encourage public engagement. Last year, for instance, police wore "spoof masks" bearing the faces of the 25 most wanted in a Bolo news conference. Bolo has also utilized life-size cutouts, online contests, advent calendars and billboards.
Police officers wearing masks bearing the faces of wanted fugitives stand during a Bolo Program news conference, in Vancouver, on Oct. 8, 2025. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

Bolo has been using AI-generated images for a few years now, Langlois told CBC News in an email statement, explaining that they use the available pictures and descriptions of the suspects from police to ensure their accuracy.
The AI images give the public a "better idea" of how the suspects may look, he said.
Experts question accuracy of avatars

While this specific use of AI could potentially be helpful, we also don't have all the information about what data was used to generate these avatars, said David Eliot, a PhD candidate in criminology at the University of Ottawa who researches AI, citizen rights and security.
When asked how the AI images were generated, Langlois said that information was confidential.

Eliot questions how Bolo verified the wanted individuals' mannerisms and body types — how much is assembled from collected data or photos, how much from witness descriptions and how much from AI or human assumptions.

items: How forensic sketch artists are adapting technology to bring their subjects to life
A sketch to remember: RCMP forensic imaging expert says drawing perpetrators is emotional work

blocks.text: "If the animation is being made with insufficient data, and making incorrect assumptions, it is possible that it may mislead investigators and the public as they uncritically accept digitally altered portrayals," Eliot told CBC News.

This has been a long-standing issue with composite images or sketches, when no photo of a suspect is available, explained Tamir Israel, director of the privacy, surveillance and technology program at the Canadian Civil Liberties Association.

The Bolo Program website displays AI models of Canada's 25 most wanted fugitives, shown in this handout image, on Thursday. An AI rendering of Satinderjeet Singh, the No. 1 most wanted, is in the top left corner. (Handout/Fondation Stéphan Crétier/The Canadian Press)

"That practice has historically been a significant contributor to wrongful convictions and wrongful arrests in a way that hits more heavily on particular demographics, like Indigenous people and Black people," Israel said.
"And this AI trend of generating images raises the same sets of concerns, particularly if low-quality images were being used to generate something that looks hyper-realistic."
The AI-generated images also appear on the landing page of the Bolo website, as well as in individual entries for each person when you click through for more information.
It's only when you keep scrolling that you see actual photos of the suspects.

Satinderjeet Singh, also known as Goldy Brar, is wanted in the 2023 murder of Sukhdool Singh Gill, Winnipeg police said in a notice issued Thursday. He is shown here in undated photos provided by Winnipeg police. (Submitted by Winnipeg Police Service)
A 'proven model'
This year's most wanted list includes fugitives wanted by police services across the country, including Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Edmonton and Delta, B.C.

At the top of the list is Satinderjeet Singh, also known as Goldy Brar, wanted by Winnipeg police on a Canada-wide warrant for first-degree murder in 2023. Bolo is offering $250,000 for any information that leads to his arrest. He's known to be a high-ranking member of the Lawrence Bishnoi gang.

items: Man believed to be top Bishnoi gang lieutenant wanted in 2023 Winnipeg killing

blocks.text: Langlois has said that Bolo's methods have a proven track record. In 2025, for instance, 13 out of 25 of the most wanted suspects were arrested — the most of any year since the program's inception in 2018, according to Bolo's annual report.

The police units working with the program also praise it. In a news release where he commented about Singh, for instance, Winnipeg police Deputy Chief Cam Mackid said, "India is looking for him. The United States is looking for him. And now, Canada, with the proven model of the Bolo Program, is looking for him."

items: As GTA police forces pause Crime Stoppers use in wake of data breach, what does it mean for investigations?

blocks.text: "The Bolo Program demonstrates the value of police services and community partners working together across Canada to extend the reach of our investigators," Niagara Regional Police Service Chief Bill Fordy said in another news release Thursday.
The Toronto Police Service noted that, since Bolo's inception, 19 of the 28 Toronto cases featured in Bolo campaigns have resulted in arrests.

But Israel, with the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, says he wonders how many false leads and accusations come from these campaigns, and what happens to the people falsely identified. This information doesn't appear to be tracked, he added.
CBC News posed the question to Bolo and has not yet received a response.
Suspected Bishnoi gangster wanted in 2023 Winnipeg murder
Private entities in police work

Both experts who spoke with CBC News said there can be serious concerns when police partner with third-party companies, such as Bolo. That's especially the case when applying AI tech, says the University of Ottawa's Eliot, adding that transparency and oversight are key for maintaining public trust.

In 2021, for instance, Canada's privacy commissioner concluded that the RCMP's use of a controversial, third-party facial recognition technology was a serious violation of Canada's privacy laws. This led to major changes in policing oversight when it comes to technology, Eliot said.

items: RCMP's use of facial recognition tech violated privacy laws, investigation finds
Privacy commissioner to investigate Canadian Crime Stoppers breach

blocks.text: "The issue raised by cases such as Bolo is how these oversights apply when policing technology is being deployed by a third party working in co-operation with the police," he said.

A third-party organization may be doing so without the same set of safeguards as the police might have had themselves, added Israel. We saw this recently with the Crime Stoppers data breach, Israel noted. A CBC News investigation last month revealed that over 1.5 million Canadian tips submitted to Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years had been exposed.
Crime Stoppers hack exposes personal information of tens of thousands of Canadians

"I would say it's the same thing for this kind of entity. If police were doing this there would be some rules in place for the need to be accurate, and what is being generated, and some safeguards in place for how these composite images will be used down the road," Israel said.
Bolo has good intentions, according to Eliot, who says he doesn't see any immediate red flags in the program, but he's still "quite cautious."
"We must ensure that the application of AI technology in policing is done with proper oversight, consultation, disclosure and consideration for Canadians' rights and freedoms."

articles.title: Gérard Depardieu and French author investigated over sexual allegations
articles.summary: A judicial investigation was launched after a complaint was filed last year over "allegations of a sexual nature".

blocks.text: Warning: this story contains graphic content
French authorities are investigating disgraced actor Gérard Depardieu and the author Michel Houellebecq over "allegations of a sexual nature", a source with knowledge of the investigation says.
The confirmation comes after reports in French media that the two were accused of being involved in a "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018 by an actress.
The source told the BBC that a judicial investigation was launched after a complaint was filed in May 2025.
Depardieu has already separately been convicted of unrelated sexual assaults. The BBC has contacted Depardieu's lawyers and Houellebecq, an acclaimed French author and occasional actor, for comment.

The actress, who has not been named publicly, accused Depardieu of penetration without consent and Houellebecq of forcing her to perform oral sex, in an interview with Mediapart, a French investigative site which first reported the allegations.
She told the outlet that none of this had been written into the script, and that she experienced "profound humiliation" and "unspeakable shame".
French law stipulates as of 2025 that all sexual acts performed without consent constitute rape.

The film's director, Guillaume Nicloux, has been accused of being complicit because he was said to have filmed the incident, Mediapart and AFP report. The BBC has contacted his agent and the Paris prosecutor's office for comment.
Nicloux told Mediapart that the scene had been improvised and he had not intervened as he had not observed "any constraints, verbal or physical opposition, or even discomfort".
The site published production documents showing footage of the scene had been destroyed.

The actress told the outlet that she had told friends, her agent and others involved in the film's production in Normandy about the incident at the time, but only filed the complaint after other women accused Depardieu of sexual misconduct.
The Asterix and Obelix star will next week find out whether he will stand trial for allegedly raping another actress, Charlotte Arnould.
On Monday, Depardieu dropped his appeal against a separate conviction for two counts of sexual assault during another film shoot, for which he was handed an 18-month suspended sentence.
Several other women have made allegations against the 77-year-old in the media.
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line

articles.title: JP Morgan boss says he will set ‘example’ in offsetting UK tax hike on banks
articles.summary:
Jamie Dimon said he would seek to claw back added costs of ‘unfair penalties’ as bank surcharge rises in January

Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to…

blocks.text: Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair.
Speaking at an event in London on Thursday, Dimon said he would seek to claw back the increase and was “setting an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”.
The bank surcharge is to rise from 3% to 6% in January as a temporary 15-month measure. It was unclear how JP Morgan, which employs 23,000 people in the UK, would make up for the extra cost.

In comments first reported by the Financial Times, citing people who attended the event, Dimon said he would set an example in making up for the added costs, and that the decision was “more in sorrow” than in anger.

blocks.caption: An artist’s impression of the proposed JP Morgan building at Canary Wharf, London.  Photograph: JP Morgan Chase/PA

blocks.text: Dimon has repeatedly lobbied Labour against raising taxes on banks, and suggested in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn tower in the Canary Wharf district of London that is expected to serve as JP Morgan’s UK headquarters.

Shortly after the chancellor, John Healey, announced the policy during his inaugural budget in October, a source familiar with the matter told the Guardian that plans for the 279,000 sq metre (3m sq ft) building were still going ahead. But the bank also said at the time that the policy “lacks principle” for singling the sector out, adding that it operated in a “highly competitive global marketplace”.

blocks.caption: JP Morgan employs more than 5,300 people at its Littledown campus in Bournemouth.   Photograph: Sam Frost/The Guardian

blocks.text: JP Morgan also has a sprawling campus in Bournemouth, where it employs more than 5,300 staff who process more than $1tn (£750bn) worth of global transactions each day. Earlier this month, the Guardian reported fears that the advance of artificial intelligence could put their jobs at risk.

Lenders in the UK pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, and the separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets, which is set for the temporary rise. JP Morgan, the biggest bank in the US, expected to pay £120m more in taxes because of the increase, the FT reported.
after newsletter promotion

Bank share prices rallied after Healey’s October announcement because the increase was less than many people in the industry had expected. The chancellor said at the time that he was “looking to our banks to help fund breathing space for British families”.
JP Morgan declined to comment.

articles.title: Feds, Ontario to meet with Stellantis execs in last-ditch effort to save Brampton plant
articles.summary: The federal and Ontario governments are meeting with auto executives from Stellantis on Friday in a last-ditch effort to save thousands of high-paying auto manufacturing jobs at the company's…

image.caption: Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly, pictured, and Ontario Minister of Economic Development Vic Fedeli are meeting with Canadian and global executives of Stellantis on Friday in an effort to save more than 2,000 jobs at the company's auto plant in Brampton. (Arlyn McAdorey/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The federal and Ontario governments are meeting with auto executives from Stellantis on Friday in a last-ditch effort to save thousands of high-paying auto manufacturing jobs at the company's recently closed Brampton plant.
'They need to protect the workers. If not, we'll get our money back,' says minister

The federal and Ontario governments are meeting with auto executives from Stellantis on Friday afternoon in a last-ditch effort to save thousands of high-paying auto manufacturing jobs at the company's recently closed Brampton plant.

"We're all going into the meeting with the same commitment, which is to protect the jobs of the hard-working Stellantis workers at Brampton," said Industry Minister Mélanie Joly at an event marking the reopening of Ford's Oakville, Ont., assembly complex.
Asked how confident she is that this meeting can save the Stellantis jobs in Brampton, Joly said only that the federal and Ontario governments will "do the work."

The minister said the meeting in Toronto will include herself, union representatives, Ontario Premier Doug Ford, Ontario Minister of Economic Development Vic Fedeli, Stellantis global CEO Antonio Filosa and Stellantis Canada CEO Trevor Longley.

items: Feds, Ontario offering Stellantis 'aggressive package'
Feds say Stellantis owes 'hundreds of millions'

blocks.text: In 2022, the Trudeau government promised to inject up to $529 million in Stellantis plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont., to help them increase production of electric and gas-powered vehicles.
More than 2,000 workers at the Brampton plant have been out of work since the company halted operations in 2023 to begin retooling so the facility could produce the Jeep Compass.
Stellantis paused that effort in early 2025, and said in October of that year that the Jeep Compass would be built at the Belvidere Assembly Plant in Illinois instead.
The Brampton plant's future had been left in limbo until last week, when Stellantis announced it was selling the facility to Canadian armoured ⁠vehicle-maker Roshel Inc.
An 'aggressive package'
Joly said last week that the federal and Ontario governments were preparing an "aggressive package" they wanted to present to Filosa in the hopes that he could be convinced to stop the sale.

The minister said that if Stellantis is willing to stay and build cars in Brampton, both governments are prepared invest in the company going forward. But if it decides to leave, the federal government says it will sue.

"They need to protect the workers. If not, we'll get our money back," Joly said. "Our goal is clear. If they go ahead and sell the plant, well then they will face legal recourses from the government of Canada of hundreds of millions of dollars."
Ford, Joly to meet with Stellantis CEO regarding Brampton plant sale

Last December, CBC News confirmed that the federal government had given $222 million to the Canadian arm of Stellantis between 2023 and 2025. Joly told CBC's Rosemary Barton Live last week that the actual total is "more than that," without specifying how much.
The company, meanwhile, says it only has to pay back $24 million.
Joly said again on Friday that contracts signed when the federal government invested in the company linked investments at the Brampton facility with investments in Windsor.
"The contracts are clear," Joly said. "We're confident in our position that they're exposed for hundreds of millions of dollars."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Peter Zimonjic is a senior writer for CBC News who reports for digital, radio and television. He has worked as a reporter and columnist in London, England, for the Telegraph, Times and Daily Mail, and in Canada for the Ottawa Citizen, Torstar and Sun Media. He is the author of Into The Darkness: An Account of 7/7, published by Vintage.
