articles.title: U.S. senator says Canada should make interim tariff agreement, let Congress 'legislate' long-term deal

image.caption: Senior Democratic Sen. Chris Coons said he will be working with his colleagues to get a better tariff deal when the new Congress is sworn in, calling tariffs on national security grounds an 'insult to Canada.' (Allison Robbert/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Politics

A senior Democrat in the U.S. Senate says he thinks Canada should seek an interim trade deal with the Trump administration — and the incoming U.S. Congress will figure out something better for the long term.
Canada-U.S. trade minister says an interim deal would likely include some tariffs

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said on Thursday that the government is seeking an interim deal with the U.S. that would see Section 232 tariffs — which covers steel, aluminum, auto and lumber — lowered and Section 338 tariffs, which came into place in September, removed entirely.
Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware told CBC's Power & Politics that if Canada can get rid of the 338 tariffs, that would "be a significant accomplishment."
"Frankly, if you can get an interim deal, I'd take it, and then put it to us in the new majority to legislate an even better deal," Coons told host David Cochrane.
If you get a deal on 338 tariffs, take it — Dems will handle the rest: U.S. sen.

The president's Republican Party suffered massive losses in the U.S. midterms and some Democrats have pledged to try to end tariffs on Canadian goods once they officially take control of the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives in January.
Coons said in a separate interview with CBC Radio's The House that removing tariffs on Canadian goods is his goal as well, though he noted that might not be shared among all Democrats.

"I know that there will be folks in my party who represent steel-producing states and who will advocate for retaining some tariffs on steel and aluminum. And I had those fights when Biden was president," Coons told host Catherine Cullen in an interview airing on Saturday.
"Section 232 tariffs are justified based on alleged national security threats. For us to impose and maintain Section 232 tariffs on Canadian imports is an insult to Canada. They should be removed."
Minister LeBlanc says Canada won’t get to zero U.S. tariffs

LeBlanc told Power & Politics that if Canada can reach an interim agreement with the Trump administration, then that would likely kickstart formal talks around reviewing the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA).
"The Americans have been clear that if we come to an arrangement to reduce the 232 and 338 tariffs, we could also begin a formal review process that's prescribed in the CUSMA agreement," he said.

LeBlanc argued that deals other countries have struck with the U.S. have all maintained some level of tariffs and that the goal is to reduce the 232 tariffs to a point where those industries could compete globally.

items: Trump says he's working on a 'fair' trade deal with Canada

blocks.text: Sources told CBC News on Thursday that the government is seeking to reach an interim trade arrangement with the Trump administration by the end of the year.
But LeBlanc says that isn't a hard deadline.
"The idea is to get the best deal we can get for Canada as soon as possible," he said. "If it takes until January or February to get that deal, we'll do that work."
The minister said Canada shouldn't see the Democrats taking control of Congress as a "magic bullet" that will end U.S. tariffs.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Florida mechanic found guilty of murdering British woman who attorney says came to US to die
articles.summary:
Dwain Hall was convicted of stabbing Sonia Exelby, a music teacher who prosecutors say suffered from mental illness

A Florida…

blocks.text: A Florida mechanic has been found guilty of stabbing to death a British music teacher, who he convinced to travel to the United States.
Dwain Hall, an auto repair and tow truck driver groomed 32-year-old Sonia Exelby from Portsmouth, England, on a fetish website before luring her to the US.
The guilty verdict came a day after prosecutors rested their case, after submitting 93 pieces of evidence and calling 30 witnesses.
Hall had pleaded not guilty to the charges of kidnap and first-degree murder.
He was charged in November last year, less than a month after Exelby had gone missing and her body was later found in a shallow grave in Marion Oaks.

The court heard from several witnesses, most of them law enforcement officials, who detailed Hall’s email, phone records, social media accounts and other records to trace his movements after Exelby travelled from the UK to meet him.

Exelby’s disappearance from her home sparked an international investigation. Prosecutors this week described how she suffered from mental illness. Investigators said that Exelby had traveled to Florida after posting online about wanting someone to end her life.

Hall’s arrest affidavit said that Exelby had previously expressed suicidal thoughts and investigators alleged that Hall knew about her struggles and used that vulnerability to bring her to Florida, the Ocala Starbanner reported.
The authorities said Exelby boarded a flight to the US seemingly with an intention “to be possibly sexually abused, tortured, and murdered by unknown individuals living in the United States”.
After Exelby traveled to the US in October 2025, authorities say Hall picked her up from the Gainesville airport in central Florida.

He drove her to an Airbnb rental, where investigators later found evidence they say connected him to her disappearance and death, including transactions on her bank cards and a video of Exelby on Hall’s cellphone.

According to the Times, Junior Barrett, Hall’s attorney, argued that Exelby took her own life. “She came here with the intention of dying, she thought she was worthless, useless, a burden on other people,” he said in his closing statement.

“This isn’t a question about what porn he likes. You can disagree with him about what he likes, but the case can’t be decided on you not liking his lifestyle. The fact he did not stop her from killing herself does not make it murder.”
Amy Beth Berndt, a prosecutor, said jurors should use their “common sense”. She added that Hall targeted Exelby for her mental illness and killed her for his sadistic pleasure.

articles.title: Spain frees wealthy US-sought activist on bail as Irish police raid Dublin home
articles.summary:
Pro-Palestinian donor James ‘Fergie’ Chambers released as court considers extradition request

In a blur of events surrounding the Trump administration’s effort to extradite James “Fergie”…

blocks.text: In a blur of events surrounding the Trump administration’s effort to extradite James “Fergie” Chambers, Spain released the wealthy US activist and donor on bail even as Irish police raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and his partner, Stella Schnabel, acting on a request from US authorities.

Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.

Speaking outside Madrid’s Aranjuez prison upon his release on Friday, Chambers called the charges against him “baseless”, adding that his release was “hopefully the first step in recognizing that internationally”.

Chambers also said: “Spain is a country that has stood on the right side of this most important issue of our time, that has stood on the right side of the genocide, and where this is some reason and some justice.”

An appeals court ordered the conditional release on Friday due to issues surrounding the legally required US translation of the extradition request’s core documents into Spanish, first reported on by the Guardian. He had been detained since 10 July, when Spanish authorities arrested him in Ibiza.
The order asserts that the translation issues cause “a diminishment, at least for the time being, in the solidity or foundation of the extradition request”.

Chambers’s release follows a separate decision on Thursday by the three-judge panel at the high court tasked with deciding on the extradition to pause the proceedings in order to evaluate the impact of the alterations the US made to the original, machine-made translation of the extradition request into Spanish.

The Guardian detailed four examples of the alterations on 7 November and the US admitted to tampering with the translation, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent” on 17 November – and citing the same four examples. Chambers’s defense team has asserted for weeks that there are as many as 30 such alterations.

The changes introduced prejudicial notions with specific legal implications that in turn wound up in the Spanish prosecutor’s report on the case, Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian earlier this week. The judges must consider the prosecutor’s report in deciding on the extradition request.

The high court was expected to rule on the extradition this week, following a 13 November hearing. But as of Thursday’s decision, the deadline has been extended indefinitely as the judges evaluate the translation, including a 345-page report submitted by the defense team that identifies 30 “incriminating changes” Trump administration officials made to a translation prepared by DeepL, “an AI-first translation platform”, according to its website.
The decision also gives the prosecutor an opportunity to address the issue in writing, after dismissing it in the 13 November hearing by referring to “supposed translation errors”.

Chambers’s views and donations to progressive and humanitarian projects have been extensively profiled in US media, including his controversial public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”
The heir to $250m from his family’s business, Cox Enterprises, is being sought in extradition because of such views, his defense team has asserted throughout the case.

Meanwhile, the Irish Garda Síochána, acting on a request from US authorities, raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and Schnabel on Wednesday, destroying the front door and removing electronic items and other possessions, according to their attorney in Ireland, Ciarán Mulholland.

Schnabel, who is five months pregnant, said: “It is difficult to see this raid as anything other than a desperate fishing expedition by the US authorities to find evidence to bolster their case against Fergie.”

The attorney told the Guardian that the raid was the result of a “mutual legal assistance” request from the US – and that such a request “wouldn’t give [the Garda Síochána] permission to kick in the doors of someone’s dwelling in Ireland”.

“It’s unusual for the Irish state to be acting in such a clandestine manner,” Mulholland said. He has asked authorities to produce a search warrant and an itemized list of what was taken. “My fear is that whatever was taken has been put on a plane and taken to the US,” he added.
“This [extradition case] shows the complete disregard for due process … that the Trump administration seems to have,” Mulholland said.

articles.title: Indian man sentenced to 19 years in prison for conspiring to kill Sikh separatist in New York
articles.summary:
Nikhil Gupta admitted to plotting with Indian government official to hire hitman to murder dual US-Canadian citizen

An Indian ⁠man was sentenced to more ⁠than 19 ​years in US prison on…

blocks.text: An Indian ⁠man was sentenced to more ⁠than 19 ​years in US prison on Friday after admitting to orchestrating a failed Indian government-backed plot to kill a Sikh separatist in New York ⁠City, in connection with what US and Canadian authorities have called a broader effort to target Indian dissidents.
Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy ⁠to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.
The US district judge Victor Marrero handed down the ​235-month sentence at a hearing in a Manhattan federal ‌court.
The discovery of alleged ‌assassination plots against Sikh separatists in the US and Canada has tested relations with India, which has ‌denied involvement in such plots.

Prosecutors accused Gupta of plotting with an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer at Sikhs for Justice in New York who has advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India.
Gupta and the Indian government official, Vikash Yadav, arranged to have $15,000 in cash delivered to a purported hitman who ‌was actually an undercover US law enforcement officer, court papers show.
Yadav is also charged in the case but is not in US custody. It is unclear ​whether he has hired a defense lawyer.
India’s government has dissociated itself from any plot against Pannun, saying it was against government policy.
Prosecutors with the Manhattan US attorney’s office had recommended a sentence of about 24 years in prison.
“This case cuts to the very core of American values,” prosecutor Ashley ⁠Nicolas said in court. “We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices ​in this country, ever.”
Addressing the ​court on Friday, Gupta said ​he regretted straying from the nonviolent example set by Indian independence leader Mahatma Gandhi.
“I’m ​sorry to Mr ‌Pannun, I’m sorry ​to the communities I hurt, ​I’m sorry to my own family,” Gupta said.
Pannun told the court that he was grateful to the US for prosecuting Gupta and said he would keep advocating for Sikh sovereignty.
“Self-determination for my people and my homeland, Punjab, is my lifetime goal,” he said.

articles.title: Misty-eyed Burnham gambles on closer ties with EU as he throws down gauntlet to Tories and Reform
articles.summary:
PM challenges rivals to rebuff plan he says could add 0.5% annual growth to economy and offer young people hope

Several sentences in to a slightly convoluted answer about where UK-EU…

blocks.text: Several sentences in to a slightly convoluted answer about where UK-EU relations might go next, Andy Burnham abruptly changed tack. “The important point is that Britain of today and the EU of today is not the one of 2016,” he said. “Life has moved on in so many ways.”
This is undoubtedly true. But Burnham’s political gamble on closer ties with Brussels hinges on the assumption that most British voters feel this way as well.

Seeking to push his deal on food checks, emissions trading and a new youth exchange scheme, Burnham was at first in full consumer politics mode, saying it would bring cheaper food – with a namecheck for Tesco, Asda and other supermarket chains – as well as lower electricity costs and a claimed 0.5% boost to overall growth.

But as the Brussels press conference went on, the prime minister became more misty-eyed, particularly in describing the youth exchange scheme as a gift to a generation stripped of choices by the 2016 referendum and then Covid. “Hope is a word,” he intoned. “And it starts now.”
For all that Burnham is a skilled political salesman, his oratory is backed up with some helpful political context matched with cooperative allies.

To begin with, not only politics but demographics are now different. A new constituency-level poll released on Friday showed that of 394 constituencies estimated to have voted leave in 2016, voters in 274 of them would now back rejoining the EU – including Burnham’s Makerfield seat.

Standing alongside the UK prime minister in the venue, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and António Costa, the European Council president, at times resembled proud parents, beaming at every positive phrase.

They, of course, began work when the EU reset was the personal project of one Keir Starmer. His name was not mentioned on Friday, and it is undeniable that Brussels finds life easier dealing with a UK leader who is both bold and popular.

Speaking to British reporters later in the day, Burnham openly challenged political opponents to rebuff a plan that, he said, could add 0.5% annual growth to the economy in the long term – more, he said, than any other single intervention.

“Why would anybody turn their back on that?” he said, with particular focus on Nigel Farage, who was, soon after Burnham spoke, hosting a retaliatory press conference of his own, 10 minutes’ walk from the EU building.

blocks.caption: Nigel Farage holds a press conference in Brussels after the UK-EU summit. Photograph: Sean Gallup/Getty Images

blocks.text: Even with the tight timing – Farage had to delay his event as the summit timetable slipped – the Reform UK leader drew a decent crowd of reporters. But there will be a sense in No 10 that beyond Farage, most of the formidable Brexit forces of 2016 have melted away.

Kemi Badenoch, who has been advised by her team to talk more about the economy and less about Brexit, spent the day on a visit in Essex. The Conservatives did send out a condemnatory press release about the EU deal, but it focused more on Burnham “reopening the divisions of the past” than the specifics.
More trenchant was a statement from Stay Out, the recently formed Brexit purity group, which floated its personal argument that rejoining the EU would cost the UK £750m a week.
after newsletter promotion

For all that the dominance of vote leave alumni in Stay Out gives the campaign the slight air of a historic battle re-enactment society, Burnham cannot ignore them. A resonant side note of the summit was how he was happy to talk about the specifics of the deal, but not much beyond that.
While it was the PM himself who provoked a debate about a future in which the UK rejoins the EU, the brakes were firmly pressed on any discussion of such ideas.

Pre-summit talk of possible closer future links with Brussels was replaced by much vaguer language about mutual “brainstorming” on what comes next, with UK officials saying any progress could be months in the making.
Another sign of the caution embedded within Burnham’s ambition was the line-up of UK cabinet ministers who watched as the prime minister, von der Leyen and Costa arrived on Friday morning.

Alongside those you might expect – Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, John Healey, the chancellor, and Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary – was Anneliese Midgley, a close ally of Burnham who has the job of chief whip, No 10’s liaison with Labour MPs.

She was there because a bill setting into UK law the new EU deal will be presented to parliament next week. Most Labour MPs agree with Burnham that the world has changed since 2016. But, as with the voters, he needs to bring them along with him.

articles.title: Despite early start, Canada's flu season may be 'far from peak' as holidays approach
articles.summary: Influenza appeared relatively early this fall, with a strain that often impacts younger adults. Medical experts aren't yet sure if this wave of infections will peter out before the holidays or if…

image.caption: A pharmacist holds up a flu shot at Remedy's Rx Pharmacy in Ottawa on Nov. 19. Though influenza A is circulating right now, and could peak before the holiday season, medical experts say it's still worth getting a flu shot given the possibility of a second wave of infections later this winter. (Pierr

blocks.text: Health·New

Influenza appeared relatively early this fall, with a strain that often impacts younger adults. Medical experts aren't yet sure if this wave of infections will peter out before the holidays or if Canada will see a second surge of flu later in the winter.
H1N1 strain circulating now can impact young, healthy individuals, and second wave of infections also possible
An early start to Canada's flu season has medical experts bracing for a range of possibilities, from influenza-free holiday gatherings to the risk of a second wave later this winter.

The latest national data shows nearly 15 per cent of flu tests came back positive in the week ending Nov. 14, up from close to 14 per cent of tests the week before. Outbreaks and hospitalizations are also up, Public Health Agency of Canada figures show, with influenza A detected in almost all test samples.

Roughly four in 10 positive tests were among older adults aged 65 and up — one of the groups at the highest risk of serious illness — though the H1N1 strain circulating this year can actually be worse for younger adults and children.

"We're really on a concerning trajectory in terms of both the volume and the speed of [the] rise of the cases right now," said Dr. Lynora Saxinger, an infectious diseases specialist and professor at the University of Alberta.
"And by the numbers, I'm very concerned about how difficult it might get."
This flu season might be worse for young people
Rise in infections putting pressure on hospitals

Influenza appeared relatively early this fall — weeks before the country's past two seasons — with the west coast bearing the brunt of those initial infections. Flu cases began appearing in B.C. by early October, and in Alberta, roughly a quarter of all flu tests were coming back positive in early November.
The ongoing rise in cases is already putting pressure on at-capacity hospitals, said Saxinger, who is based in Edmonton.
"[This week] I was seeing people in an ambulance bay. Many have basically been there for days," she told CBC News.

items: Early start to flu season may test Alberta hospital capacity
Ontario offers free flu, COVID-19 shots for general public starting Monday

blocks.text: It's a mixed bag elsewhere in the country, said Dr. Allison McGeer, a Toronto-based infectious diseases specialist with Sinai Health System.
"B.C. is probably close to the peak of the wave by now. The peak in Ontario and Quebec is probably going to be early to mid-December," she said.
"And then, hopefully, that's it."
But she acknowledged that an early end to flu season — before the holidays are fully underway — may be wishful thinking, given the unpredictability of influenza in any given year.
H1N1 strain can impact kids, young adults
Canada-wide, Saxinger said the season is likely "far from peak," with the potential for another surge of flu in the months ahead.

In some years, the virus rises and falls twice in the same season. Though H1N1 is dominant this fall, it's possible another strain could spike later in the winter, leading to a distinct second wave of infections.

items: As flu cases rise, Quebec only province without free flu shots for all

blocks.text: "We have had recent years where things have been very strange and we've actually switched strains partway through," said Saxinger. "And it's also very common to have influenza B come up at the end."
What you need to know about this year's flu season in Ontario
Still time to get flu shot, experts say
The takeaway for Canadians? It's still worth getting a flu shot, even for young and healthy individuals.

Multiple experts agreed the early dominance of H1N1 this year could hit both kids and younger adults harder than usual, as many lack prior exposure to the similar virus strains that circulated decades ago among older generations.

"[B.C. has] seen a lot of emergency room visits, doctor's office visits; it's really gone up for young children, particularly zero to five, and then the young elementary age children," said Dr. Bonnie Henry, B.C.'s provincial health officer. "But we're not seeing it so much in adults yet."

items: Winnipeg health officials encourage people to get vaccinated against respiratory viruses
Moderna's mRNA flu and flu-COVID combo vaccines have been approved by Health Canada

blocks.text: Young adults who skipped the flu shot may have a higher risk of infection this year, Saxinger warned, though overall numbers still show more older adults testing positive.
"We will probably see a higher number of otherwise healthy people getting more severely ill this season," she said.
Flu season strikes Quebec early — and most people now have to pay for the shot
COVID, RSV seasons underway as well

COVID and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are also circulating at varying levels this fall, with the latest federal numbers showing more than six per cent of tests were recently coming back positive for COVID while less than one per cent of tests showed RSV.

After multiple severe RSV seasons in the wake of the COVID pandemic, McGeer said this "quieter than usual" year is giving the country a reprieve from a lesser-known infection that typically sends both the youngest and oldest into hospital.

items: Some Alberta pharmacists say they’re having trouble getting enough stock of COVID-19 vaccines
'Quite frustrating': Demand surges for N.S. fall vaccine appointments

blocks.text: With B.C.'s respiratory virus season the furthest along, Henry remains hopeful it won't be nearly as severe as other recent years given the relative lack of RSV cases. "We're happy that we're not having influenza and RSV at the same time," she added, "because that's where you really see the impact on … children's hospitals."

McGeer also stressed that highly effective vaccines and monoclonal antibody shots are available to protect against RSV — for infants, children, pregnant individuals and older adults — on top of the shots meant to ward off COVID and flu.
"This is going to be an 'everybody should take precautions' flu season," Saxinger said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Lauren Pelley is a senior health and medical reporter for CBC News. She's a two-time RNAO Media Award winner for in-depth health reporting in 2020 and 2022, a silver medallist for best editorial newsletter at the 2024 Digital Publishing Awards, and a 2024 Covering Climate Now award winner in the health category. Contact her at: lauren.pelley@cbc.ca.

items: @LaurenPelley

articles.title: Denmark to expel Russian diplomat over attempt to kill US-Ukrainian rapper
articles.summary:
Moscow suspected of being behind plan to kill Kyivstoner before a performance in Denmark

Denmark’s foreign minister has said Russia’s defence attaché in Copenhagen would be expelled after…
articles.byline: Guardian staff and agencies in Copenhagen

blocks.text: Denmark’s foreign minister has said Russia’s defence attaché in Copenhagen would be expelled after Moscow was suspected of being behind an attempted killing of a US-Ukrainian rapper.

“We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attaché from Denmark” within seven days, Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a news conference.
“We are saying this very clearly: we have exposed you,” he said.

The announcement came after Danish police said they had averted an attempt by Russian intelligence services ⁠to kill the US-Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner in September before a planned performance in Denmark.
Rasmussen also said that Denmark was mulling suspending Schengen visas to Russians.
“We have launched work at the European level to further tighten the rules governing access of Russian nationals to Europe,” he said.
“We are now stepping up our efforts towards a halt to all non-essential visas.”
“The strongest response Denmark can give is not to waver and to support Ukraine. And we fully intend to continue supporting Ukraine,” he said.

Police ⁠thwarted the alleged ⁠plot when ​they arrested three men with links to the Danish criminal underworld shortly before the rapper was due to give a ⁠concert on 25 September, which was then cancelled, officials said. Kyvistoner, whose real name is Albert Viktorovich Vasiliev, holds both US and Ukrainian nationality.

“It is our clear assessment that the assassination attempt was planned by the Russian ⁠intelligence services,” Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, head of Denmark’s national security and intelligence service, PET, told a ​press conference.

According to prosecutors, the suspects were driving towards the concert venue north of Copenhagen with two loaded pistols and two knives when police arrested them at about 9.55pm (1955 GMT), five minutes before the concert was due ‌to begin. A fourth suspect was arrested later that evening, police said.
One of the suspects had bought a ticket to the concert, according ​to the charges.

The suspects are charged under Section 108 of Denmark’s Criminal Code, which covers assisting a foreign intelligence service, as well as attempted murder. They denied wrongdoing in court, broadcaster DR reported.
“A Russian assassination attempt is not something we’ve seen in Denmark before, ⁠and that gives me an impression of an increasingly aggressive and ​risk-taking Russia,” Kieffer-Kristensen said.
“We believe ​that the case is important ​for understanding the threat that Denmark faces from Russia.”

articles.title: Alberta separatist leaders pursue different paths back into UCP fold
articles.summary: The United Conservative Party wants to be united once again, but fallout from the referendum is making that difficult.

image.caption: After Albertans voted decisively against another vote on independence, separatist leaders, from left, Chris Scott, Mitch Sylvestre and Jeff Rath are all charting different paths back into the United Conservative Party. (Mantai Chow/CBC, CBC, Jason Franson/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Moving on is hard to do.

A month after Albertans voted decisively to reject the prospect of a future vote on independence, many in the governing United Conservative Party are struggling with how to heal the breach blazed by the separatist sentiment that, polling says, was particularly entrenched in their ranks.

items: 15 United Conservative constituency presidents won't sign agreement to publicly back Alberta referendum result
UCP board candidates must sign declaration to abide by Alberta's vote to stay in Canada

blocks.text: The party line is now one of unity. And the party has moved to enforce that, requiring both aspiring board members and leaders of local riding associations to sign a pledge to abide by the results of the referendum, prompting further questions about how unity is actually achieved, and how much disagreement must be embraced, tolerated or stamped out in pursuit of it.

The challenge is personified by the former separatist leaders themselves, several of whom spent months spreading the gospel of an independent Alberta before those dreams were crushed — who now must grapple with their own futures within Alberta’s governing party.

It’s a dilemma that has left Danielle Smith wobbling on a highwire as she tries to keep her party together while the independence movement, never that cohesive to begin with, has begun to turn on itself.

“As a sovereignty-minded individual, I have choices to make,” Chris Scott, founder of a group called Let’s Talk Alberta, told CBC News. He spent months crisscrossing the province in a branded motorhome but, after not getting the result he wanted in October, is now running for a seat on the party’s provincial board.
“Am I going to flog the dead horse for the rest of my life, or am I going to find alignments with those that have disagreed with me?” said Scott.
Chris Scott of the pro-independence group Let's Talk Alberta is seeking a spot on the UCP's provincial board. (Mantai Chow/CBC)

Speaking on stage as part of a board candidate forum in Calgary Wednesday night, Scott told the audience that despite his disappointment, he didn’t see a future in trying to rip the party apart or take down the premier. There are plenty of people on both sides who want to strengthen Alberta sovereignty, he added.
“If we can set our emotions aside and start treating each other as what we’re supposed to be, which is one group instead of enemies, we really only can go up from here,” he said.

Two days after the referendum, Smith released a video in which she drew a line in the sand. Hers was not an independence party, and those few who “remain intent on dividing and turning our party into a vehicle for the independence movement” were invited to go elsewhere, she said.

items: Q&A: Premier Danielle Smith says she doesn’t need Alberta separatists’ support

blocks.text: The first time he watched the video, he was angry, Scott says. He saw it as the party leader telling those who believed in independence to find a different party. But once he set emotion aside, he watched it again and changed his mind. He concluded that Smith only meant that all members were welcome — but shouldn’t try to seek leadership positions and turn the UCP into a separatist party.

His bid for a board seat is a continuation of what he’s been doing all along, he says, in that he will continue to push for a strong and sovereign Alberta. But he plans to do it in a way that puts independence on ice, at least for now.
In his view, that puts him in compliance with Smith’s directive.

When he received the form sent to board candidates, asking them to respect the referendum, he signed it. He suggests that his fellow travellers in the independence movement who can’t move on aren’t able to see past their own anger.
“Any reasonable person would accept and abide by the outcome of the referendum,” he said. “That’s how democracy works.”
But not all of the separatist figureheads share Scott’s convictions.
Mitch Sylvestre maintains that in his neck of the woods, meaning the farmland and oil country around northeastern Alberta, separatism remains a going concern.

The sporting goods store owner, who helped craft the first petition calling for a separatism referendum, argues that the independence-leaning part of the party helped bring Smith to power, and she won’t stay there without them.
Mitch Sylvestre, CEO of the Alberta Prosperity Project, spoke to reporters after the remain side was projected to win in the Alberta referendum. (Kory Siegers/CBC)

Unlike Scott, Sylvestre already has a firm perch in the United Conservative Party, as president of the Bonnyville-Cold Lake riding association. He’s one of the presidents who have refused to sign a pledge to respect the results of the referendum and signed his name to public letters calling on the requirement to be dropped.
He intends to stay with the party and continue what he sees as his ongoing educational campaign, but said he couldn’t answer a question about whether that meant pushing for independence.
But he took a less positive view about the calls for unity expressed at the recent meeting of UCP members.
“We’re not the problem,” he told the CBC News, speaking the morning after the Calgary event.
“I’ve been saying forever that we’re going to work within the UCP, but they’re trying to kick us out,” he added. “The unity has to come from their side.”

It would be impossible for Smith to remove all the separatists from the party, given how many there are, says Duane Bratt, a political scientist at Mount Royal University. In the weeks before the vote, polling suggested that slightly more than half of party voters favoured separation.

Instead Smith has appeared to implement a “don’t ask, don’t tell,” policy, Bratt said, citing a phrase first applied to Smith by political blogger David Climenhaga. There are longstanding rumblings about the convictions of some of her MLAs, but she has turned a blind eye to those who haven’t spoken publicly, he said.

But if the challenge for the party is unity, Bratt said, the general public — who showed up to the polls to firmly reject the idea of independence — is going to want to know that their governing party is not a separatist one.

To do that, Smith will likely have to remove a few high profile separatists, Bratt argues. The party has already kicked out Jeff Rath, another high profile separatist whose membership was recently revoked after publicly clashing with Smith over her leadership.
Jeff Rath, the lawyer for the Stay Free Alberta petitioners, says the premier can't ignore Alberta separation anymore. (Emily Fitzpatrick/CBC)

In an email, the party’s executive director told Rath his “words and actions” made clear that he did not support Smith or the party. Rath told CBC News that the party declined to tell him which of his social media posts triggered the move and that leaving the party hadn’t hampered his efforts to remove Smith from leadership.
He also attended the recent UCP meeting and said the unity talk had fallen on deaf ears.
“The people that she wants to unify with, she’s basically told it’s her way or the highway,” he said.
The question now, Bratt said, is whether Rath’s ouster will be enough to convince Albertans that the separatists are no longer in control over the party.
“The question, ultimately, is how many bodies have to be tossed,” he said.
Removing Rath may not be sufficient, he said, and it would be far harder for Smith to remove someone like Sylvestre, who already has standing with the party.
“That’s a challenge for her,” he said.
But as far as Sylvestre is concerned, the demands by, and on, the premier aren’t his concern.

“We’ve had three different premiers in the last 12 years,” he says, alluding to the political turmoil that saw Jim Prentice, Jason Kenney and Smith all take turns as head of an Alberta conservative party.
“Leaders can come and go.”

articles.title: No one else in Reform is suitable to lead the party, Nigel Farage says
articles.summary:
Farage issues warning to potential rivals and says he will fight next election as leader if ‘still here and fit and healthy’

Nigel Farage has said he does not see another person who could do…

blocks.text: Nigel Farage has said he does not see another person who could do his job as leader of Reform UK, in a warning shot to potential rivals who might seek to replace him.
The Reform UK leader delivered a message that he was going nowhere despite his worries over his personal safety in the wake of the killing of the Reform politician Ann Widdecombe.

There has been speculation over Farage’s future in light of police and parliamentary investigations of Reform’s financial affairs. The Commons standards watchdog is due to report soon on whether he should have declared a £5m personal gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne before the last election. If he gets a substantial suspension from parliament, he could face a second byelection, contested by other main parties, in his Clacton constituency.

However, Farage sounded a note of defiance in an interview with the Sun, saying: “These are very thoughtful moments, but, you know what, if I’m not here doing this job right now, who else could? Who else would? I don’t see that person. So I’m gonna do it.”

A number of other Reform UK politicians are potential contenders to succeed him, including the party’s economics spokesperson and former Conservative, Robert Jenrick, the home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, and the former leader Richard Tice. Another possibility is the return of Rupert Lowe, who left Reform in acrimonious circumstances and founded his own party, Restore Britain, but who is popular on the online hard right.
The party is going through a difficult period after slipping from first place in the polls to second or third behind behind Labour and sometimes the Conservatives.
Asked by the Sun if he had “blown” his chances of reaching No 10, Farage said: “No, far from it.”
He admitted there had been “self-inflicted wounds” in the past year but said he still had a chance of becoming prime minister.
He told the newspaper that he would fight the next election as Reform leader if he was “still here and fit and healthy”.
He also batted away questions about the £5m, which he has insisted was to pay for his personal security despite the fact the party has been providing this.

“What’s it got to do with you? Drugs, sports cars, desert islands. It’s a gift,” he said, adding that although the party had had “ebbs and flows” and had made mistakes after growing “too far and too fast”, he was confident it was “more than through the worst of it”.

On the prospect of another battle over Europe as Andy Burnham weighs the case for rejoining the EU, the Reform leader said: “If you ask me, have I got the energy and the enthusiasm to do this again? I would say to you, hold my jacket. I’m ready for it.”
after newsletter promotion
He also warned of people taking to the streets with “direct action” if Brexit is reversed.
In a separate interview with the Times while travelling to Brussels, where Burnham was attempting a reset deal, Farage said he believed the issue of Europe would dominate the years to come.
“It’s going to be absolutely huge. It’s going to be much bigger than anyone realises. The genie is out of the bottle; it literally can’t be stopped now,” he said.
He also ruled out joining a new campaign called Stay Out, led by former Tories, suggesting he would make his own case for keeping Brexit.

articles.title: Indian man sentenced to 19-plus years in plot to assassinate US-based Sikh separatist leader
articles.summary: Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February.

blocks.text: A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.

Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge said he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.

US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.
India has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.

Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019. He previously told the BBC, "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".

India has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs.
Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.
Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in New York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors said.

At his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors said. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.
Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in New York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court.

"He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton said in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.

Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.
Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event".
"It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed."

India crushed a violent armed Sikh insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s aimed at demanding the creation of Khalistan. The movement has little support in India now although some in the Sikh diaspora continue to advocate for Khalistan.
Pannun is facing serious charges, including in connection with terrorism, in India, but he denies the allegations, saying he is an activist who just believes in Khalistan.
Gupta's case placed increased scrutiny on a separate incident, involving the 2023 murder of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia, which led to increased tensions between India and Canada.

In September 2023, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said there were "credible allegations potentially linking" India to the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another advocate for the creation of Khalistan and an associate of Pannun's.
Nijjar was shot and killed by two assailants outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia. India also has denied involvement in his death.
The day after Niijar's murder, US prosecutors allege that Gupta told the undercover officer Nijjar "was also the target" and "we have so many targets."
Nadine Yousif contributed to this report.

articles.title: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
articles.summary: The UK-EU deal agreed on Friday covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

blocks.text: Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.
European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".
Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.
Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.
The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.

The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.

The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.
The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.
A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.
There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.
Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."

The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.
Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".
He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.
Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.
"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."
Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.
The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.
Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".

Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".

Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".
She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".

Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."

In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

articles.title: At COP31, conflict over climate science slows action on global warming
articles.summary: Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?

image.caption: Distractions and disinformation risk obscuring the scientific data climate negotiators rely on to make key decisionsImage: Osmancan Gurdogan/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's plans to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.
But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.

"We are extremely concerned about the situation," said a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.

The IPCC's scientific assessments, published every six to seven years, provide the basis for major international climate agreements, including the 2015 Paris Agreement. The IPCC began evaluating the latest climate science in 1988 and its most recent report was published in 2023.
Oil interests and climate promises collide at the COP31 summit
Researchers should have actually already started work on the next edition but the last plenary session was put on hold in October at the urging of Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kenya.

"The IPCC finds itself in a difficult situation," a spokesperson from the German Environment Ministry told DW at COP. "We stand ready to help resolve this issue, so that the panel can continue its work. To that end, we are holding many discussions with various countries to explore possible solutions."
2028 climate report card risks delay
At the core of the dispute is the question of whether future UN climate talks base their negotiations on the latest scientific knowledge — or not.

That's especially relevant for the next "global stocktake," due in 2028, a report card on the world's climate efforts, which will shape action plans for countries around the world to lower planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

The European Union, Brazil, the United Kingdom, small island states and several other countries especially at risk of the effects of climate change have called for the IPCC's seventh assessment report to be published in 2028, so it can be used to inform next steps for climate action. The report cover climate protection and impact.
"It's much more difficult without these scientific reports. Otherwise, we're just talking to ourselves or relying on information that's no longer current," said a delegation source.
But Russia, Iran, India and Saudi Arabia want the IPCC report postponed until 2029, after the global stocktake.
The official reason: the tight timeline would be detrimental to the quality of the research, and could hinder the participation of researchers and governments representing developing countries.

blocks.caption: Poorer countries are calling on the nations responsible for the largest share of greenhouse gas emissions to assume financial responsibility for adaptation effortsImage: Yasin Akgul/AFP

blocks.text: Disagreements over budget issues have also held up the IPCC's work. Among other expenses, the funds are used to pay the travel arrangements for the hundreds of volunteer scientists, especially those from poorer countries, to attend the IPCC sessions.
"No budget means no more IPCC," said a member from another delegation, also speaking off the record.
It hasn't come to that point yet, but without planning certainty the whole process risks being delayed — along with the climate negotiations that depend on this knowledge.

Researchers with the IPCC, however, have said the timeline is attainable. "We have no time to lose," said an open letter released in October signed by more than 100 researchers from 36 countries — including India and China. "We stand committed to continue working to deliver the [seventh assessment report] in a manner that is rigorous, timely and inclusive."
But while the dispute over the timeline won't alter the scientific findings themselves, it could delay their political impact.
EU stresses need to 'protect the integrity of climate science'
In its pre-COP communications, France accused the countries delaying the report's publication schedule of attempting to "obstruct science in order to lower the ambition of the global stocktake."

The IPCC isn't a stranger to attempts at political persuasion: at past climate conferences, delegates from many countries have regularly negotiated the exact phrasing of the summary reports intended for policymakers.

Speaking at COP31 on November 17, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said it was "fundamental to protect the integrity of climate science and the role of the IPCC as the source of best available science."

Although there is no vote on the IPCC at COP31, it's possible that its significance and a timeline for the next report will be included in the final declaration of the climate talks, expected this weekend.

The IPCC has been warning for years that disinformation is hindering global climate action. And the struggle for information and control over the narrative in Antalya hasn't just been limited to the IPCC.

DW was able to obtain a copy of a presentation which included misleading statements on the COP's electrification targets, one of the key goals at this year's talks. Turkey has proposed boosting global electrification to 35% by 2035, to reduce the world's reliance on planet-warming fossil fuels.
The contents of the presentation, said to have been leaked to some states in advance, was confirmed to DW by two countries. Its origin, however, could not be verified.

The presentation portrays electrification as a business venture undertaken by wealthy countries at the expense of poorer nations. The International Energy Agency, however, has calculated that developing countries could save around $100 billion (€90 billion) in fossil fuel imports by 2035 through electrification.

The presentation also gives the impression that all countries must meet fixed electrification targets. In fact, according to the UN, the 35% target represents a global goal, with individual countries free to determine their own national pathways.
This article was originally written in German.

Qatar to invest €15 billion more in German defense tech, says Merz
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday announced that Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani had pledged €15 billion ($16.5 billion) in new German defense and technology investments.
During a Berlin press conference with the emir, Merz said, "This strengthens both of us, particularly in future technologies such as artificial intelligence, semiconductors and aviation."

The Qatar-Germany collaboration is aimed at improving security and defense projects that also include defending against cyberattacks, with Merz saying, "We are particularly open to new partnerships in the defense industry."
That cooperation comes as both nations look to beef up defenses amid regional conflicts with global consequences.

The chancellor and the emir also stressed the fundamental importance of diplomacy in the resolution of conflict, with the two leaders' focused largely on Iran and the Middle East — and the need to get the flow of shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz closer to pre-war levels.
The emir called for deescalation, saying, "We are convinced that true political resolution is the only way to achieve lasting peace."
Merz added that the two agreed on the war in Ukraine, saying: "Russia must stop its time-wasting diplomatic games. Moscow has to finally sit down for real peace negotiations."
Merz was straightforward on Iran, saying Germany wants peace in the Middle East because it needs affordable energy.
He later called out Russian maritime marauding on the Black Sea, labeling it a threat to global food security.

Two men have been killed after their glider crashed into Loch Leven, a large body of water in Perth and…

blocks.text: Two men have been killed after their glider crashed into Loch Leven, a large body of water in Perth and Kinross, on Friday morning.
Police Scotland said their bodies were recovered from the loch by the emergency services after the alarm was raised at 11.05am on Friday.

The force said next of kin had been told and the incident was not being treated as suspicious. Two Coastguard helicopters and an air ambulance were sent to the scene, along with a fire service appliance and a specialist crew.
The pair had flown off from the Scottish Gliding Centre at Portmoak airfield near the loch’s eastern shore in a Perkoz two-person glider on a training flight.

A spokesperson for the gliding centre said: “The incident is currently under investigation by air accident investigation branch of the Department for Transport and the police in conjunction with the British Gliding Association.
“Our club is co-operating fully with these organisations. At the present time, there is no indication as to the cause of the accident.”

An Air Accidents Investigation Branch spokesperson said: “A multi-disciplinary team including inspectors with expertise in aircraft operations, engineering and recorded data have been deployed to gather evidence and make inquiries.”

articles.title: Better educated than ever – yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future
articles.summary: Never before have young people faced so many challenges. Young Germans are asking: Will I be better off later in life than my parents are now?

image.caption: GenZ makes its voices heard, also on the streets of BerlinImage: Ralf Hirschberger/AFP

blocks.text: It is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing professional training or university. And finding an affordable place to live in a big city and finally starting to live independently is nearly impossible.

Nor do young people feel that politicians are finally taking action on issues that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It therefore shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe are taking to the streets this Friday to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 cities, coinciding with World Children's Day.

What particularly infuriates young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example from the political realm was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran the headline: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today."

"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," says Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests," he argues.

blocks.caption: Erik Sczygiol was deputy secretary-general of the German Conference of Student Representatives until recentlyImage: Oliver Pieper/DW

blocks.text: Gen Z is better educated but faces a bleaker future

However, eighteen-year-old Erik Sczygiol is an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW).This year's report is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z. The report is titled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future."

The United Nations surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries. Some of the findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them. Today, 78% of adolescents complete at least upper-secondary education. Yet finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise across the globe.

This economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, financial independence is often not achieved until one's mid-to-late twenties, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities until one's early-to-mid thirties.
Young people are underrepresented in the German parliament

Nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30."

Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," says Brod.

At least Brod is somewhat closer to the political decision-making process. He has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an important step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

blocks.caption: Florian Brod has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two yearsImage: Oliver Pieper/DW

blocks.text: Political participation often remains purely symbolic

Nevertheless, both Florian Brod and Erik Sczygiol, who represents students, have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," says Brod.

Sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people."
'Small extremist minority' turn Germany's youth protests violent
The promise that 'our children will have a better life' no longer holds true

Medical student Amélie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva this May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

Her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have said, 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We, young people, need to be able to believe in our future again!"

articles.title: Police search for teacher who missed sentencing after indecent assault conviction
articles.summary:
Sally-Anne Bowen was found guilty of having sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the 1980s

Police are searching for a missing chemistry teacher convicted of sexual…

blocks.text: Police are searching for a missing chemistry teacher convicted of sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the late 1980s after she did not turn up to her sentencing hearing.

Sally-Anne Bowen, 65, was not found at her Hemel Hempstead home by Metropolitan police officers after her failure to attend Harrow crown court in north London on Friday, where a warrant was issued for her arrest.

Bowen’s barrister, Mark Kimsey, told the court she was in contact with solicitors on Thursday and had engaged with a pre-sentence report, adding there had been “concerns as to her welfare due to the content of the messages” from her.

The former teacher, who was in her 20s when she had sex with one pupil up to 30 times and kissed a second boy when they were aged about 14 to 15, was convicted in August of seven counts of indecent assault and granted bail before her sentencing.
Judge Karim Ezzat issued a warrant for her arrest, which he said was “not backed by bail”.
Neelam Gomersall, prosecuting, said Bowen’s partner of 36 years, Darren Scotchbrook, was at the home address when officers arrived, but Bowen was not.
Gomersall earlier told the court there was “no evidence” that Bowen could not attend the sentencing, and that information from her partner was “suggestive of refusal rather than inability” to attend.

The Met said: “On Friday 20 November, officers were made aware that a 65-year-old woman had failed to appear at Harrow crown court for sentencing. A warrant has been issued for her arrest, and inquiries to locate her are ongoing.”
The trial heard that Bowen was in her mid-20s when she taught at Christ’s College in Finchley, north London.
Jurors heard she had worn short, tight skirts and flirted in class, with one former pupil comparing her behaviour to “a Sabrina Carpenter video”.
after newsletter promotion
One victim told jurors he had had sex with her “about 20 or 30 times” over several months, considered her his girlfriend and kept it secret. He said it had led to “the destruction of my education”.
The second victim described spending lunchtimes with Bowen in a cafe, where he was “goaded” into kissing her by other boys and recalled touching her breasts.

Bowen denied the allegations as “total fabrication” and claimed a medical condition made sex difficult and painful. She denied flirting, saying: “I didn’t flirt with students, I was just friendly.” Defending her clothes, she said she “wasn’t going to dress like Margaret Thatcher”.

items: Former PBA star Peter June 'PJ' Simon passed away at the age of 46 after collapsing during a basketball game.
Simon had a legendary 16-year career with the Purefoods/Magnolia franchise, earning multiple accolades including eight PBA All-Star selections and a Grand Slam title in 2014.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Former PBA star Peter June “PJ” Simon died on Friday, November 20, after collapsing in a basketball game. He was 46.
The Purefoods/Magnolia franchise confirmed his passing in a social media post.

“Isa si PJ sa pinakamagandang ehemplo ng isang professional basketball player (PJ is one of the best examples of a professional basketball player),” the team said. “You competed with quiet confidence, carried yourself with humility, and wore #8 with a pride everyone could feel.”
“You represented the franchise in the best way possible, and that is why you are beloved not just by Hotshots fans, but every Filipino basketball fan.”

Though no official cause of death was given, multiple videos online showed Simon being fanned by teammates on the sideline and eventually carried off-court after an apparent mid-game collapse in what looked like a recreational match in Davao City.

Drafted 43rd overall in 2001, Simon quickly established himself as one of the greatest PBA draft steals, eventually carving out a legendary 16-year career entirely with the Purefoods/Magnolia franchise, and earning the iconic moniker “The Scoring Apostle.”

Forming a feared guard duo with fellow franchise icon and shooter James Yap, Simon provided excellent production mostly off the bench, enough to earn him eight PBA All-Star selections and win Mr. Quality Minutes twice.

Alongside fellow stars like Yap, Marc Pingris, and Mark Barroca, Simon immortalized himself in PBA lore in 2014 after helping Purefoods — named the San Mig Coffee Mixers at the time — win the ultimate PBA title trifecta, the rare Grand Slam, under head coach Tim Cone.
“This is so sudden, Part. I didn’t expect it at all,” Yap wrote in Bisaya in a social media post.
“Thank you for everything, Part, for all the times we spent together that I will never forget. We still have a basketball tour to do. This is painful, Part.”

In 2019, Magnolia handed Simon the rare honor of retiring his iconic jersey No. 8, after the Cotabato native helped the franchise win eight PBA titles with averages of 10.1 points in under 22 minutes across nearly 700 games.

After the 2001 PBA draft, Simon started to make a name for himself in the defunct Metropolitan Basketball Association and the Philippine Basketball League, becoming a two-time PBL champion and one-time MVP, before finally suiting up for Purefoods in 2004.

After retiring from the PBA in 2020, Simon made a brief return to the pro ranks in 2024 with the Davao Occidental Tigers of the Maharlika Pilipinas Basketball League before again hanging up his sneakers a year later.

“We’ll always remember the eight championships and the Grand Slam. We’ll miss that signature one-hander from midrange. We’ll always think of the clutch shots and heat checks of ‘The Scoring Apostle,'” the Purefoods/Magnolia franchise said.
“Most of all, we’ll miss the person we got to share those moments with.”
Simon is survived by his wife, Jehza, and two children. – Rappler.com
