articles.title: DepEd gives Antipolo teachers laptops, tech training
articles.summary: The Department of Education (DepEd) has launched a hands-on technology training program for public school teachers alongside its nationwide distribution of laptops, as part of efforts to accelerate…

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 6:18pm

The Department of Education (DepEd) has launched a hands-on technology training program for public school teachers alongside its nationwide distribution of laptops, as part of efforts to accelerate digitalization in basic education.

Education Secretary Sonny Angara led the launch of GuroXL, a customized professional development program, during the distribution of laptops to 1,441 public school teachers from 62 schools in Antipolo City.
The teachers received MacBook Neo laptops under the DepEd Computerization Program (DCP) and immediately participated in guided training sessions on how to use the devices for classroom instruction.

"What this is all about is giving you the best that we can give you. Because we know teachers give their best, even without laptops, you give everything you can and go above and beyond what is required. That is why you continue to inspire us, and the President is behind you one hundred percent. We at DepEd are behind you one hundred percent," Angara said.

“Please maximize these tools because there is so much that they can do for you and for your learners. Let us take time to listen because they will explain to you the potential, and they will make you more productive, save you time, and enable you to be a better teacher,” he added.
The rollout builds on the nationwide laptop distribution program launched by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Angara in Dagupan City on November 9.

DepEd has awarded contracts for 231,725 teacher laptops, consisting of 169,008 MacBook Neo units and 62,717 Windows-based laptops. Another 3,646 MacBook Neo units were procured for administrative officers.
The delivery and deployment of the devices are expected to continue through March 2027.

Coordinated through the National Educators Academy of the Philippines (NEAP), the DepEd Information and Communications Technology Service, and the Bureau of Learning Delivery, GuroXL allows teachers to train using the same laptops assigned to them.
The laptop packages were procured through competitive public bidding at approximately P43,000 per unit, significantly below suggested retail prices.
Each package includes a five-year warranty, built-in productivity software, logistics, technical support and professional development assistance.
DepEd said the nationwide rollout aims to narrow the digital divide in public education while reducing teachers' administrative workload.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: South Korea catches 111 students with new measures against exam cheating
articles.summary: The students were caught with banned smart devices while taking the high-stakes Suneung exam.

blocks.text: South Korea's education ministry says 111 candidates were found with unauthorised smart devices during a high-stakes nationwide exam, after officials introduced urgent measures to tackle rising cases of AI-assisted cheating.
Five of the candidates were caught red-handed using smart devices during the exam, authorities said on Friday.
Half a million students sat for the college entry exam, also known as Suneung, which took place this week under the shadow of several recent high-profile cheating scandals.
Prior to the Suneung, authorities announced anti-cheating measures such as emergency alerts sent to every single mobile phone in the country to detect unauthorised devices in exam halls.
On Friday, Prime Minister Lee Jae Myung called for an overhaul of the exam system to tackle AI-assisted cheating.

In South Korea, public examinations "significantly affect the distribution of opportunities and resources", Lee said, adding that using AI to cheat in such tests "rocks the basic order of our society by undermining fairness and trust".
Concerns over academic dishonesty had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
Last month, two candidates were caught cheating with AI glasses during university entrance exams.
The education ministry said earlier this month that four students across middle and high schools were caught using AI glasses to cheat this year.
These fears came to a boil over the weekend, when the top scorer of South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam admitted to cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," said the candidate, 34-year-old Han Won-seok, in a video published on Sunday.
His confession, days ahead of the Suneung, prompted authorities to introduce last-minute measures to prevent cheating during the national exam.
The measures included nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.

Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea tapped on its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
All this made even honest test takers paranoid.
Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times that he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.
Another told news outlet Yonhap that he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.
Held every November, the Suneung is an infamous eight-hour marathon of back-to-back exams.
Students attempt about 200 questions across various subjects, which include Korean, maths, English, social and natural sciences, among others.
The country itself comes to a standstill - construction work halts, planes are grounded and military training gets suspended to facilitate an optimal testing environment.
Many South Koreans see the Suneung as a culmination of years of formal education - and a turning point that determines their university placements, careers, and social statuses.

articles.title: Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?
articles.summary: German automakers are pulling back on investments at home, sparking fresh anxiety about the auto sector's future. Some industry watchers think there is still a narrow window to stem the decline. But…

image.caption: Mercedes-Benz has halted all further investments in German manufacturing for the time being and is also weighing plant closuresImage: Bernd Weißbrod/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.
In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.
Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure."
The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, said it was shelving plans to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant.
Can crisis reinvent the car again?
German auto industry faces restructuring

Germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure.
Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country.

"We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot."

A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Bergeragreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation."
In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable.

blocks.caption: In Germany, Mercedes has three assembly plants and seven facilities that manufacture drivetrains and componentsImage: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

blocks.text: Unions dig in amid fight for survival

Many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek. The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached.
Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic.
Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he said was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation.
"We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW.
China's EV-makers can bring a new model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage.
Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500.

blocks.caption: Mercedes plans more than 40 model launches by next year — a growing share will be built outside GermanyImage: Joan Cros/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Does Germany have a 'false sense of security?'

A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security."
PwC said Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China.

These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those new technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms.
"The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany.
With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit.

Wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi, which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year.
"Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned.
Production remains resilient despite decline
Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well.

Domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA).
IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability.

In Italy, "the politics and the unions blocked any attempt by Fiat to cut overcapacity," Puls told DW. "What's the result? They have a capacity of 1.1 to 1.2 million cars and utilization of about 250,000."
Last year, those same Italian plants built just 214,000 passenger cars, according to the FIM Cisl trade union, the fewest since 1954.
Analysts call for faster reform
For Germany, the issue isn't a lack of expertise or ambition; it's that reforms to huge industries often get weighed down by caution and red tape.

As the country's auto giants try to push through painful cuts, RWTH Aachen University's Kampker warned that if they fail to address their shortcomings, "we will see more production sites closing and a substantial shift of industrial investment and employment away from Germany."
"There is still an opportunity to reverse this trend, but the window of opportunity is narrowing," Kampker concluded.

articles.title: Global stock markets slump as Anthropic IPO fails to stem AI sell-off
articles.summary: Asian markets on track for their worst week since 2020, with European and US stocks also way down

blocks.text: Global stock markets have slumped as Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.

Asian stock markets were on track for their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell on Friday. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chipmaker TSMC down about 6%.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets were heading for their worst week since March, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.3% in the first 90 minutes.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by over 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

Anthropic’s shares jumped 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the frontier AI firm began. But they were heading for losses on Friday, down 6% at $91.30, falling back towards the IPO price of $83.

Anthropic’s floation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
after newsletter promotion
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index hit a five-month low on Friday morning. It has dropped by 4.8% this week, and is heading for its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

articles.title: Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports
articles.summary: According to a letter obtained by the media, Lufthansa's executive board said the German company is losing €20 million every month. In addition to job cuts, operational cuts are also planned.

image.caption: Lufthansa is also the largest airline in Europe, in terms of passengers carriedImage: Ardan Fuessmann/Eibner-Pressefoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany's flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.
The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa CEO Jens Ritter and four other board members.
Why is Lufthansa cutting 1,000 jobs?
This is reportedly down to ongoing financial losses. In the first nine months of the year, the airline recorded an operating loss of €180 million ($197 million).
VW on the brink

The executive board said on average the loss amounts to €20 million every month, according to media reports. The board stated in the letter that "this is the third year in a row of not being financially successful."
"Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said.
At the end of 2025, the Lufthansa group employed some 67,100 people, up 1% from the previous year.
How else is Lufthansa planning to save money?

The company also plans to cut employee travel benefits, restructure its hub operations to reduce crew overnight stays abroad, and reduce short- and medium-haul capacity by replacing some A320 aircraft with A220 jets.

Furthermore, it plans to equip ten aircraft per month with Starlink, a satellite internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The airline hopes to generate "additional revenue” by monetizing onboard internet access, according to the letter.
The time frame of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were a part of a previously announced downsizing.
In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4,000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.
In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.

articles.title: Jinggoy Estrada's 'fees' linked to Bulacan pumping stations, solar lights --witness
articles.summary: Senator Jinggoy Estrada"s P213 million worth of "commitment fees" or “kickbacks” stemmed from P355 million worth of pumping stations and P500 million worth of solar street lights in Bulacan, a…

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 5:34pm

Senator Jinggoy Estrada’s P213 million worth of "commitment fees" or “kickbacks” stemmed from P355 million worth of pumping stations and P500 million worth of solar street lights in Bulacan, a prosecution witness said Friday.

Carlo Rivera, a former engineer at the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Bulacan First District Engineering Office (DEO), gave testimony during the ongoing hearing on the bail petition filed by Estrada before the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division.
Estrada is facing a P573 million plunder charge over his alleged involvement in the flood control kickback scheme.

“Ang sabi po niya prepare a list for Senator Estrada…iyong P300 million pumping station, i-tag kay SJE,” Rivera said, referring to this former boss, state witness and ex-Bulacan First DEO District Engineer Henry Alcantara.
It was Alcantara who previously told the anti-graft court that Estrada got a 25% commitment fee per project. Alcantara, however, did not specify the nature of these Bulacan projects.
“The total amount of solar street lights is P500 million,” Rivera said.
Another prosecution witness, Edrick San Diego, said he served as a driver for Alcantara but was paid as a lot technician.
Likewise, San Diego said his task was only to deliver the boxes to state witness and the DPWH Undersecretary Roberto Bernardo, not to Estrada.
“Hindi ko alam ano nangyari [sa mga boxes] after madeliver sa Diamond Hotel,” San Diego said.
After San Diego’s testimony, the prosecution informed the Sandiganbayan that San Diego would be its last witness.
As a result, the Sandiganbayan gave the prosecution 10 days to submit its formal offer of evidence. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Defense witness: No reason for Cale88 income to go beyond P208M
articles.summary: The defense witness from the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte said Friday there was no reason for Cale88 Foods Corporation to surpass its…

blocks.text: FROM 2022 TO 2025
Published November 20, 2026 5:25pm

The defense witness from the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte said Friday there was no reason for Cale88 Foods Corporation to surpass its declared sales of P208 million during the years 2022 to 2025.

On Day 45 of the impeachment trial, Senator-judge and Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian asked DTI Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo about Cale88, the food company linked to Duterte's husband Manases Carpio.
"From 2022 to 2025, ang audited sales ng Cale88 is P208 million, tama po ba (is that correct)?" Gatchalian said, citing DTI documents.
"Opo (Yes), honorable judge," Rodolfo replied.
Gatchalian then presented data from the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC), which showed that Cale88 had an inflow of P776 million compared to an outflow of P154.611 million.

"Ang inward remittance is about P776 million… sa inyong karanasan, dahil alam ko na expert kayo pagdating sa incentives, matagal na rin kayo sa BOI (Board of Investments), ano 'yung possible reason dito dahil ang laki ng discrepancy? Mayroon bang undervaluing of sales, hindi nagdedeklera nang tama? Base sa inyong analysis," Gatchalian asked.

(The inward remittance is about P776 million… in your experience, because you are an expert when it comes to incentives, you have been with the BOI for a long time, what is the possible reason for the large discrepancy.)
Gatchalian added that based on a submitted balance sheet, there was also P20 million in advances from shareholders. Despite this, it would still not explain the large amount, he said.

"In relation po, Honorable Judge, doon sa operations po ng kumpanya at saka po doon sa sinubmit sa aming dokumento, wala ako ng makitang rason para tumaas po sila ng more than dito po sa declared sales revenue po nila na sinubmit sa amin," Rodolfo said.
(In relation, Honorable Judge, to the operations of the company and the submitted documents, I do not see a reason for this to go higher than the declared sales revenue that was submitted to us.)
The DTI also submitted bank certifications to the impeachment court, including one in 2023 indicating $352,000 in sales or about P22.48 million with the current exchange rate.
In 2025, there was another inflow of $368,000, or about P23.5 million.
Rodolfo said this amounted to $721,283 (about P46 million). The Senate President noted that this was still far from the amount found by the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC).
Last October, AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura testified said that Cale88 had aggregate transactions amounting to P1.25 billion from 2022 to 2025.
Buenaventura also said Cale88 received P319 million from China and Hong Kong, based on AMLC's covered transaction reports (CTRs) and suspicious transaction reports (STR).
Unavailed tax incentives
Meanwhile, Gatchalian also noted that Cale88 did not avail of any tax incentives from the BOI such as the income tax holiday (ITH).

"Why go through all the trouble tapos hindi ka rin mag-a-apply ng VAT zero rating? Sabi nga kanina ni former senate president Tito Sotto, pati other incentives like ITH, 'yung customs duty exemptions, bakit hindi sila nag-apply?" Gatchalian asked, referring to value-added tax.
(Why go through all the trouble and then not apply for VAT zero rating? Former senate president Tito Sotto pointed out that other incentives like the ITH, customs exemptions, why did they not apply?)
Rodolfo explained that given that Cale88 was export-oriented, the VAT zero rating was highly competitive.
"VAT zero rating 'yung isa sa mga pinag-aawayan. It has to be very facilitative. Within that context po, hindi ko rin alam kung bakit hindi siya nag-apply," Rodolfo said.
(The VAT zero rating is fought over. It has to be very facilitative. Within that context, I do not know why they did not apply.)
— VDV, GMA News

articles.title: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
articles.summary:
State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors

California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that

blocks.text: California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.

Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors.”
The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.

Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China.
Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.
Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.

“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”
after newsletter promotion
Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.

Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, said the company had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back.
Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.

articles.title: Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?
articles.summary: From record-breaking heat to devastating floods and wildfires, the warning signs are everywhere. Can rising temperatures still be brought under control?

image.caption: Has the world acted too late to stop catastrophic climate change?Image: Abriansyah Liberto/REUTERS

blocks.text: When world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment. Hope rippled from Paris, where the historic deal was made.

Since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply. But they still account for around 86% of the world's energy.
"We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.

And that has consequences. The United Nations now says overshooting the temperature threshold agreed in Paris 11 years ago is inevitable. That means even more extreme weather events, like storms, flooding, droughts and deadly heat waves and resultant crop failures and water shortages across the world.

The impacts are already being felt globally. This summer, Europe alone recorded 50,000 heat-related deaths in urban areas. In Delhi, India, summer heat waves saw temperatures soar above 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit). Even in the relative cool of the evening, there was little respite.
"It feels like your eyes are burning," said Disha Ravi co-founder of the India chapter of youth climate movement Fridays for Future (FFF). "I always describe it as being cooked alive in an oven."
Heat waves and other weather extremes are killing people now, says Ravi, and she is aware that as the global average temperature continues to rise, life is only set to become tougher.
"Even at this moment where we haven't even reached the worst of what it could be, it's already difficult," she said.
"We should have dealt with climate change 10, 20 years ago," Maslin said.
Shoulda, woulda, coulda: Is it too late to bring temperatures under control?
The UN now says that the world must keep the time it spends in overshoot as brief as possible, bringing global heating back down by the end of the century.

The longer the planet spends above the threshold, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible, self-perpetuating tipping points, such as massive forest die-back and permafrost melting that would release huge amounts of carbon into the atmosphere.

blocks.caption: As permafrost melts, it releases carbon dioxide which adds to the greenhouse gas effect that continues to warm the planetImage: MAXIM SHEMETOV/REUTERS

blocks.text: A recent report by science-based assessment Climate Action Tracker says limiting overshoot will require policies to rapidly and steeply reduce the emissions warping the climate.

"The stark choice for governments is to continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to — or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever," the authors said.

Failure to cut emissions quickly has made it significantly harder to get climate change under control, and the window for doing so is rapidly closing. But Maslin refers to a Chinese proverb: "When is the best time to plant a tree? Yesterday. When's the next best time to plant a tree? Today."

He points to the massive expansion in renewable energy as reason not to despair. Wind, solar and hydropower accounted for around 34% of global electricity production in 2025 and are increasingly being used to meet rising demand.
Last year, record growth in solar power meant that clean energy met all new global electricity demand, stifling new fossil fuel generation, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember.

blocks.caption: Solar energy has experienced record growth for years Image: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "At the moment, $2 trillion is being invested in new renewable energy projects around the world, which is twice as much as fossil fuels," Maslin said.
But no country is weaning itself off fossil fuels quickly enough to limit the time spent in overshoot. "The transition is happening, it's just not happening fast enough," he added.
The countries pushing for a fossil fuel phaseout

One of the problems is that most climate and energy plans focus on building a green energy system rather than creating policy to shift away from fossil fuel use and production, according to recent report on how to manage the transition by nonprofit research organization, World Resources Institute.
A group of 57 states is working together to manage and accelerate the complicated task of phasing out oil, coal and gas by creating specific roadmaps to do so.

Under the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels initiative (TAFF) initiative, Brazil has published a global roadmap that suggests various measures that can be tailored to each country's financial circumstances and capabilities.
So far, a small but growing number of countries, including, Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Finland, have released national roadmaps.
COP31: Can electrification replace fossil fuels?

Yet renewables advocacy group Oil Change International says they largely repackage existing commitments rather than offering new ones, when "what we need is an accelerated timeline for a clean, secure energy system."

France is sticking to a previously announced deadline of phasing out fossil fuels entirely by 2050. The Netherlands has not published binding dates for quitting oil and gas, and will continue to extract gas in the North Sea.

Germany, however, explicitly mentioned transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045 for the first time, in line with its existing climate neutrality target. The country has also reduced its emissions by 48% compared to 1990 levels.

And while Finland has not set a hard and fast target for phasing out the fossil fuels that still account for 26% of its total energy consumption, it already generates more than 96% of electricity from non-fossil sources.

"None of these examples is a perfect template," according to the WRI report. "But together, they show that countries are already developing many of the core ingredients of a fossil fuel transition plan."
Every fraction of a degree matters
Limiting the time spent in overshoot would mean fossil fuel use falling 20% by 2030 and being phased out completely by 2070, according to research institute Climate Analytics.
It also means removing hundreds of billions of tons of CO2 from the atmosphere using carbon removal technologies that remain unproven at scale, as well as nature-based approaches like reforestation.
And it requires fast action on the short-lived but highly potent greenhouse gas methane. A 45% cut would reduce warming by 0.3%, according to the UN.

blocks.caption: Each fraction of a degree of warming will bring with it escalating climate extremes so it's still all to play for, say scientistsImage: Apu Gomes/AFP

blocks.text: Scientists stress that every fraction of a degree matters as the world blows past the threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) of warming above pre-industrial levels. That's because every increment will bring more extreme heat, heavier rainfall, rising seas, and greater and more catastrophic risk for everyone around the world.
Still, even in the face of accelerating climate change, FFF co-founder Ravi rejects the idea that it is too late to act.
"I refuse to believe we'll ever run out of time. No matter how bad it gets," she said. "We owe it to ourselves. We owe it to each other to always try to get out of this mess."

blocks.text: Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.

articles.title: PNP identifies 70 social media posts encouraging protests, violence

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 5:00pm
The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Friday said it has identified around 70 social media posts allegedly encouraging people to participate in protests and engage in violence.
At a press briefing, PNP spokesperson Police Brigadier General Allen Rae Co said the PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group is working to identify the individuals or groups behind the posts.
“Marami po, marami ang na-ano natin na, several. Siguro nasa mga 70, more or less, 70,” Co said.
(There were several. Maybe more or less 70.)

Among the posts monitored by authorities were messages urging people to take to the streets, join demonstrations, oust certain government officials, and resort to violence over alleged government’s wrongdoing.
Co said the PNP is still validating the identities of those behind the posts.
According to him, authorities have noticed similarities in some of the messages, including the use of identical punctuation marks and spacing.
“It could have come from a single source na marami pong naglalabas (and many people posted them),” he said.
Co said the PNP is examining possible violations of Philippine laws in connection with the posts.
During the ASEAN Summit 2026, protesters expressed opposition to the Pax Silica initiative as well as the visit of United States President Donald Trump to the Philippines. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: A Montrealer died in Istanbul. Authorities blame food poisoning but what we found suggests something else
articles.summary: A young Canadian woman travelled to Turkey after graduating from medical school. In her last days there, she fell ill and died within hours. Authorities there blame food poisoning, but a joint…
articles.byline: Michelle Gagnon, Jacaudrey Charbonneau, Judith Plamondon

image.caption: Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino visited Capadoccia, Turkey, in 2025 as part of a trip celebrating her recent graduation from medical school. During that trip, the 24-year-old Montrealer died suddenly in Istanbul. (Submitted by Deveaux-Cattino family)

blocks.text: Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino, a healthy 24-year-old Montrealer, died suddenly in Istanbul on June 17, 2025.
A Turkish autopsy report concluded the cause of death was food poisoning.
But for her family, that doesn't add up.
A joint investigation into Deveaux-Cattino's death by Enquête and the fifth estate revealed a different poison at work and 12 similar deaths.
The recent medical school graduate had decided to celebrate by taking a trip with a few of her closest friends.
"She'd never been to Turkey," said her sister, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. "She thought it was a super beautiful, vibrant country."
The group hit the tourist trail and its highlights, including the requisite balloon ride in Cappadocia.
Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino had never been to Turkey before her trip in 2025, says her sister, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. ‘She thought it was a super beautiful, vibrant country.’ (Radio-Caanda)
With only two days to go, Bérengère and one of her friends headed for Istanbul, a city she'd longed to visit.

items: Watch the full documentary, "The Invisble Killer," from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m.

blocks.text: They checked into Room 108 at the Seven Days Hotel and went straight out to explore. They soaked up the sights and street food, then settled down for a proper meal, a chicken casserole followed by Turkish tea and baklava.
The next morning, they woke violently ill.
Laurie recalls the final days

The details of those final days come from Laurie, the woman who travelled to Istanbul with Bérengère. What happened on that trip left her traumatized and we've agreed to protect her identity and not use her real name.
She said that within minutes of waking, Bérengère was throwing up.
"Then I started feeling unwell," Laurie said, "and suddenly we were taking turns running to the bathroom to vomit until we realized that whatever it was, it wasn't just going to pass."
They called the front desk and an ambulance took them to hospital.
‘My sister is younger than me,’ said Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino, right. ‘I’d never imagined a life without her.’ (Submitted by Deveaux-Cattino family)
'Things aren't going well'
That same day, across the ocean in Montreal, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino saw her screen light up: Laurie was FaceTiming her.

"I thought: 'This isn't normal. Something's off. This is going to be bad news,'" said Deveaux-Cattino. "She says 'Élo, we're in the hospital in Istanbul, and things aren't going well. I've been told to contact the family.'"
Deveaux-Cattino and her father, Henri Cattino, scrambled to find flights to Istanbul. While waiting for their connection in Paris, Deveaux-Cattino called the embassy.
"I said: 'Please, can you tell me if my sister has died?'" said Deveaux-Cattino. ”And she said: 'I'm very sorry, Éléonore, but your sister is dead.'"
Three days into their trip to Istanbul in November 2025, the Böcek family from Hamburg fell ill. Five days later, all four family members were dead, poisoned by phosphine gas. (@ismailsaymaz/X)
The Böcek family
The Deveaux-Cattinos repatriated Bérengère's body and asked the Quebec coroner's office to examine it. They buried their daughter and sister without confirmation of the cause of death.
As they waited for answers from Turkey, the family speculated about what else could explain Bérengère's death: Organ trafficking? Alcohol poisoning? Medical malpractice?
Then, in November, as we were investigating, a diplomatic source texted with a tip that pointed to an entirely different explanation.
"A family of four has just died in Istanbul. Watch this report."
The Böceks, a Turkish-German family from Hamburg, were visiting Istanbul. Their hotel was blocks from where Bérengère and Laurie stayed. All four fell ill and died within days of each other.

Investigators initially suspected food poisoning there, too. But within days, authorities concluded that another poison had been at work: aluminum phosphide, a highly toxic agricultural pesticide used to kill rodents and insects.
The 'bomb'

Exterminators call aluminum phosphide "the bomb." It is used in pellet form. Once the pellets are exposed to air, they release phosphine gas. Exterminators say that when placed in a sealed room, the gas kills every living, breathing thing within 72 hours. In Turkey, it's illegal to use in urban areas.
But, like all big cities, Istanbul has a bedbug problem.
Safe extermination of bedbugs
Exterminator Birkan Cihan said he can barely keep up with calls from desperate home and hotel owners. Some ask whether he treats bedbugs with "gas." He doesn't.
"We tell them their neighbours could die from it, and that they could, too. But they say: 'We have no choice, it's the only thing that works,'" Cihan said
The phosphine gas these pellets emit is so potent and volatile that it can spread through a building, even if the area being treated is sealed.
In the case of the Böcek family, fumigation in the neighbouring room was determined to be what killed all four of them.
Investigations by Enquête and the fifth estate have found similar cases. In 2012, two sisters from Quebec, Audrey and Noémi Bélanger, died of phosphine poisoning in Thailand.
In 2012, two sisters from Quebec, Audrey and Noémi Bélanger, died of phosphine poisoning in Thailand. (Submitted by Bélanger family)
'That doesn't make any sense'

Just before Christmas 2025, the Deveaux-Cattinos received the autopsy report from Turkey. It concluded that food poisoning caused Bérengère's death. Unconvinced, they handed the report to the Quebec coroner's office.

"The coroner here ran some tests, and she couldn't confirm that food poisoning was the cause of death because, usually, there are signs of intestinal irritation," Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino said. "There were none in my sister's case."
We showed the Turkish autopsy report to another Quebec pathologist. Although not authorized to speak publicly, he also questioned the autopsy's conclusions.

"Two young, healthy women who end up in the hospital with food poisoning — OK, I'll buy that. But to die of it so quickly, without any signs of bloody diarrhea or other complications, that doesn't make any sense."
Turkish freelance journalist Ayse Adanali covered the story of the death of the Böcek family in Istanbul in 2025. (Radio-Canada)
Women and children
In Turkey, we started working with Ayse Adanali, a freelance Turkish journalist who'd covered the Böcek story.
Together, we documented nearly 30 cases of phosphine poisoning, including a dozen deaths, since 2023 in Turkey.

Some were tourists, like the two Dutch teenagers found dead by their father in their Istanbul hotel room in August 2025. But most of the victims were Turkish, like Karan Yazıcı, a three-year-old boy poisoned in Istanbul in April 2025 following a fumigation in the neighbouring apartment.

The majority of the victims are women and children. Members of the same family were often poisoned together. While some survived, others died. In most cases, food poisoning was initially blamed for making them sick.
'This is not food poisoning'
Şebnem Korur Fincancı is a human rights activist, professor emeritus and leading forensic pathologist in Turkey.
She's studied aluminum phosphide and knows how difficult it is to identify victims poisoned by phosphine gas.
Turkish forensic pathologist Şebnem Korur Fincancı has studied aluminum phosphide and knows how difficult it is to identify victims poisoned by phosphine gas. (Radio-Canada)
She'd never heard about Bérengère; her death had not been covered by Turkish media.
"This is not food poisoning," she said after reading the Turkish autopsy report.
"I don't think that this is food poisoning because there is no story of diarrhea, only throwing up."
She added that the timing of Bérengère's decline suggests food poisoning couldn't be the culprit.
"Rather, it is the pesticide poisoning."

Fincancı sees one undeniable detail in this report, a finding common to all victims of phosphine gas poisoning she's examined: something called metabolic acidosis, which increases the levels of acidity in the body.
"There is the metabolic acidosis, which also indicates the pesticide intoxication," she said. 'It is one of the main findings of these kinds of cases."
She believes there could be more cases of phosphine poisoning than currently reported.
"With all these misdiagnoses, we have to consider the situation."
Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino and her friend, Laurie, stayed at the Seven Days Hotel in Istanbul. (Radio-Canada)
150 bites
We scoured hundreds of Google and Tripadvisor reviews for the Seven Days Hotel to see if they'd had a bedbug problem around the time of Bérengère and Laurie's stay.
One stood out: A tourist claiming he'd been bitten 150 times during his stay in June 2025.
We tracked him down. He confirmed he stayed in Room 107, the room next door to where the two women stayed 10 days later.
The windows in those two rooms open onto each other.
That left one critical question: Had Room 107 been treated after his stay? And, if so, with what?
We contacted hotel manager Bahattin Demir. He remembered Bérengère and Laurie and had gone to the hospital after they'd been admitted.
We told him about the tourist in Room 107 and asked him whether extermination work in that room could have killed Bérengère.
"I don't think so, because if it was that product, I'm sure that, you know, everybody would have this problem," he said.
Inside Room 108 at the Seven Days Hotel where Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino and Laurie stayed. (Radio-Canada)
He said exterminators spray the rooms in the hotel monthly. He offered to contact them and find out what product they use, but then wrote back, referring us to them for more details.
The extermination company is called Wolves.
A contact called them for us. We're protecting her identity because undercover work can lead to jail time in Turkey.
Posing as an Air BnB owner in Istanbul's Fatih district, she claimed to be struggling with bedbugs.
The employee was cautious on the phone.
He didn't name the product specifically, but his detailed description is similar to how aluminum phosphide is used.
"For 72 hours, nobody goes in, the doors are locked and nothing living enters."

items: Deaths of Quebec women in Thailand may have been caused by pesticide
Phosphine pesticide used to kill bedbugs causes Fort McMurray baby's death

blocks.text: We called Wolves for an interview. The employee who answered the phone was not authorized to speak, but denied using aluminum phosphide.
Neither the hospital that treated Bérengère nor the Forensic Medical Centre where her autopsy was performed replied to our inquiries.
The tourism police similarly declined our interview request.

Going over notes Laurie had shared, we noticed she and Bérengère had left the window open the first night. But the next evening, to avoid being woken by the call to prayer, they closed it and turned on the air conditioning. And that was the night they got sick.
We asked pathologist Şebnem Korur Fincancı whether phosphine gas residue could build up in air conditioners.
"Of course," she said.
'Those who are gone'

The Böceks' case went to trial in June 2026. The defendants were charged with criminal negligence causing the deaths of this family of four. The ruling came down within days. The owners of the extermination company were found guilty and sentenced to 18 years in prison. The hotel owner and employees received 12 to 13 years.
While awaiting the verdict, the paternal grandfather, Yilmaz Böcek, commented that even the stiffest penalty could never bring back his children and grandchildren.
"Those who are gone never come back."
Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino wants Bérengère to be remembered.
"My sister is younger than me. I'd never imagined a life without her. We used to be two against the world … now I'm all alone," she said.
"But I'm stubborn. And since she can no longer speak, I'll speak for her. I'll never let her go."

In the summer of 2026, the government of Canada added a new entry to its travel advisory for Turkey, alerting travellers to "cases of poisoning linked to the use of chemical pesticides in tourist accommodations in Istanbul."
After this story first aired on Oct. 15, 2026, Turkish consular officials contacted us, confirming the investigation into Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino's death in Istanbul remains open.

articles.title: Marcos signs law expanding vouchers for K to 12 students in private schools
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has signed into law a measure that institutionalizes government vouchers to help eligible Filipino students pay tuition at private schools, particularly…
articles.byline: JON VIKTOR D. CABUENAS, GMA News

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 4:26pm

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has signed into law a measure that institutionalizes government vouchers to help eligible Filipino students pay tuition at private schools, particularly those who cannot access nearby public schools due to overcrowding or distance.

Under Republic Act No. 12327, or the Basic Education Voucher Assistance Act, signed on November 12, the government will provide financial assistance to Filipino students from middle-middle-income households and below, or those belonging to equivalent income classifications.
The law mandates the Department of Education (DepEd) to implement the program and determine the eligibility requirements, voucher amounts, and participating private schools.

“To achieve quality education, the State shall address classroom backlog and congestion of public schools through the Basic Education Voucher Assistance Act, which shall form part of the broader national strategy to address quality education by resolving classroom shortage,” the law states.

Voucher assistance may be provided, in order of priority, to students enrolled in public schools identified by DepEd as congested, those living in areas without nearby public schools, and those residing in communities with congested public schools.
A public school may be considered congested if its enrollment exceeds classroom capacity based on DepEd standards, or if it has resorted to multiple shifts or alternative delivery modes.

Students living in areas without a nearby public school may also qualify, including senior high school students in areas where public schools do not offer subjects or electives aligned with their chosen pathways. The law defines the covered area as within a walkable distance of three kilometers from the student's residence.

The program budget will be distributed equitably among all regions, including the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), based on official data on public school congestion, available capacity, and open seats, with priority given to areas with the highest public school congestion.

Qualified beneficiaries and their families will be allowed to choose their preferred private basic education institution from a registry maintained by the DepEd. Schools will be required to provide information on their location, available slots, student capacity, tuition fees, and other relevant details.

The law requires DepEd to implement safeguards against fraud, including a centralized system for verifying learner eligibility, stronger audit and monitoring procedures, and mechanisms to protect whistleblowers.

Schools or individuals found to have committed fraud or other prohibited acts may face administrative and legal penalties, such as suspension, disqualification from the program, reimbursement of funds, blacklisting, and prosecution.

The law also requires the government to disburse payments to participating schools within 60 days after the submission of complete documents to the DepEd. Local government units, private sponsors, and other scholarship providers may supplement the assistance.

It also assists private basic education institutions and their teachers, including in-service teacher training, teachers’ salary subsidies, scholarships for qualified private school teachers, and support for school development.

The program will initially cover kindergarten and elementary students beginning in School Year 2027-2028. Meanwhile, existing beneficiaries of the Educational Service Contracting Scheme and the Senior High School Voucher Program will continue to receive assistance until they complete basic education. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Andy Burnham heads to Brussels as UK and EU close in on Brexit reset deal – live
articles.summary:
UK and EU have provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme.

Senior correspondent

France’s insistence…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 2m agoUK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries
10m agoRow over voting rights dispels myths that UK comes to negotiations from position of strength - snap analysis
16m agoTalks went down to the wire this morning
17m agoMorning opening: Second post-Brexit EU-UK summit gets under way in Brussels

blocks.text: UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries
Rajeev Syal and Lisa O’Carroll
The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document.

blocks.caption: A migrant leaves an abandoned warehouse, where some migrants are taking shelter during the winter months, in Marck, near Calais, northern France. Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”.
Until now, the Home Office has been seeking bilateral agreements with third countries allowing the removal of migrants, but with no obvious success.
Last week, five EU countries – Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands – announced an agreement in principle with Rwanda to establish a migrant “return hub” there in 2027.

Burnham hinted at possible cooperation with EU countries last week when he told reporters that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that [the five-country deal] with interest, learning from what went on in the past”. He said: “The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
The UK has been fighting for deeper cooperation with the EU on migration, with the new deal on a “strategic dialogue” secured in the last two weeks by negotiators in Brussels.

It is a key part of the UK-EU reset pact, which also covers a youth mobility scheme, tariffs on Chinese imports, food and drink exports to the EU and a wider restatement of commitment on defence and security.
Informed sources confirmed this was the first time the UK and the EU had agreed to “open a dialogue on returns” after the launch of the bloc’s Channel action plan in June this year.
Whitehall sources said the UK was now open to the possibility of sending rejected claimants to Rwanda – a recent pivot from the position under Keir Starmer’s government, which rejected the move.
According to a draft of the joint agreement, negotiations over third-country hubs will be part of increased cooperation to tackle irregular migration.
Row over voting rights dispels myths that UK comes to negotiations from position of strength - snap analysis

blocks.caption: Lisa O’Carroll

blocks.text: Lisa O’Carroll
Senior correspondent

France’s insistence that the UK could not have voting rights at any stage during the shaping of legislation on food standards and public health risks relating to food and agri products is a line in the sand for Andy Burnham.

blocks.caption: Journalists arrive as preparations are made for the EU-UK Summit at the European Council building in Brussels. Photograph: Virginia Mayo/AP

blocks.text: The last night tensions at the ambassadors meeting will be a sharp lesson for anyone in the UK who clings to the idea that negotiating with the EU comes from a position of strength: the UK is not a member of the EU and despite the warm feelings to the Labour government in European capitals, benefits of the club are not extended to non members.
It also underlines the feeling expressed by several large member states this week that the way forward after this summit is not more iterative reset summits or mini-deals.

Yes, there will be negotiations on allowing the UK into the energy single market as this is in the joint interests of both sides in the wake of the Ukraine war. But no talks on pharma or chemicals, according to some capitals.
As one diplomat said:
“It puts down a marker warning the UK that cherry picking bits of the single market mean you are a rule taker.”
“It makes the choice for Britain starker and more binary” and shows that “the alternatives are basically muddling along with a version of the status quo or rejoining,” they said.

blocks.caption: Jennifer Rankin

blocks.text: Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels
UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be welcomed with a rendition of God Save the King and the Ode to Joy when he attends the opening ceremony around 10.30am local time.

blocks.caption: Musicians rehearse the British national anthem and the European anthem ahead of the EU-UK summit in Brussels, Belgium. Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPA

blocks.text: Talks went down to the wire this morning
Talks to seal today’s reset in relations between the UK and the EU went write down to the wire this morning.
In what is known as a “silence procedure”, the EU issued a late night compromise text to all member states after a meeting of crunch hours long meeting of ambassadors in Brussels last night.
Under the procedure if no member states breaks the silence the text is considered “adopted” and would then be made available for signing by the UK – bar any last minute hitches on its side.
This morning diplomats said “no one had broken the silence”. The headline agreements are:

items: Food and drink deal, setting up sanitary and phyto sanitary common area
An electricity carbon emissions deal
Cap of 100,000 EU citizens under 31 years old to come to the UK under a new youth mobility scheme
The issue of tuition fees kicked down the road - a supplementary agreement has been reached to sort this out within the next six months
This allows the UK to hold up the youth deal if the EU does not give it what it needs in the Made in Europe legislation which is expected to reach its final negotiations stages by Easter too.

No voting rights for the UK when the EU comes to writing new laws about food standards; this was never a realistic option as the UK is not a member of the EU, but the French led the resistance as the UK pushed for it equally as hard, instead the UK will be consullted at key stages
Industry groups say that must mean UK regulators are in the room at the early stages. Food regulation is very technical, the say and this is where the real decisions are taken.
The two sides will also open talks on UK entering the energy single market.

blocks.text: Morning opening: Second post-Brexit EU-UK summit gets under way in Brussels

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc.

blocks.caption: A member of protocol arranges the Union flag and EU flag as preparations are made for the EU-UK Summit at the European Council building in Brussels. Photograph: Virginia Mayo/AP

blocks.text: It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa.
As our Brussels correspondent, Jennifer Rankin, explained:

“The two sides hope to announce three deals, which were initiated under Starmer’s government. First, a food and drink agreement that will remove a lot of Brexit red tape on animal and plant products, making it easier to trade meats, cheese, wine and flowers. To secure the deal, which is not expected to take effect until 2028, the UK will align with EU standards, meaning the government, for example, must abandon a planned ban on foie gras imports. A second agreement will link the British emissions trading system with its bigger EU cousin, restoring a link severed by Brexit. It is a significant step for industry because EU and UK businesses will be exempt from each other’s charges on high-carbon imports such as steel, cement and electricity. This agreement also requires alignment with relevant EU rules. The third deal has proved the most contentious: a youth mobility scheme that will give those aged 18-31 the right to live, work, travel and study on both sides of the Channel for up to three years. The scheme may not be up and running until 2030 – which is bad news for anyone in their late 20s.”
The leaders are expected to arrive 9.30am GMT (10.30am Brussels time), with “the leaders’ meeting” between Burnham, von der Leyen and Costa to follow.

A plenary session with UK ministers and EU commissioners is expected at 10.45am GMT (11.45am Brussels), and if all goes well we should then see the leaders tell us what they agreed around half past midday (1.30pm Brussels time).
I will bring you every single detail of the day here today. You won’t miss a thing.
It’s Friday, 20 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.summary: The House prosecution panel raised questions Friday regarding the alleged possible connection of Vice President Sara Duterte's tree planting activities with Cale88 Foods Corporation.

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 4:11pm
The House prosecution panel raised questions Friday regarding the alleged possible connection of Vice President Sara Duterte's tree planting activities with Cale88 Foods Corporation.

Cale88, the food firm linked to Duterte's husband Manases Carpio, has come under scrutiny during the vice president's impeachment trial over its profits earned with only two employees and its supposed financial inflows from China.
During the cross examination of Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo on Day 45 of the trial, private prosecutor Erwin Matib flashed photos of Duterte planting trees.
The defense counsel initially objected on the basis of relevance, but Presiding Officer Francis Escudero allowed Matib to continue, granted that he is on a short leash.

"Tama po ba na itong pagtatanim ng mga puno ni Vice President Sara Duterte ay connected sa pag-comply ng Cale88 Foods sa tree planting activities na requirement ng Board of Investment? In fact, ang requirement ng Board of Investment ay magtanim dapat ang enterprises ng at least 100 forest trees. May ganoong requirement, tama po ba?" Matib said.

(Is it correct that Vice President Sara Duterte tree planting is connected with with Cale88's compliance with the tree planting requirements of the Board of Investment? In fact, the requirement of the Board of Investment is to plant at least 100 forest trees. There is a requirement for this, right?)
Before Rodolfo could answer, defense counsel Justin Gular objected.

"Objection, your honor, misleading. There is no prior testimony coming from the witness wherein he testified that the vice president participated in the compliance requirement of tree planting," Gullar said.

"The insinuation being made by the prosecution that the pictures being shown or that was displayed of the vice president planting trees had any relation to Cale88 Foods Corporation's registration is misleading, malicious and callous, your honor," he added.
Escudero sustained Gular's objection, telling Matib to carry on to the next point.
Rodolfo affirmed that tree planting was part of Board of Investment's (BOI) requirements. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Vape users hospitalised after losing consciousness, prompting public health warning in New South Wales
articles.summary:
NSW health issues public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas

Three people who lost consciousness and…

blocks.text: Three people who lost consciousness and were hospitalised in New South Wales after using certain vapes have tested positive for the unregulated anaesthetic agent etomidate, health officials have said.

NSW health on Friday issued a public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia.
The three people who were hospitalised had used non-nicotine refillable vapes, the state health department said. Testing of their blood and urine confirmed the presence of etomidate.
The department would not confirm how old the three patients were, where they were hospitalised, or their condition on Friday.
The discovery of etomidate in vapes in NSW comes about four months after Victorian health officials announced they had found the powerful anaesthetic agent in an illicit vape sold in Melbourne.
On Friday, NSW health warned vapes sold as space pods, space oil, kpods, piu piu vapes, or zombie vapes may contain etomidate, or other substances, including ketamine, THC and potent opioids.
The medical director of the NSW poisons information centre, Dr Darren Roberts, said etomidate’s effects were unpredictable when used in a vape.
Roberts said etomidate could cause confusion, drowsiness, slow breathing, vomiting, muscle spasms or movements that were hard to control, and people who took it could become unresponsive.
These effects could be life threatening, especially if used with other drugs that could cause sedation, such as alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, and GHB, Roberts said.
He said etomidate could also cause long term harm when used regularly, including the disruption of hormones produced by the adrenal gland.
These hormones are important in regulating stress responses and need to be replaced if they aren’t produced naturally, he said.
“The contents found in non-nicotine vapes vary,” Roberts said. “You can’t assume what’s inside.”
He urged anyone considering using a vape to ask themselves what could be in it.
“You won’t get into trouble for seeking medical care,” he said. If you feel unwell, or if your friend feels unwell, after using a vape, do something about it.”
NSW health officials said it recommended people administer Naloxone to anyone who became responsive after using any drug, in case they had ingested opioids.
Naloxone is an opioid overdose treatment, which is free at pharmacies and does not require a prescription.
Naloxone won’t reverse the effects of etomidate, as the sedative does not belong to the opioid class of drugs, but it is still safe to give, health officials said.
The officials said anyone who witnessed someone experiencing unexpected symptoms after using drugs should call triple zero immediately or seek urgent medical attention.

articles.title: Baby born with heart abnormalities ‘didn’t have a chance’ after non-medical free birth, NSW inquest hears
articles.summary:
Inquest into the deaths of four babies after free and home births hears routine checks and follow-up may have saved their lives

Four babies who died in New South Wales – three after free…

blocks.text: Four babies who died in New South Wales – three after free births and one after a home birth – might have survived if they had had routine checks and follow-up , a coronial inquest has heard.
Baby DH, Baby D, Baby R, and Baby B died in the state’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024.
The inquest in Lismore has heard women chose free or home births for reasons including traumatic experiences, a lack of trust in clinicians, and a lack of services.

Baby DH died about eight hours after he was born in a free birth – with a doula but no medical professionals present. The court earlier heard he turned purple, was struggling to breathe and had became floppy.
His parents gave evidence they were worried but the doula kept reassuring them their baby was OK, then left.
The doula denied many of their claims, and denied that she gave them any clinical advice.

Expert neonatologist, associate professor Nicholas Evans, said on Friday Baby DH’s complex heart abnormalities “would have been readily detectable” in a routine pregnancy scan after which he would have been referred to a paediatric cardiologist.
It was a “missed opportunity”, he told the court.
Paediatric cardiologist Dr Paul Brooks said it was “highly likely” all the abnormalities would have been identified in a routine scan before birth.
Even if the extent of the abnormalities wasn’t clear, he told the court, the scan would have shown the baby needed to be born at a major hospital with cardiac surgery capabilities.
“The site of [Baby DH’s] birth meant that he didn’t have a chance.”
Baby D’s mother did not know she was having twins, and at first thought she’d delivered Baby D’s placenta, only to realise it was a stillborn second twin.

Experts at the inquest agreed it was impossible to know exactly why Baby D died. They discussed the possibility it was because self-described birth keeper Sita Tara Kali did not clamp the umbilical cord before cutting it, but ultimately, Evans told the court, it was most likely from respiratory distress because of his compromised heart function.

Baby D might have survived if someone who could do advanced resuscitation arrived in under 10 minutes, he said, but the “root cause” was that it was not known the mother was carrying twins before the births.
“If [twins] had been diagnosed, at 18 weeks, as it would usually in pregnancy, there would have been very close monitoring.”

Baby R likely died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day in a free birth. The standard is to induce birth or perform a caesarean section at 42 weeks, as the ageing placenta puts the baby at risk.
The mother had been for an ultrasound at 12 weeks, which had put the date of birth at 28 July, 2020.
But the mother distrusted hospitals and trusted Kali, her birth keeper, the court previously heard.
Kali told her to calculate her due date from the date of conception, an unreliable measure that put the date of birth in mid August.
That recalculation, Evans wrote in his report to the court, was the “root cause” of the issue.
“The standard practice now is that you don’t allow a pregnancy to go beyond 42 completed weeks,” Evans said on Friday.
Expert midwives earlier told the court they don’t have statistics for babies born beyond 43 weeks, because it’s so rare.

A 19 August ultrasound showed the pregnancy had become a medical emergency – but Kali advised her to “go home and rest”. It is “more likely than not” that the baby would have survived had she gone to hospital after the ultrasound, Evans said.

Baby B’s mother was warned multiple times that she needed to go to hospital to give birth to her twins, but she was determined to have a home birth. Rather than let her have a free birth, four midwives assisted her and the head midwife repeatedly counselled her about the risks.
The mother declined ultrasounds as well as a test for early onset group B streptococcus (GBS) – an organism present in 15 to 20% of women that infects the babies of about 2% of carriers.
Baby B likely died of GBS, pneumonia and sepsis, Evans told the court on Friday, while his twin fell ill but survived. Many infected babies survive in hospital thanks to antibiotics, he added.
The inquest is ongoing.
