articles.summary: Orla Guerin speaks to seven people trapped in Taiz by the Houthis who reveal what life is like under siege.

blocks.text: Image source, Ahmad Al-Basha/AFP via Getty Images
Houthi attacks on Taiz have killed more than 140 civilians since August, local government officials say
ByOrla Guerin
Senior international correspondentReporting fromIstanbul
In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.

"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."
Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.
Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.
Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.

They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Burning piles of rubbish are producing toxic smoke that hangs over the city

blocks.text: Burning piles of rubbish are producing toxic smoke that hangs over the city

On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.
From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.
Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.

Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.
"Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.

"It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous."
She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.
"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Taiz has been a major battleground in Yemen's civil war for more than a decade

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Taiz has been a major battleground in Yemen's civil war for more than a decade
War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.
Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.

More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.

In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.
A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.
In Taiz, it is a threat to survival.

blocks.caption: Four-panel map series showing the expansion of Houthi-controlled territory in western and southern Yemen between August and November 2026. Houthi-held areas are shaded pink. Top left (August 2026): Houthi forces control much of western Yemen, including Sanaa, and launch an offensive south along t…

blocks.text: An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.
Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.

The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him."
Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.
They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.
He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Taiz's hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity and 120 health centres have closed, its governor says

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Taiz's hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity and 120 health centres have closed, its governor says
If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards.
"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.
It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us.
"The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents."
He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.
On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.

He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.
The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.
That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.

blocks.caption: 3D satellite graphic showing Houthi-controlled territory (red) and contested areas (purple) around the government-controlled city of Taiz, southern Yemen, as of 18 November 2026

blocks.text: What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.
He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.

"Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".
Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.
How long can the city hold out, I ask.
"Until the population perishes," he replies.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling

blocks.text: Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling
Many in Taiz are resisting.
They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.
They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.
Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.
Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.

When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.
Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.
He tells us this fight is different to 2015.
"This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he says. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves."
He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.
But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He says that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".
The armed group is currently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union.
"They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Almost 350,000 people have been displaced by the fighting in recent months

blocks.text: Almost 350,000 people have been displaced by the fighting in recent months
But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest.
"Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes."
The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he says, "because we don't see any move to help us."
Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.
But could they fight their way in?
Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does.
"Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says.
His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.
Like Ashwaq, the teacher, he tries to explain it away.
"I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party."
As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community.
"Please don't forget Taiz," she says. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports."
Additional reporting by Wietske Burema and Albaraa Mansoor

articles.title: From premature baby to social media star - Famed hippo Fiona dies
articles.summary: The beloved hippopotamus died days after swallowing a knitted hat that accidentally got into her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo.

blocks.text: The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona has died just days after swallowing a knitted hat that slipped into her enclosure.

Fiona was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo in 2017 and at first struggled to survive. At birth, she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species. She reached 1,000 lbs in 2018.

Over the years, Fiona became a favourite among visitors and a star on social media. This video captures moments from her life, from her early days as a calf to celebrating her fifth birthday and receiving treatment just a few days ago.

articles.title: Putin proposes second humanitarian ceasefire — is it a trap?
articles.summary: Russian President Putin has suggested evacuating civilians from the embattled Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka. But experts warn this could serve military, not humanitarian, aims. What should Kyiv do?

image.caption: A Ukrainian soldier from an anti-drone unit patrols a street in Kostiantynivka (January 2026)Image: Diego Herrera Carcedo/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a humanitarian mission in the city of Kostiantynivka similar to a recent operation in Oleshky. According to Putin, Russia has control of the city in the Donbas; the remaining civilian population, he says, could be evacuated. It would take five days to clear the access roads. The Russian leader has suggested that human rights organizations from Ukraine and Russia and delegates from the foreign press be incorporated into the mission.

Putin's proposal comes after discussions between the Russian government and US representatives, who have been negotiating to try to bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. Experts say that while Russia is indicating a readiness to make agreements, at the same time it is propagating its own depiction of the situation on the front line.

In July, Russia announced that it had taken Kostiantynivka but did not provide any proof. Ukraine says the fighting there is still ongoing. Experts from the Ukrainian open-source interactive map of military operations project DeepState say that the city is still controlled by the Ukrainian army, but that the situation there is "extremely difficult."

blocks.caption: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visited the main command post of a brigade defending Kostiantynivka in March 2026Image: Ukrainian Presidential Press Service/AFP

blocks.text: Responding to the proposal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists: "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city." He emphasized that Ukraine had always given the civilian population in Kostiantynivka opportunities to leave, and said that Russia had used the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky to bring military equipment and weapons into the city.
What is the situation for civilians?

Kostiantynivka is the southernmost city in the so-called Donetsk "fortress belt," which also includes Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. Taking Kostiantynivka would open the way for Russian troops to advance to Druzhkivka, and on to the conurbation of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military expert at the Dmytro Tymchuk Center for Security Studies, a Ukrainian think tank, said Kostiantynivka's role is similar to that of Bakhmut, Avdiivka or Chasiv Yar — towns whose defensive installations were able to hold back Russian enemy forces for years.

Local authorities say the humanitarian situation in the city, whose population before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion was around 70,000, is catastrophic and that some 340 civilians remain. They add thatKostiantynivkahas no central water, electricity or gas supplies, there is no public transport, and since the spring of 2026 people have only been able to evacuate on foot.

"Those who stayed in Kostiantynivka need to be evacuated, they need a chance of a better life," military analyst Denys Popovych told DW. However, he added that an evacuation was virtually impossible without a ceasefire, as Russian troops had occupied the road between the town and Druzhkivka and drones were being deployed throughout the region. Ukraine, therefore, could not carry out such an operation unilaterally. "It still takes two to tango — to evacuate the people, that is," he said.
Humanitarian proposals as leverage

Kovalenko believes that Moscow is simply using the humanitarian issue for purposes of manipulation and to strengthen its negotiating position. The Russian army, he said, wants to gain time in order to reinforce units fighting in the vicinity.

Yevhen Zakharov, the director of the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group, has similar concerns. "I'm afraid that this proposal by the Russians has very different objectives to those they claim to pursue," he told DW. He described Putin's initiative as suspect, and said the Ukrainian side should treat it with the utmost caution.

blocks.caption: The aftermath of a Russian attack on a residential building in Kostiantynivka in November 2024Image: Ukrinform/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Kyiv is in a difficult position, as the idea of a mission for Kostiantynivka is also being pushed by US intermediaries. "If we reject it, they'll say to us: 'You're rejecting peace proposals, you're not taking care of your own citizens, why should we keep talking to you, Zelenskyy wants to continue the war.' This is precisely the calculation behind it all," said Popovych.
Ceasefire as military tactic

After the end of the ceasefire in Oleshky, which was in place from October 27 to November 1, the Ukrainian General Staff announced that, in that time, the Russians had rotated their troops, entrenched their positions, reinforced measures to repel drones and brought in ammunition.

Kovalenko is convinced that the reason Russia is proposing a ceasefire is because its army is gradually losing ground in Kostiantynivka. From Moscow's perspective, the Russian troops that are meant to be storming the city are in urgent need of reinforcements, which they can't get because of the fighting on the ground.

"If a so-called humanitarian mission were to take place in Kostiantynivka, it would be a disaster for Kyiv, because Russia would use that time to consolidate forces that would enable it to take the city," he warned.

blocks.caption: Apartment buildings and a church in Kostiantynivka were damaged in Russian attacks in December 2025Image: National Police of Ukraine/AFP

blocks.text: How should Kyiv respond to Moscow's proposal?

Popovych, however, does not think Ukraine should reject the Russian proposal. In his view, Kyiv should base its tactics on experiences with previous ceasefires and insist on very clear conditions in advance. "If there is a ceasefire, soldiers currently at their posts should stay there and not move," he suggested.

Oleksandr Pavlichenko from the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union believes Ukraine should submit a counter-proposal, which envisages the withdrawal of Russian troops from the Ukrainian city and the unimpeded departure of the civilian population.

The human rights activist said that, for a genuine humanitarian mission to be put in place, a strong, neutral third party should be brought in to supervise and ensure safe passage. In his view, the only party with such a mandate is the International Committee of the Red Cross. "If a proposal comes from only one side, and from a side such as Russia, it doesn't inspire confidence," he said.
This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
articles.summary: Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will…

image.caption: 'We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming,' Beatrice Atim Anywar, Uganda's environment minister, told DWImage: DW

blocks.text: Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.

"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods."

In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.
"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change.
"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.

blocks.caption: People search for missing belongings buried under landslides triggered by heavy rainfall in Kaptang village in Uganda in October 2025Image: Abubaker Lubowa/REUTERS

blocks.text: Climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.
Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.
Ramping up electricity production
As it deals with the affects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.

In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.

While using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.

"Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar said. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives."
As pipeline nears finish, resistance in Uganda holds firm
Drilling for oil

At the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.

Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.
The Climate Accountability Institute said it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.
Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.

"That has been also a sticky issue. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way."

blocks.caption: Climate activists in New York protesting JP Morgan Chase bank's support of Total Energies East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP), which is displacing farmers in Uganda and TanzaniaImage: picture alliance / ZUMAPRESS.com

blocks.text: The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.

"You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar said, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming."
Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.
Carbon trading 'breakthrough?'
Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar said, describing them as a potential "breakthrough."

Carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.
"Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar said.

blocks.caption: Uganda is rich in biodiversity, including lush tropical forests with plenty of wildlifeImage: C. Kaiser/blickwinkel/picture alliance

blocks.text: Carbon credits have been promoted as an important source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.

"We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar said, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.
"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed."
This interview also appeared as a video.

articles.title: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel
articles.summary:
Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent

The

blocks.text: The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.

In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.
The lengthy judgment will have been read particularly carefully by Israel, the only other country currently before the ICJ accused of genocide.
It is also relevant to Germany, which has been brought before the court by Nicaragua on the accusation it has facilitated and failed to prevent genocide in Gaza.

“I think it’s a judgment that brings the genocide convention alive,” said Philippe Sands, a leading human rights lawyer who was part of the Gambian legal team. “It gives the convention practical, real meaning. And if the alternative view had been taken, the convention would essentially become a dead letter.”

Amnesty International’s secretary general, Agnès Callamard, called the ruling “a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”. But it was also an assertion of humanitarian law in an increasingly lawless world.

“This is a good day for international law. We needed it,” said Dr Iva Vukušić, an assistant professor in international History at Utrecht University and a war crimes expert. “It is really important, clarifying a lot of law, and that’s going to be very helpful going forward.”

There will be a spillover from this ruling to its sister tribunal in The Hague, the international criminal court (ICC), providing a benchmark for when genocide charges could be made against individual perpetrators.

The Trump administration, instinctively hostile to international legal institutions, is also watching critically. The US ambassador to the UN told the ICJ before this judgment not to “lower the legal threshold for proving genocide” lest it be “weaponised” against US and allied soldiers.
The court did not directly lower the standard for demonstrating genocide, and the Gambia – which brought the case to The Hague – did not ask it to.

The judges kept the existing benchmark for judging genocide intent as the “only reasonable inference” of Myanmar’s actions and referred extensively to prior case law. But it went a long way towards clarifying how that standard should be applied in assessing atrocity crimes committed by states.

Before this case, only Serbia had faced the charge of genocide at the ICJ, in cases brought by Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Bosnian ruling in 2007, Belgrade was found to have failed to prevent the 1995 genocide in Srebrenica, but in both cases it was cleared of committing the genocide directly.

The new ICJ judgment finds the Myanmar military directly responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority targeted in a ferocious counterinsurgency campaign that reached its peak in 2017.

In assessing the Myanmar campaign, the ICJ looked not just at the death toll of about 10,000 in assessing the scale of the atrocities, but at the total Rohingya population targeted in northern Rakhine state, 815,000 people. Significantly, it cast its net wider than just the death toll, considering mental damage done to the survivors, particularly victims of sexual violence, and the impact on reproduction in the Rohingya community.

Most importantly, the ICJ judgment provided a guide to interpreting the standard set by Serbian cases, in which a finding of genocide could be made only if there were not other plausible motives for mass killing.

In this judgment, the court ruled that Myanmar could have had other motives, such as the desire to displace or punish the Rohingya population, but that those motives could exist alongside genocidal intent. The judges said genocidal intent was the “only reasonable inference” from the “totality” of evidence.

In justifying that conclusion the judges pointed to several factors that international law experts say are relevant to the Gaza case, which is now hearing written pleadings and is expected to take at least another three years.

The common factors include the targeting of children, which the court described as striking at the “foundation” of the Rohingya as a group – the ICJ said up to 2,109 Rohingya children under the age of five had been killed, while more than 5,000 Palestinian children under five years old have been killed in the Gaza war.

Another incriminating factor cited by the court was the “bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance” after the destruction of villages, followed by “rapid construction” including security installations, which has been the hallmark of Israeli army occupation of over 60% of the Gaza Strip.

“It’s full of messages for Israel,” said William Schabas, an international law professor and expert on genocide at Middlesex University. “There are obvious differences, of course, the evidence will be different, but if you exchanged the word Myanmar with Israel, you wouldn’t have to change much in the judgment.”

The fact that there were six dissenting voices on the bench suggested that substantial parts of the majority’s reasoning were not beyond dispute, and lawyers involved in the case cautioned that it did not necessarily mean that the same bench would find Israel guilty of genocide in Gaza. But the same lawyers added that the opposite was almost certainly true. If this case had failed, the case brought by South Africa against Israel would have been all but over.

articles.title: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
articles.summary:
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake

Donald Trump was, again,

blocks.text: Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.

Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump, California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway.
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.

“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump with his eyes closed during an NBA finals game between the Spurs and the Knicks at Madison Square Garden in New York on 8 June 2026.   Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep. Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump apparently asleep next Pete Hegseth at the White House on 2 December 2025.  Photograph: Carolyn Van Houten/The Washington Post/Getty Images

blocks.text: Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News.

Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health, often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

articles.title: ‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling
articles.summary:
Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world

There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands…

blocks.text: There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.

For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.

By the time they spilled into the court’s halls, the relief was evident. A Rohingya community leader threw a big thumbs up as he left the courtroom and others immediately took out their phones to call family in the refugee camps.

Salma, 30, a Rohingya survivor who lost family members in the 2017 genocide, said: “Everyone worked hard and struggled for this justice, for this cause. When they hear it today, everyone will be happy, thank God. I don’t know how to express it or even what to do with myself.”

blocks.caption: The Gambian justice minister Dawda Jallow, centre, speaking at the ICJ in The Hague on Thursday: ‘The victory belongs to the Rohingya. They survived. They testified. And today, they will believe.’ Photograph: Jeroen Jumelet/ANP/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Another Rohingya present, who cannot be named because of safety concerns, said they cried as the judge went through each of the rulings.

“During the last few minutes I couldn’t even sit down any more, I had to move to the back because I didn’t know how I’d react,” they said. “I saw some of the other Rohingya around me crying. They were so emotional.
“Now the responsibility is with the international governments. It has been declared genocide now and they have to act.”

In Bangladesh, where most of the Rohingya population have lived – in the world’s largest refugee camp – since being forced to flee in 2017, the verdict was translated into the Rohingya language for the crowds who had gathered to watch on screens specially set up for the purpose.

They immediately leapt up, cheering, applauding and shouting gratitude for the Gambia – the faraway African nation that brought the case to the ICJ on behalf of the stateless minority. Many held posters that read “Thank You Gambia” and “Justice = Safe Return”.

“Since we arrived here, we have been waiting and looking forward to this justice,” said Farida Khatun, 50, who has been a refugee in Bangladesh since 2017, when her village, Tula Toli, was targeted by soldiers. The village in north-western Myanmar, near the Bangladesh border, was the scene of a massacre in August of that year, with reports of mass killings and gang rapes.

She said, however, that she does not expect to be able to return home. Tula Toli was completely destroyed by Myanmar’s forces and no longer exists. “Even though today’s verdict makes us happy, my heart still cannot believe that they will take us back in true peace.”

The case has taken seven years to reach this point, with Rohingya researchers working to collect testimony from survivors. The initial hope for justice had faded during the long wait for a ruling. Many were also left deflated during early hearings when the one-time pro-democracy hero Aung San Suu Kyi defended the Myanmar military at The Hague.

blocks.caption: Yusuf Ali, a Rohingya justice campaigner, outside the ICJ in The Hague on the day of the ruling.  Photograph: Kaamil Ahmed/The Guardian

blocks.text: Before today’s ruling, some were optimistic, others were prepared to be disappointed, but all said they knew themselves that they were victims of genocide.

The tension was finally released when the court declared Myanmar was responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, highlighting the use of sexual violence and attacks on children alongside the killing of Rohingya who tried to flee violence, which it said meant the violence amounted to more than ethnic cleansing.
The court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations for the Rohingya and end continuing breaches of the genocide convention.

blocks.caption: Rohingya refugees in Cox’s Bazar thank the Gambia for its role as they watch a live broadcast of the ICJ Myanmar genocide ruling.  Photograph: Yassin Abdumonab/EPA

blocks.text: There is now also an international criminal court investigation into the violence of 2017, looking specifically at the crime of mass deportation, and for which prosecutors in 2024 sought an arrest warrant for Myanmar’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing.
With continuing violence against the Rohingya, the possibility of a return to Myanmar, as happened after previous exoduses to Bangladesh in 1978 and the early 1990s, remains unlikely.
But many hope the ICJ ruling will be the start of a process of ensuring justice and lead to real international pressure to ensure their safety in Myanmar.
“We will be able to return to our homeland – with our rights, with our citizenship, and having received our full security. We will be able to return,” says Salma.

articles.title: Anthropic trading tests investors' appetite for AI
articles.summary: Shares in Anthropic start trading on the Nasdaq after its record $81 billion IPO. Its performance will put investor confidence in AI and the Claude maker's $1.5 trillion valuation to the test.

image.caption: Anthropic's public listing is being seen as a key test of investors' confidence AI will continue to make them moneyImage: Dado Ruvic/REUTERS

blocks.text: Shares of US artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic see their first day of trading on Thursday on the US tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange.
Anthropic is one of the global leaders in AI technology and is best known for its Claude chatbot.

Actual trading data is delayed, however, as the Nasdaq matches millions of buy and sell orders to set a starting price. With mega-IPOs like Anthropic's, the first real-time trades are expected 2 to 4 hours after the opening bell.
The company's share performance is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.
The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude AI tool has offered 980 million shares at $83 (€76) per share, raising a record $81 billion.
This valued the firm at $1.5 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.
First of the AI giants to go public
Anthropic is the first big AI company to go public. Its main competitor, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI, has reportedly pushed its IPO to 2027.
Issuing shares on the stock market is essentially a way to raise money and avoid taking on debt.
Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt and is not yet making a profit. At the same time, it faces massive bills for computer power and data centers.
That specific financial situation is one of the reasons for persistent concern that the AI boom might be a bubble that will eventually burst.

articles.title: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
articles.summary: Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’

blocks.text: China, Russia and the US have said they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran triggered by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.

The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.

blocks.caption: Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Donald Trump in front of the other world leaders at the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP

blocks.text: “We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and a “mutual understanding” had taken place.

Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed advances by Trump to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.

The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued before by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK. “The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.

Analysts had warned that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.

First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”

The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.

Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”

Xi, his status as a global powerbroker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. He made an appeal for regional harmony, saying: “Members of Apec are like passengers riding the same ship. To navigate the waves of the Pacific, we must unite as one and look out for each other.”

blocks.caption: Trump shakes hands with Xi Jinping. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP

blocks.text: However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce.

Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – with the US president calling the Russian his “friend”. The peace declaration said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.

Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he warned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.

Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.

Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

articles.title: No mention of fossil fuels in latest COP31 draft deal
articles.summary: One of the most fraught debates at the UN climate talks in Turkey has revolved around the future of coal, oil and gas. Now all mention of fossil fuels has been removed from the summit's new draft…

image.caption: Protestors at the COP31 in Antalya Turkey calling for a phaseout of fossil fuels, the burning of which is the main driver of climate changeImage: DW

blocks.text: Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a new draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.

The latest text released Thursday at the UN climate conference in Turkey stripped out two references to a transition away from coal, oil and gas and a call for an accelerated phaseout that had been in an earlier draft.
This slimmed down version follows days of tough negotiations with representatives from nearly 200 countries on issues such as the future of fossil fuels and climate funding for developing countries.
The text also includes a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35% by 2035 — up from around 20% today — a proposal that had been pushed by host Turkey.

blocks.caption: COP31 negotiators are once again gearing up to fight to have fossil fuels mentioned in a final decision in the yearly UN climate summitImage: Dilara Senkaya/REUTERS

blocks.text: It did not specify whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources, a point that has drawn criticism from some countries. But it did link the target to efforts to triple renewable energy capacity globally alongside other energy efficiency measures.
What else is in the draft text?

The draft text also expressed "deep concern" that global warming is projected to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels — the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avoid runaway climate change.
It acknowledged that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems."

It also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" cuts to greenhouse gas emissions and called for efforts to ramp up action targeting the potent greenhouse gas methane. The greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet are largely caused by burning fossil fuels.
COP31: Can electrification replace fossil fuels?
The text additionally calls for the deployment of technologies that can remove carbon from the atmosphere to be sped up — those technologies are as yet largely unproven at scale.

Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign to boost climate finance for developing countries said the second draft "trims away inconvenient mandates and accountability while leaving behind lofty rhetoric that won't protect a single vulnerable community."

"It is actively more regressive, stripping out hard-won accountability, timelines, and legal anchors just as frontline communities in the Global South are paying the steepest price for climate breakdown," said Singh in a statement.
Talks in crunch time
The climate conference officially ends on Friday, but it's not uncommon for the annual talks to run overtime. The latest text is expected to face further revisions before it can be adopted.
Decisions on the language need approval from all countries, meaning an objection from one party is enough to scupper a deal.
On Thursday, Panama said it would block any agreement that does not meet its demand for a cap on oil production and steps to eliminate the potent greenhouse gas methane.
The country's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said Panama "not lend its name" to "complacent or ineffective language" in the final pact.

blocks.caption: A glacier collapse linked to planetary heating killed thousands in Nepal in AugustImage: Francis Mascarenhas/REUTERS

blocks.text: The stakes are high for this edition of the COP summit, which comes in a year of major climate-related disasters, from wildfires and deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.
It's also taking place against the backdrop of an intensifying "super" El Nino weather pattern, and geopolitical shocks that have sent energy prices rising globally.

It's the first conference taking place with the acknowledgement by the UN that keeping the average global temperature under 1.5C is no longer realistic. Instead, scientists are talking about limiting the time spent above this threshold and bringing temperatures back down rapidly by the end of the century.
More to come…

articles.title: Car rams into Palestinian residents four times in Israeli city, injuring eight
articles.summary:
Arab MPs accuse Israeli politicians of fuelling hostility as footage shows driver accelerating towards pedestrians at several locations in Kafr Qasim

Eight people were injured on Wednesday…

blocks.text: Eight people were injured on Wednesday evening when a driver struck Palestinian residents at four separate locations in Kafr Qasim, a city in central Israel.

Footage shared on social media appears to show the car accelerating towards people, all Palestinians, at several locations in the city, striking them before driving away. Three of those injured were in moderate condition, and several of the victims were women leaving a nearby wedding, the Times of Israel reported.

Haaretz has reported that investigators are examining whether the driver struck people deliberately. Avi Levy, a police district commander, said the incident appeared to be a hit-and-run and that the driver had tested positive for drugs. He said the Shin Bet security service was taking part in the investigation and added that “as of this moment, nothing is coming up. The suspect has no criminal record.”

The incident prompted Arab lawmakers and activists to accuse Israeli politicians of fuelling hostility towards Arab citizens. Benjamin Netanyahu has called Arab parties “terror supporters” and said partnering with them would put Israel’s security at risk. The parties won a record 19 seats in the Knesset in the country’s recent election.

Yousef Jabareen, the chair of the Joint List, said the incident “raises difficult questions about the claim that the driver lost control”. He said: “I’ve been warning for weeks that the incitement against Arab citizens will turn into assaults and even assassinations.”

blocks.caption: An election billboard in the predominantly-Arab city of Kafr Qasim in central Israel. Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Said Issa, a community activist in Kafr Qasim, described the incident as an “act of terror”.
“Someone who loses control of his vehicle might hit one or two vehicles, but not multiple people in several different places,” Issa said. “The attacker struck at four locations, one after the other.”

In a separate incident in the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian foreign ministry called on Monday for an Israeli settler to be held accountable after eight Palestinians were run over and injured in Tuqu, south-east of Bethlehem. Local sources told the Anadolu news agency that the driver first struck three young men, then returned and ran over five others who had gathered to help them.

articles.title: Myanmar committed acts of genocide against Rohingya minority, world’s top court rules
articles.summary:
Judgment ends seven-year legal battle and is seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of all state crimes

Myanmar committed acts of genocide against its Rohingya minority during…
articles.byline: Kaamil Ahmed in the Hague, and Oliver Holmes

blocks.text: Myanmar committed acts of genocide against its Rohingya minority during “clearance operations” nearly a decade ago, the world’s highest court has ruled.

The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle and is seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.

“The court is fully convinced that Myanmar committed acts falling under … the genocide convention with an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in Myanmar,” the ICJ president, Yuji Iwasawa, said during a reading of the judgment.

A 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, with refugees arriving with stories of mass killings of adults and children, gang-rapes and burned-down villages.

Governments have been anxiously awaiting the decision, handed down in The Hague, the Netherlands, where the UN-run court is based, in part because the ruling will set a precedent for genocide claims, notably a high-profile case against Israel.

Genocide, defined after the Nazi Holocaust by a 1948 UN convention, is harder to prove than war crimes because it requires evidence of specific “intent” to destroy a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Myanmar’s case was raised by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, on behalf of Myanmar survivors. It rested on claims of genocidal statements and “patterns of conduct” that showed attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state, including gunning down people as they fled and blocking their return.

In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear from survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. More than 1 million Rohingya still live there in the world’s largest refugee settlement, and fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Buddhist-majority Myanmar.

blocks.caption: Mumtaz Begum, pictured in 2017 in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. She fled to Bangladesh shortly after an attack on Tula Toli village in Myanmar, in which she said the military burned homes, gang-raped women and killed her husband and son in front of her. Photograph: Allison Joyce/Getty Images

blocks.text: Refugees who fled to Bangladesh told the Guardian in 2017 of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, mass graves and the drowning of children in a river. That village, which satellite footage later showed had been burned down, was one of several analysed by rights investigators and built a case for genocide.
During hearings, the Gambian justice minister, Dawda Jallow, told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”.
“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”

Legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention says the crime can include acts with the intent to “prevent births”. Investigators have said gang-rapes and accounts of soldiers mutilating women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.
Myanmar denied carrying out a genocide and claims its actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted guerrilla-style attacks. Its military responded with massive “clearance operations”.

The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-2017 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals and not states like the ICJ, on allegations of crimes against humanity.

blocks.caption: Bangladeshi guards stand by as thousands of Rohingya refugees fleeing from Myanmar walk along a muddy rice field after crossing the border in Palang Khali, Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh.   Photograph: Paula Bronstein/Getty Images

blocks.text: The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.

Israel and its chief ally, the US, have been closely following the Myanmar case as the decision provides the strongest hint of how judges might assess the Gaza case, brought by South Africa. UN independent investigations, as well as genocide scholars, have already said Israel committed acts of genocide in Gaza.
A judgment finding Myanmar had breached the convention has been predicted to lead to the US imposing sanctions on ICJ judges, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay.

blocks.caption: A Myanmar border guard police stands near a fence, behind which are Rohingya refugees and makeshift houses at the ‘no man’s land’ zone between the Bangladesh-Myanmar border in Rakhine State, western Myanmar, in 2018. Photograph: Nyein Chan Naing/EPA

blocks.text: Washington had considered the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration. However, the Trump administration has been on the offensive against international rights bodies, including imposing sanctions on the ICC.

Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the 1990s Balkans wars fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops at the Srebrenica massacre.
Other UN tribunals have established genocide in only a handful of cases since the Holocaust, including Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge rule in the 1970s and the 1994 mass killings in Rwanda.

articles.title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
articles.summary:
The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits

Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs…

blocks.text: Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.
The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.

The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.
The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.

Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”

Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.
“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.

The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.
Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.
“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”
Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.

The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”

Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.
The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.
A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

articles.title: Violent protests and killings in Bangladesh ahead of exiled Sheikh Hasina’s planned return
articles.summary:
Awami League party called for ⁠nationwide protest on Thursday after the government rejected Hasina’s request for passport

Parts of Bangladesh were shut down Thursday as protests by…

blocks.text: Parts of Bangladesh were shut down Thursday as protests by supporters of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina sparked clashes, bomb blasts and arson attacks, with the ancestral home ⁠of former leader Muhammad Yunus set ablaze in the violence.

Hasina’s Awami League party had called for a ​week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support ‌for Hasina’s planned return in December, culminating in a ‌nationwide lockdown on Thursday.

Hasina, who has lived in exile in neighbouring India since she fled Dhaka following violent ⁠protests demanding her resignation in August 2024, has requested a new passport and identity card to facilitate her return. Her supporters are protesting against the government’s rejection of that request.
To deter ⁠violence, 97 platoons of the Bangladesh Border Guard fanned out across seven districts, including Gopalganj and Faridpur, considered to have many Hasina supporters, a spokesperson ⁠said.
Police said former interim leader Yunus’ ancestral home in Chattogram, about 300km (186 miles) south-east of Dhaka, ​was set on fire late on ‌Wednesday.
It is likely that flammable ‌substances were thrown into an unused ground-floor room, police told Reuters, adding that Yunus’ paternal family members, who live on the upper floors, are safe.

blocks.caption: Fire engulfs the Tungipara police station in Gopalganj on 17 November amid unrest after the arrest of activists of the banned Awami League party.  Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Reuters could not immediately reach the Yunus Centre thinktank that speaks on his behalf to seek comment. Yunus and his government, which led Bangladesh after Hasina’s ouster, have faced hostility from her supporters.

During the last 10 days of protests, police have reported dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of ‌vehicles being set afire in at least 28 districts, injuring several police officials and members of the public, media have said.
Late on Tuesday, an activist of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist party (BNP) was allegedly killed by unidentified people during a protest near Hasina’s home district of Gopalganj, police said.

On the same night, a crude bomb exploded outside the Dhaka residence of cultural affairs minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury, and the house of a BNP lawmaker and shops ‌belonging to BNP supporters in Gopalganj were set on fire, police added.
On Wednesday morning, a bus company helper was burnt to death in the southern district of Pirojpur after two buses ​were set on fire, authorities said.

Tuesday marks a year since Hasina was ​sentenced to death by a local court that found her guilty of ordering a deadly crackdown on a student-led uprising against her in 2024. She has lived in exile in neighbouring India since fleeing Dhaka.
On Thursday, authorities detained former education minister Nurul Islam Nahid, who faces charges ⁠over several killings during the 2024 protests, from his house in Dhaka, police told Reuters.

At ​least 37 branches and offices of ​Grameen Bank, set up by Yunus, have been targeted in arson attacks or ​attempted fires since 10 November, ‌with 14 more ​attacked since midnight ​on Tuesday, the bank said.

On Tuesday, the home minister Salahuddin Ahmed accused Awami League leaders abroad of inciting supporters to destabilise Bangladesh and torch property, adding that those involved in violence would be identified and prosecuted.
Awami League leaders, most of them in hiding, could not be reached for comment.

articles.title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
articles.summary:
Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds

One in four women around the world has no power of consent if their husband or…

blocks.text: One in four women around the world has no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.

“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”

The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.

“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.

He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.

In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.

Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.

Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”
She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.

“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.
